1. A diaspora in the US who wants to go but can't participate in her mother's burial because of the travel ban
Affected Groups: Women from countries under active U.S. travel restrictions — primarily nationals of Afghanistan, Iran, Syria, Yemen, Somalia, Libya, and Cuba — residing in the US on F-1 student, J-1 exchange, H-1B work visas, or Temporary Protected Status (TPS). This disproportionately affects women who are the primary visa holder, not a derivative dependent, making their immigration status entirely contingent on continuous physical presence and program compliance.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: Presidential proclamations and State Department travel bans suspend visa issuance and re-entry for nationals of designated countries. Departure from the US voids single-entry visa status, and consulates in or near affected countries are often closed or non-functional, making re-entry visas impossible to obtain abroad. USCIS humanitarian advance parole — the one legal off-ramp — has processing times of 3–12 months and is frequently denied for nationals of banned countries. Emergency expedite requests require documented proof but offer no guaranteed timeline. For TPS holders, travel authorization requires separate approval that can be revoked.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: When a mother dies, the burial in Islamic, Jewish, and many African and Asian cultural traditions must occur within 24–72 hours. This processing reality means the bureaucratic timeline is structurally incompatible with the human emergency. A daughter cannot say goodbye, cannot wash or shroud her mother's body as religious rite demands, cannot lead mourning rituals, and cannot fulfill her role as next of kin — not because she chose her career over family, but because the legal architecture offers no mechanism fast enough to honor both her immigration status and her most fundamental human obligations.

—

Travel ban took the chance to show my father the life I built here in the U.S.; he passed away without ever seeing it. I can’t not say goodbye to him. Now I have to choose between saying goodbye to the hero of my life or finish my PhD on the single entry visa I have. What should I do?

2. An Afghan girl who wants to go to school but can't because of the Taliban banning girls from education
Affected Groups: Afghan girls aged 6 and above, and young women of all ages, across all 34 provinces of Afghanistan — cutting across ethnic lines including Pashtun, Tajik, Hazara, and Uzbek communities. Particularly devastating for girls in rural and semi-urban areas who had no alternative access to private or underground schooling, and for young women mid-way through university degrees or professional training in medicine, law, and engineering.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: Following the Taliban's return to power in August 2021, a series of decrees systematically dismantled female access to education. Secondary schools for girls were closed immediately in September 2021. Universities were banned for women in December 2022. The Ministry of Education — now entirely male-staffed — enforces compliance through physical presence at school gates. Female teachers were dismissed from public employment, collapsing the pipeline needed to even deliver gender-segregated instruction. NGO-run community schools and informal learning spaces have been raided and shuttered. The de facto legal framework carries no appeals process, no exemption mechanism, and no judicial review.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: An entire generation of Afghan girls is being structurally locked out of literacy, credentials, and economic participation in a single policy stroke. A 13-year-old who was in 6th grade in 2021 is now 18 with no secondary certificate, no path to university, and no legal right to pursue one. For girls in medical training, their absence creates a compounding public health crisis — Afghan women can only be treated by female providers under Taliban gender codes, yet the ban simultaneously eliminates the next generation of those providers. The consequence is not lost time. It is the permanent foreclosure of an entire female generation from public life.

—

Everyday I watch my twin brother getting ready for school. Everytime that I ask maman why I can’t go to school like him, she says that girls can’t go. Sometimes I see her crying but she hides it from me. What is school like?

3. A Somali girl who has undergone FGM and is now experiencing a health consequence she cannot name or explain.
Affected Groups: Girls and young women in Somalia and among Somali diaspora communities globally, where FGM prevalence remains among the highest in the world at approximately 98% of women and girls. Most acutely affects girls aged 5–15 who underwent Type III infibulation — the most severe form involving near-total closure — and are now experiencing delayed health consequences in adolescence or early adulthood. Disproportionately impacts girls in rural and nomadic communities with no proximate healthcare, and diaspora girls caught between two cultures with no safe linguistic or institutional space in either.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: FGM creates a permanent anatomical alteration with cascading medical consequences — chronic infections, obstructed urinary flow, keloid scarring, nerve damage, and during menstruation, hematocolpos, where blood cannot exit normally and accumulates painfully. These are not episodic symptoms but structural, ongoing medical conditions. Yet the procedure itself exists in a zone of enforced silence: in Somalia it is culturally normalized and until recently legally unaddressed; in diaspora countries it is criminalized, meaning a girl who discloses it implicates her own family. Healthcare systems in Western countries are frequently untrained in FGM-related presentations, misdiagnosing symptoms as UTIs, anxiety, or psychosomatic pain. Medical intake forms carry no culturally safe disclosure pathway. Interpreters in clinical settings are often community members, collapsing confidentiality entirely.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A girl experiencing severe menstrual backup, chronic pelvic infection, or urinary obstruction has no medically or socially safe language to describe what was done to her or why her body is responding as it is. She was not given a name for the procedure. She was not told what was removed. She knows only that something happened, that it hurts, and that naming it destroys her family. In diaspora settings she may present to emergency rooms repeatedly with the same symptoms, be discharged with antibiotics, and return again — her actual condition never identified, never treated, never spoken. The silence is not cultural sensitivity. It is a medical system's failure to build the infrastructure that would allow her to be seen.

—

It takes me forever to urine, and it hurts so much. My girl roomates tell me there is something wrong with me but back in Somalia, it was normal for all the girlsد. I can’t describe how the pain is. What should I do to stop it?

4. A newly married Jewish woman in an Orthodox community who has just had her head shaved and must now wear a wig for the rest of her life.
Affected Groups: Newly married women entering Orthodox and Ultra-Orthodox (Haredi) Jewish communities — including Modern Orthodox, Hasidic sects (Satmar, Chabad, Bobov), and Yemenite Jewish communities — where the practice of head shaving or hair covering upon marriage is halachically mandated or communally enforced. Most acutely affects women who entered these communities through marriage rather than birth, women with no prior informed exposure to the practice, and women in tightly bounded geographic enclaves — Borough Park, Williamsburg, Bnei Brak, Mea Shearim — where communal surveillance of compliance is constant and departure from the community is socially catastrophic.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The requirement derives from halachic interpretation of tzniut (modesty law), under which a married woman's hair is classified as ervah — sexually charged exposure forbidden to be seen by any man other than her husband. In the most stringent communities, wigs (sheitels) are mandatory in all public and semi-public spaces including within her own home when male guests are present. The enforcement mechanism is not statutory but communal and economic: non-compliance risks her husband's standing in his yeshiva or business network, her children's acceptance into community schools, and the family's access to communal social services. Rabbinical authority holds binding interpretive power with no formal appeals process available to women. There is no halachic forum in which she has standing to contest the ruling as it applies to her body.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A woman who undergoes head shaving experiences an irreversible physical transformation she may have understood abstractly but could not have fully consented to without having lived it — the sensation of permanent baldness beneath a wig in every temperature, every illness, every moment of private grief or joy. The wig itself, a high-quality sheitel, can cost $3,000—$5,000, creating immediate economic dependency on her husband for the basic requirement of leaving her home. Her natural hair — a dimension of her physical identity she has carried her entire life — is gone, and its regrowth is socially impermissible to display. She has no secular legal recourse because no law was broken. She has no communal recourse because the authority that mandated the practice is the same authority that would hear her objection. The consequence is a woman who must mourn a loss she is not permitted to name as a loss.

—

Since I got married, whenever I see myself in the mirror, I don’t recognize myself. I feel I’m not my own! Everyone is Brooklyn say this means I’m a woman now and I should be happy  but watching my friends get up early to style their hair, feels like I miss something that I will never have again. How can I feel like myself again?

5. A student in Pakistan who was slapped by a teacher for contradicting him in class and cannot report it because the teacher is the authority.
Affected Groups: Primary and secondary school students across Pakistan — most acutely affecting children in public sector schools in rural Punjab, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Balochistan, and interior Sindh, where teacher-to-student power differentials are steepest and institutional oversight is most absent. Disproportionately impacts students from lower socioeconomic backgrounds whose families depend on the same teacher's goodwill for grades, promotion, and school-leaving certificates. Further compounded for girls, religious minority students (Christian, Hindu, Ahmadi), and students from lower-caste or bonded labor families, for whom any confrontation with institutional authority carries consequences far beyond the classroom.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: Pakistan's Constitution and the Punjab Protection of Teachers Act, alongside provincial education codes, technically prohibit corporal punishment — but enforcement infrastructure is structurally absent. Complaint mechanisms route through the same school administration that employs and protects the teacher. The District Education Officer receives complaints in writing, a literacy and access barrier for many rural families. Teachers in Pakistan hold a socially sanctioned disciplinary authority rooted in both Islamic pedagogical tradition and colonial-era institutional hierarchy, meaning physical correction is culturally framed as legitimate instruction rather than assault. A student who reports is immediately recast as disrespectful — the original act of contradiction that provoked the slap is treated as the primary offense. Parents who escalate risk their child being failed, transferred, or expelled through administrative mechanisms that require no documented justification.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A child who was struck for thinking out loud — for doing precisely what education is designed to produce — learns in that moment that intellectual contradiction of authority is a punishable act. He or she internalizes not just silence but the specific shape of the silence: do not contradict, do not question, do not be visibly more correct than the person above you. Reported or unreported, the slap functions as a systemic instruction. Multiplied across millions of classrooms over generations, it is not an isolated disciplinary failure — it is the active manufacturing of a population trained to equate curiosity with danger, and deference with survival. The child does not just lose the argument. They lose the belief that their mind is something they are permitted to use freely.

—

I didn’t want to offend our teacher; he is one of the best teachers in Lahore. I was only curious. He said 500 was the middle of 1,000, and I just said there is no middle for 1,000 as this is even. He slapped me in front of my classmates. What should I do? I didn’t mean it.

6. An elderly widow in India facing social pressure not to remarry because remarriage after loss is treated as shameful.
Affected Groups: Widowed women across India, most acutely affecting those in rural Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, and West Bengal — states where upper-caste Hindu orthodoxy most rigidly governs widow conduct. Disproportionately impacts women widowed young, women from Brahmin, Rajput, and Bania castes where ritual purity codes are most strictly enforced, women in joint family structures where they are economically dependent on in-laws, and women in communities where the deceased husband's family retains legal and social custody of her personhood after his death. Dalit widows face a compounded vulnerability — stripped of caste protection while simultaneously subject to the same remarriage stigma, with additional exposure to sexual exploitation framed as their inevitable social destiny.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act of 1856 technically legalized widow remarriage, and the Hindu Succession Act provides inheritance rights — but legal permission and social permission operate in entirely separate jurisdictions. A widow who remarries forfeits her claim to her deceased husband's property and her children in many customary arrangements that courts rarely intervene in. Her in-laws, who may be her sole housing and economic infrastructure, withdraw support the moment remarriage is pursued. Panchayat systems — extrajudicial village councils with no formal legal standing but enormous operative power — issue social sanctions including community ostracism, family boycotts, and in extreme cases violence, with no accountability mechanism. Priests and religious authorities frame remarriage as cosmic transgression, telling women their husband's soul will be dishonored or that their own spiritual merit will be destroyed.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: An elderly widow who has spent decades in mandated white clothing, excluded from auspicious ceremonies, forbidden from remarrying, and treated as a living embodiment of bad omen, faces her final years in compounding isolation — economically dependent on children or in-laws who enforce her compliance through the threat of abandonment, socially invisible in the community she has lived in her entire life, and religiously instructed that her own desires constitute a form of desecration. If she pursues remarriage she loses her home, her grandchildren, her community, and her standing. If she does not, she loses the remainder of her life to a grief she is not permitted to move through. The system does not merely discourage remarriage. It constructs the architecture of her total dependence so thoroughly that the question of what she wants becomes, over time, genuinely unanswerable — even to herself.

—

It’s been 20 year since my husband died, recently my co-worker at kolkata’s hospital has proposed. I’m scared of bringing it up and lose my family. What would they do?

7. An illegal Afghan girl trafficked to begging on Tehran's streets
Affected Groups: Afghan girl children — predominantly aged 6–16 — trafficked into Iran through the Nimroz, Herat, and Farah border corridors, drawn almost exclusively from internally displaced families fleeing Taliban territorial consolidation, drought, and economic collapse. Most acutely affects girls from Hazara, Tajik, and rural Pashtun communities whose families were either deceived by traffickers promising domestic work placements, or who knowingly surrendered children under conditions of absolute destitution with no remaining alternative. Compounded for unaccompanied minors separated from families during border crossings, and for girls already carrying the layered vulnerability of FGM, early marriage, or prior displacement trauma.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: Afghan nationals in Iran exist in a three-tier legal hierarchy — registered refugees with Amayesh cards, undocumented residents with no status, and newly arrived illegals with full deportation exposure. Girls trafficked for street begging overwhelmingly occupy the third tier, carrying no documentation, no legal identity, and no access to any state protection mechanism. Iran is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention, meaning no formal asylum framework exists to receive them. The traffickers who control begging networks operate with functional impunity — Iranian law enforcement periodically conducts sweeps that result in the deportation of the girls rather than the prosecution of the network controllers. The girls are simultaneously criminalized as illegal migrants and victimized as trafficked minors, with no legal category that holds both truths at once. Afghan consular infrastructure in Iran is too under-resourced and politically compromised to intervene meaningfully on behalf of undocumented girls whose own families may be complicit in their placement.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A girl who arrived in Tehran as a child has by adolescence been stripped of every developmental resource simultaneously — no schooling under Taliban decree in Afghanistan, no schooling as an undocumented illegal in Iran, no physical safety on the street, no bodily autonomy under trafficker control, no legal identity in either country, and no family structure capable of protecting her even if located. She is beaten for insufficient earnings, withheld food as a control mechanism, and cycled between begging locations to avoid police pattern recognition. If swept up in an enforcement raid she is deported to an Afghanistan where the Taliban now governs her future, her education is permanently banned, and the family poverty that produced her trafficking remains entirely unchanged. She does not fall through the cracks of two systems. She was never inside either system to begin with. The crack is her entire world.

—

I wish I could send some money to my family in Kabul so they could get my brother a surgery but the mister takes all of it and tells me that this is in return for the food he gives me. I get jealous of the Persian kids I see at the metro. I wish I could go shopping with my mom like them. How can I send my family money?

8. A widow in a community where she is expected to marry her deceased husband's brother.
Affected Groups: Widows in communities practicing levirate marriage across sub-Saharan Africa (particularly among the Luo in Kenya and Uganda, the Zulu in South Africa, and various communities in Nigeria, Ghana, and Zimbabwe), parts of South Asia, and certain communities in the Middle East. Most acutely felt by young widows with children, where remarriage to a brother-in-law is framed as the only legitimate mechanism for keeping her children, her home, and her social standing within the family structure. Particularly devastating for widows whose deceased husband died of HIV/AIDS, where the inheritance marriage directly delivers her into the same transmission chain that killed him.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: There is no single law compelling levirate marriage in most of these contexts, which is precisely what makes it so difficult to escape or contest. The enforcement is social and economic rather than legislative, meaning there is no courtroom in which to challenge it and no rights violation a state authority will recognize. Upon a husband's death, property, land, and children default in practice to the husband's family under customary law frameworks that exist parallel to and often override formal national law in rural and peri-urban settings. In Kenya for example, statutory law technically grants widows inheritance rights, but customary land tenure systems operate at the community level with the backing of family elders and are rarely challenged through formal courts because doing so requires resources, legal literacy, and a willingness to be permanently expelled from the community. Refusal to accept the levir is not processed as a personal decision but as a forfeiture. She does not simply decline a marriage. She surrenders her children, who belong to the patrilineage. She surrenders her home, which was never legally hers. She surrenders her right to remain in the community without being marked as a woman who has violated her obligations to the family that absorbed her. Churches and local administrative structures that might otherwise offer recourse frequently normalize the practice or actively facilitate it.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A widow whose husband has just died, who is in acute grief, is immediately placed inside a negotiation she did not initiate and cannot exit without paying a price most women in her position cannot afford to pay. The emergency is not hypothetical or downstream. It is happening at the funeral. The husband's family is already determining which brother she will go to. Her own grief has no protected space because her future legal and physical status is being decided in the same week as the burial. If she refuses, she may be forcibly evicted from her home within days, her children retained by the paternal family as members of that lineage, and herself returned to her birth family in a condition of social failure that carries its own set of consequences there. If she acquiesces, she enters a marriage she did not choose with a man who may already have a wife, who may have been her husband's brother in name only and a stranger in every other sense, and in communities where HIV prevalence is high, she absorbs a compounded mortal risk with no mechanism to negotiate condom use within a marriage framed as her obligation. The grief and the coercion arrive at exactly the same moment, by design.

—

It’s only 5 days since my husband passed away. My kids are so little. They keep asking me why their uncle hugs me instead of their father. I wish I could just take my kids and go to Tehran. I really can marry him. How can I disagree? I’m still their bride how can they do this to me?

9. A woman who was raped in Iran and is now being pressured to marry her rapist.
Affected Groups: Women and girls across Iran, with particular concentration among those in rural and semi-urban communities where family honor structures operate as the primary social governance mechanism, and where formal legal institutions are either inaccessible or actively hostile. Most acutely felt by unmarried girls and young women, where the rape is reframed by family and community not as a crime done to her but as a contamination of her marriageability and by extension her family's standing. Particularly devastating for minors, for whom the pressure to marry the perpetrator can be initiated and completed by male guardians without her consent being a legally required factor.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The mechanisms here do not fail her, they are structurally arranged against her from the first moment. Under Iranian law as governed by Islamic penal code, proving rape requires either a confession from the perpetrator or the testimony of four male witnesses to the act. This standard is not an administrative oversight. It functionally ensures that rape is nearly unprovable in any contested case. In the absence of proof meeting this threshold, a woman who reports rape faces a serious legal risk of being charged with zina, illicit sexual intercourse, for admitting to sex outside of marriage. The law does not distinguish between coerced and consensual sex outside marriage in any practically enforceable way that protects her. This means reporting to authorities is not a neutral act. It is a gamble in which she is the only party who can lose. Simultaneously, in communities governed by honor-based family structures, the rape is processed socially as a problem of her purity rather than his criminality. The solution the community generates is marriage to the perpetrator because it retroactively legitimizes the sexual contact, restores a version of her marriageability, and keeps the matter inside the family or community rather than exposing it to outside scrutiny. Her male guardian, a father or brother, has the legal authority to contract her marriage in many circumstances, and the social authority to make her life unlivable if she refuses. There is no shelter infrastructure, no legally protected pathway out of the family home, and no restraining order mechanism available to her in any practical sense.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A woman who has just survived a rape is immediately placed inside a system where every available institution, her family, her community, her legal framework, and her religious authority, is processing what happened to her as a problem she caused or a condition she now carries rather than a crime committed against her. The emergency compounds in real time. Reporting to police risks a zina charge. Telling her family risks being married to her rapist within weeks to manage the social fallout. Staying silent allows the perpetrator to remain in her life, often in close proximity through family or community ties, with full impunity. If she is a minor her guardian can legally formalize the marriage without her consent. If she becomes pregnant the pregnancy is both evidence of the act and a accelerant of the pressure, because a child born outside marriage carries consequences that make the marriage to the perpetrator feel to her family like the only available resolution. She is being asked, at the moment of maximum trauma, to accept her perpetrator as her permanent intimate partner as the price of social survival. The architecture of that pressure was not assembled in response to her case. It was already there, waiting.

—

It was not my fault I swear. He forced himself on me. I said no but who believes a girl over a boy in this small town? My father is telling me I have to marry the guy because our family’s credit at Gonabad is more important. How can I convince him to not do this?

10. A Pakistani boy in a brick kiln whose family's debt to the kiln owner means he cannot leave.
Affected Groups: Children and families trapped in bonded labor across Pakistan's brick kiln industry, concentrated in Punjab and Sindh provinces, where an estimated 4.5 million people work in kilns and a significant proportion are locked into hereditary debt bondage. Most acutely felt by children born into kiln families, where the debt predates their birth and their labor is absorbed into repayment before they are old enough to understand the arrangement. Particularly devastating for Christian and low-caste Hindu minority families, who are disproportionately represented in kiln bondage because their social marginalization limits their access to any alternative economic entry point, and because their minority status removes whatever residual community protection a Muslim family might invoke.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act was passed in Pakistan in 1992, which on paper canceled all existing bonded labor debts and prohibited the system entirely. This law has functioned almost exclusively on paper. The peshgi system, the advance loan given by a kiln owner to a laborer family, is the mechanism of capture. The loan is offered at a moment of acute vulnerability, a medical emergency, a wedding, a funeral, a crop failure, and accepted because there is no other available credit instrument for a family with no assets, no bank account, and no collateral. Once accepted, the debt does not behave like a loan. Interest accumulates at rates set unilaterally by the kiln owner. Repayment is calculated against wages also set by the kiln owner. Bricks are counted and priced by the kiln owner. The entire accounting system is controlled by the single party who benefits from the debt never resolving. Children are counted into the labor ledger not by formal contract but by the physical reality that a family producing more bricks services the debt faster, meaning a child's labor is absorbed structurally regardless of whether anyone explicitly commands it. District administration and local police are frequently on informal payroll relationships with kiln owners, who are often significant local landowners with political connections. A family that attempts to leave without settling the debt risks physical detention, violence, and police involvement on behalf of the owner rather than on their behalf. Legal aid organizations exist but require the family to first physically escape the kiln premises to access them, which is the step the entire system is designed to prevent.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A child in a brick kiln is not making a series of bad choices inside a functioning system. He was born into a ledger. His body is the repayment instrument for a debt he did not incur, denominated in a currency his family cannot earn fast enough to retire because the person setting the wage is the same person who sets the debt. When he is sick, he cannot rest because production slowdowns extend the debt timeline and kiln owners apply direct pressure, social, physical, or through debt acceleration, to keep bodies working. There is no school because school attendance removes a labor unit from the kiln floor and nothing in the structure incentivizes his education. If his father dies, the debt transfers to him as the eldest male child. The emergency is not a single moment. It is the permanent condition of his entire childhood, structured so that the exit requires resources, legal access, and physical freedom that the system is specifically organized to ensure he never simultaneously possesses.

—

Last week a piece of hot brick fell on my foot. It is very bad and swelling. It hurts so bad. I always ask my dad when we can leave and he responds with nothing. I miss the days I could play with my friends at Punjab. How can I have a better life?

11. A village woman in Iran falsely accused of adultery who must face an elder council.
Affected Groups: Women in rural and peri-urban communities across Iran, particularly in provinces with strong tribal governance structures such as Kurdistan, Sistan-Baluchestan, Khuzestan, and Kermanshah, where customary elder councils operate as the primary dispute resolution mechanism and where formal state legal institutions are geographically distant, culturally foreign, and practically inaccessible. Most acutely felt by women in communities where tribal or clan identity supersedes individual legal standing, and where a woman has no independent social existence outside her relationship to a male guardian. Particularly devastating for women whose accusers are from a more powerful family or clan within the same community, where the elder council's composition and conclusions are shaped by existing power hierarchies before she enters the room.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The mechanisms trapping her operate on two parallel tracks that never intersect in her favor. Under Iranian statutory law, zina carries catastrophic penalties including flogging and death by stoning, and the evidentiary standard formally requires confession or multiple witnesses. But the formal legal system is not her primary threat in a rural village context. The elder council is. These councils, known variously as jirgas, shuras, or tribal assemblies depending on region, operate outside formal legal jurisdiction but with total practical authority in the communities they govern. They are composed exclusively of elder men. She has no right to speak in her own defense in most council formats, and where she is permitted to speak, her testimony carries a fractional evidentiary weight compared to male testimony by convention. The accusation itself functions as the primary evidence because her denial is structurally discounted. There is no defense counsel, no rules of evidence, no appeal mechanism, and no external oversight. Iranian state authorities do not intervene in council proceedings as a matter of policy and practical resource allocation, and local police and administrators frequently have clan affiliations that align them with the council rather than with her. Her male guardian, the person who might theoretically advocate for her, is simultaneously the person most socially invested in resolving the accusation quickly in whatever way best preserves family honor, which may or may not require her survival or freedom.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A woman falsely accused of adultery in this context is not navigating a flawed justice system. She is inside a room where the verdict is a social negotiation between men about property, honor, and clan standing, and she is the property being negotiated. The accusation alone is sufficient to destroy her marriage, her custody of her children, her position in her household, and her physical safety regardless of any formal outcome, because the community has already begun processing her as guilty from the moment the accusation became public. If the council finds against her the consequences range from forced divorce and expulsion to sanctioned violence carried out by her own male relatives as an honor restoration mechanism, which Iranian law has historically treated with significant leniency at the prosecution and sentencing level. If the council finds in her favor she returns to a community that heard the accusation and will not unknow it. The false accusation is not the beginning of her emergency. The moment it was spoken aloud in a structure with no mechanism for her defense, the emergency was already complete.

—

Nobody believes me in this small village in Kerman. He just told me that he is going to get another wife and when I told him that I’ll get divorced he spread the rumors that I have had adultery. All the people in the town looks at me with anger. The elders are his uncles. What should I do?

12. A North Korean teenager who found a USB drive with foreign content and is reported.
Affected Groups: Teenagers and young adults across North Korea, with particular concentration among those in northern border provinces like Ryanggang and North Hamgyong where USB drives containing Chinese media have historically entered the country through informal cross-border trade networks. Most acutely felt by children from songbun classes below the privileged core class, where the state's loyalty classification system means their family has less political capital to absorb the consequences of an accusation and fewer connections to bribe their way out of investigation. Particularly devastating for teenagers who consumed the content with siblings or friends, where a single report triggers an investigation that radiates outward to everyone present, and for those whose families have any prior mark on their songbun record, where a second infraction compounds into a classification collapse that affects the entire family unit across generations.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: North Korea's 2020 Reactionary Thought and Culture Law formalized what was previously enforced through party discipline and social pressure, criminalizing the consumption, distribution, or possession of foreign media with penalties scaling from forced labor to execution depending on the volume of content and evidence of distribution intent. The law is not the primary mechanism of capture. The inminban is. The inminban is the neighborhood watch unit, a block-level surveillance cell of approximately 20 to 40 households overseen by an appointed monitor, almost always a woman, whose explicit function is to report ideological infractions, unusual behavior, and signs of foreign influence to the Ministry of State Security. This system means that in the physical geography of a North Korean neighborhood, there is no private space in which to consume foreign content that is not already inside a surveillance perimeter. A report does not require evidence beyond the monitor's word. Once reported to the Bowibu, the State Security Department, the investigation does not function as a truth-finding process. It functions as a pressure escalation designed to extract confessions and identify additional names. Interrogation techniques include sleep deprivation, prolonged stress positions, and threats against family members. There is no legal representation, no right to silence, no independent judiciary, and no appeal mechanism outside the party structure that initiated the investigation. The USB drive itself, if found, is forensically examined for viewing history and any evidence of the content having been shared, which transforms a solitary act of curiosity into a distribution charge carrying substantially higher penalties.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A teenager who picked up a USB drive out of curiosity, who may have watched a South Korean drama or a foreign film for the first time in his life, enters a machinery that does not distinguish between him and a deliberate political dissident because the law is not designed to make that distinction. The report to the inminban monitor may come from a neighbor, a classmate, or someone in his own household who feared that not reporting would implicate them. From the moment of report his family cannot protect him by telling the truth because the truth is the crime. They cannot protect him by lying because the investigation is designed to find inconsistencies. His parents face their own interrogation and their own songbun consequences regardless of his outcome. If he is sent to a political prison camp, a kwanliso, he enters a system with a documented mortality rate so high that a sentence of any significant length is functionally a death sentence delivered slowly through forced labor, starvation rations, and systematic violence. The content on the USB drive, a piece of culture that exists freely on the other side of a border a few hundred kilometers away, has activated a state apparatus whose response is calibrated not to the harm caused but to the totality of control the state requires to maintain itself. His curiosity is the emergency. It was the emergency the moment someone else decided to report it.

—

I accidentally found a USB and when I just looking at it, I saw one of our neigbors that was talking to Kukgabo-iwisong  and pointed at me. What should I do?

13. A mother in Iran whose 15-year-old son has been sentenced to execution because of protesting.
Affected Groups: Mothers and families of juvenile protesters across Iran, concentrated among communities that have been most active in protest movements including the 2019 fuel protests, the 2020 plane shootdown aftermath, and the 2022 Mahsa Amini uprising. Most acutely felt by families in working class and lower income urban neighborhoods and in ethnically minority regions including Kurdish, Baluch, and Azeri communities where protest participation has been highest and where state repression has been most severe and least internationally visible. Particularly devastating for single mothers or mothers whose husbands are themselves imprisoned or otherwise removed from the household, where she is simultaneously the only advocate her son has and a person with no institutional standing from which to advocate.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: Iran has signed the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, which prohibits the execution of individuals for crimes committed under the age of 18. This signature has functioned as a diplomatic instrument rather than a domestic legal constraint. Under Iranian law as interpreted through the Islamic Penal Code, offenses classified as moharebeh, enmity against God, or efsad fil-arz, corruption on earth, carry mandatory death sentences that judges have applied to protest-related charges including the broad and elastic charge of being at war with God, which prosecutors have attached to acts including throwing stones, burning a trash can, or being present at a demonstration where violence occurred nearby. The juvenile justice framework that technically exists in Iranian law is overridden in practice when charges are elevated to this category, because the religious legal framework treats the severity of the offense against God as superseding the age of the offender. Revolutionary courts, which handle these cases, operate without transparent procedure, without meaningful access to independent legal counsel, and without public records. A mother attempting to navigate this system confronts a structure that does not publish its docket, does not notify families of hearing dates reliably, and has in documented cases executed prisoners without informing the family until after the execution was carried out, meaning she may be actively campaigning for a son who is already dead without knowing it. Lawyers who take these cases face their own disbarment and imprisonment. International pressure triggers a nationalism reflex in state communications that reframes outside criticism as foreign interference, which the government then uses domestically to justify accelerating rather than reconsidering the sentence.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A mother in this situation is not waiting for a miscarriage of justice to be corrected. She is inside a system that has correctly understood its own logic and is applying it. Her son was sentenced for threatening the state and the state is responding with the instrument it has decided is proportionate. Every action available to her carries a cost that the system has pre-calculated. Speaking to foreign media risks her own arrest for collaborating with hostile foreign entities and may be used to add charges against her son. Hiring a lawyer risks the lawyer's freedom and may signal to the court that the family has resources or connections that invite closer scrutiny. Staying silent preserves her immediate physical safety and accomplishes nothing. Organizing with other mothers, as the mothers of Laleh Park did, creates a visible solidarity that the state monitors and periodically dismantles through arrest. She may not know her son's execution date. She may call the prison and be told he is fine and then be told days later to come collect his body, a documented pattern used by Iranian authorities that forecloses even the possibility of final contact. Her son was fifteen years old when he stood in a street and the state decided that act was worth his life. She is now living inside the administrative processing of that decision with no lever to pull that does not risk making his situation or her own measurably worse.

—

It was two weeks that he was lost, then he called from the prison saying they have arrested him. He is sentenced to execution just because he was in the Tehran’s protestings. He’s only 15. How can I save my child?

14. Venezuelan trying to send money internationally during economic collapse.
Affected Groups: Venezuelans across all income levels — but most acutely working-class families, small business owners, elderly pensioners whose bolivar savings have been destroyed by hyperinflation, and families dependent on remittances from relatives abroad. Also severely affects the Venezuelan diaspora in Colombia, Peru, Chile, and Spain attempting to send money back to family members who remained. Particularly devastating for households relying on imported medicine, food, or emergency evacuation funds where access to hard currency is literally the difference between survival and death.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The Bolivarian government's successive currency control frameworks — CADIVI, CENCOEX, and DICOM — criminalized unofficial dollar transactions while making official exchange rates functionally inaccessible to ordinary citizens. Simultaneously, US and EU sanctions including OFAC designations caused international correspondent banks to sever or severely restrict relationships with Venezuelan financial institutions wholesale, not only government entities. Venezuelan banks are largely cut off from SWIFT in practice. PayPal, Zelle, and major fintech platforms block Venezuelan accounts or require foreign phone numbers and addresses that Venezuelans inside the country cannot obtain. Western Union and MoneyGram have repeatedly suspended Venezuelan corridors entirely. Cryptocurrency offered a partial workaround but requires smartphone access, reliable internet, and financial literacy that millions lack, and the government's own Petro surveillance apparatus actively monitors and attempts to control crypto flows.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A family member abroad wires emergency funds for insulin or chemotherapy and the transfer is blocked at the correspondent bank layer before it ever reaches Venezuela. A grandmother inside Caracas receives a successful transfer but the bolivar conversion at the official rate strips two-thirds of its value before it reaches her hands. A family attempting to pay for emergency evacuation during a political crisis cannot access any regulated channel fast enough and is forced into black-market exchange networks where they are robbed or reported. A small business owner who needs to pay a foreign supplier to keep medicine on shelves cannot execute the transaction through any legal mechanism and watches the supply run out. The defining cruelty of this trap is that the sanctions designed to pressure a government are experienced at ground level entirely by the civilian population — the people the policy claims to protect are the ones for whom every financial exit door has been simultaneously sealed by their own government's controls and the international community's response to them.

—

I need to send money to my son at minnesota for hospital. But the government has shut all the exchange offices in Petare down or they ask for triple the money to do it. What should I do?

15. Cuban entrepreneur under embargo trying to do anything online.
Affected Groups: Cuban entrepreneurs, freelancers, independent artists, software developers, and small business owners attempting to participate in the global digital economy — a population that expanded significantly after Cuba's limited liberalization of private enterprise in 2021. Also affects Cuban academics, journalists, and civil society organizations attempting to access international platforms, tools, and funding. Particularly devastating for the emerging class of self-employed Cubans — known locally as cuentapropistas — who were explicitly encouraged by state reform to build independent livelihoods but were never given the international financial infrastructure to sustain them. Affects the Cuban diaspora in Miami, Madrid, and Havana simultaneously, as transactions between them are structurally blocked regardless of which side initiates.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The US embargo — codified most severely through the Helms-Burton Act and enforced through OFAC's Cuban Assets Control Regulations — prohibits American companies from providing services to Cuban nationals or Cuban-based users, and because American technology infrastructure underlies most of the global internet, this prohibition radiates outward far beyond US borders. Google, Apple, Microsoft, Adobe, Slack, Zoom, GitHub, Stripe, PayPal, and virtually every major SaaS platform either blocks Cuban IP addresses entirely or prohibits Cuban account registration under OFAC compliance requirements. A Cuban developer cannot download developer tools from GitHub without a VPN. A Cuban designer cannot receive payment through any major international payment processor. A Cuban journalist cannot purchase a domain name through any US-based registrar. Cuba's own domestic internet infrastructure, controlled entirely by the state telecom monopoly ETECSA, is expensive, slow, and intermittently throttled or shut down entirely during periods of civil unrest — meaning the technical access that does exist is itself weaponized by the state as a political instrument. The combination produces a complete pincer: the US embargo closes the door from the outside, and the Cuban state controls the door from the inside.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A software developer who taught herself to code using pirated materials and built a functional product cannot deploy it on any major cloud platform, cannot receive payment from a single foreign client, and cannot access the collaboration tools her international competitors use as a baseline. An independent musician whose work gained international streaming traction cannot collect a dollar of royalties because every rights management and payment platform is blocked at the account registration stage. A small restaurant owner who survived the pandemic by pivoting to delivery cannot use any internationally integrated point-of-sale or inventory system and manages everything in cash notebooks while her costs spiral. A Cuban journalist documenting government abuses cannot securely upload materials to international outlets using standard encrypted tools because those tools require account registration that OFAC compliance blocks. The defining paradox of this trap is that the embargo was architecturally designed to pressure a communist government by strangling its economy — but the entrepreneurs it most directly immiserates are precisely the people attempting to build independence from that government. The policy that was meant to encourage a private sector is the same policy that makes operating one structurally impossible.

—

I sent my customer’s orders to him. It takes three days for the shipment to arrive from Bayamo to Miami. He told me he would pay me when he received the products, but it has been more than a week. I haven’t received any payment, and he is not answering my phone calls. What should I do?

16. Undocumented worker in any country trying to access healthcare.
Affected Groups: Undocumented migrants globally, spanning economic migrants, asylum seekers whose claims are pending or rejected, trafficking survivors, stateless persons, and individuals who overstayed visas across every income level and origin country. Most acutely felt by those in countries with explicitly exclusionary healthcare frameworks like the United States, the United Kingdom post-Brexit, Germany, Greece, and Malaysia, where entitlement to care is administratively linked to legal status verification. Particularly devastating for women requiring maternal or reproductive healthcare, children requiring vaccinations or pediatric intervention, individuals managing chronic conditions like diabetes, HIV, or tuberculosis where treatment interruption has compounding consequences, and trafficking survivors whose immigration status was controlled by their trafficker and who have no documentation because documentation was the instrument of their captivity.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The mechanisms vary by country but converge on the same structural problem: healthcare systems require identity verification at the point of entry, and identity verification triggers status checks that feed into immigration enforcement infrastructure. In the United States, while federal law requires emergency stabilization treatment under EMTALA regardless of status, non-emergency care is effectively gatekept by insurance requirements that undocumented individuals cannot meet, and hospital financial assistance applications require documentation that simultaneously flags immigration status. The 1996 welfare reform legislation formally excluded undocumented individuals from Medicaid except in acute emergency situations, meaning chronic and preventive care, the medicine that keeps emergencies from happening, is structurally unavailable. In the UK, the National Health Service's hostile environment policy introduced data sharing arrangements between NHS trusts and the Home Office, meaning that seeking care generated a paper trail usable for immigration enforcement. This arrangement was partially walked back after significant public pressure but the institutional memory of it remains embedded in migrant communities as a lived deterrent that policy revision has not erased. In Malaysia and across Southeast Asia, undocumented migrants face not only denial of care but active risk of detention during hospital visits, with documented cases of immigration officers conducting raids on healthcare facilities. In countries where no such explicit enforcement exists, the barrier is financial: care requires payment upfront that undocumented workers, excluded from formal banking and earning below minimum wage in cash informal economies, structurally cannot produce.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A person who is undocumented and experiencing a medical emergency is performing a risk calculation at the worst possible moment of their life. The calculation is not irrational. It is based on accurate information about what presenting at a hospital has cost people in their community before them. A mother whose child has a dangerously high fever waits to see if it breaks on its own because the last person from her community who went to the emergency room was detained before discharge. A man with appendicitis manages the pain at home until rupture because he cannot produce the upfront payment the hospital requires and does not know that emergency law technically protects him. A trafficking survivor with internal injuries does not seek care because her trafficker controlled her documents and she has no way to prove who she is or explain her situation in a language the intake system understands. A diabetic whose insulin ran out rations what remains and begins the slow organ damage that will eventually produce an emergency that costs the healthcare system ten times what the prescription would have. The cruelest dimension of this particular trap is that the fear of the system is doing most of the work. In many jurisdictions the legal protections technically exist on paper, emergency care is required, data sharing is officially prohibited, financial assistance is theoretically available, but the community knowledge of past enforcement, past raids, past deportations initiated at hospital doors, has already built the wall. The law changed. The fear did not.

—

Last week at the construction site in Sa’adat Abad, a bag of cement fell on my foot, and it is now swollen. My wife told me to use the medicine she sent from Herat, but it made it worse. I don’t have health insurance. What should I do?

17. Elderly person in a village with no digital infrastructure trying to solve a problem their grandchildren told them to google.
Affected Groups: Elderly rural populations globally, most acutely in sub-Saharan Africa, South and Southeast Asia, rural Latin America, and post-Soviet states, but equally present in the rural interiors of wealthy nations including the United States, Canada, and the UK, where geographic isolation produces the same exclusion regardless of national income. Particularly devastating for those over 70 with limited formal education, those whose primary language has minimal digital representation, those with physical limitations like deteriorating eyesight or arthritis that make device interfaces hostile, those living alone whose only point of contact with institutional systems is now assumed to be digital, and those whose entire generation was never given a single moment of structured digital literacy training because the technology did not exist when their education occurred.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The mechanism here is not a single law but an accumulated architectural assumption embedded across every layer of modern public and private service delivery: that a person interacting with a system has reliable internet access, owns a functioning device, possesses an active email address, can navigate a browser, and has the literacy to parse interfaces designed by and tested on demographics that share none of their characteristics. Government benefits portals, healthcare appointment systems, banking platforms, utility bill payment, pension management, prescription refill systems, and social service applications have undergone systematic digitization framed as modernization but functioning as silent exclusion. Physical offices were closed as redundant once digital alternatives existed. Phone lines were automated. Forms were discontinued in paper. The assumption of digital access became load-bearing infrastructure for citizenship itself, quietly, without legislation, without transition support, and without anyone formally deciding that the elderly rural poor would simply be left outside.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A 74-year-old woman in a village with intermittent electricity and no smartphone needs to renew her pension documentation. Her grandchildren, who migrated to the city, tell her to google it. She does not own a device. The nearest internet caf— is twelve kilometers away and she does not drive. The government office that used to process this in person closed three years ago. The phone number on her paperwork connects to an automated system that requires her to navigate seven menu options in a language she speaks but cannot read fluently, and then asks her to confirm her identity via a code sent to an email address she does not have. Her pension lapses not because she is ineligible but because the system that was redesigned to be more efficient processed her out of existence without ever registering that it had done so. The cruelest dimension is the grandchildren. They are not wrong that the answer is online. They are not wrong that this is how the world works now. What they cannot see from the city is that telling someone to google something when they have no google is not advice. It is an accidental reminder of exactly how far the world has moved without her.

—

I live in a small village near Shiraz, and we don’t really have the kind of connections people in cities do. I have a phone my grandson gave me, but I only know how to answer calls on it. Whenever I ask him something, he just laughs and says “just google it.” What does that even mean, and how am I supposed to do it?

18. Diaspora trying to contact family inside with internet blackout.
Affected Groups: Diaspora communities from countries with documented histories of internet shutdowns and communication blackouts including Iran, Ethiopia, Myanmar, Sudan, Cuba, Belarus, and Nicaragua, spanning every legal immigration status from naturalized citizens to asylum seekers whose pending cases are directly affected by conditions on the ground they can no longer verify or document. Most acutely felt by first generation immigrants who have elderly parents, sick relatives, or family members in active conflict zones where the blackout is not an inconvenience but a severance of the only thread connecting them to people whose physical survival is uncertain. Particularly devastating for asylum seekers in active proceedings who need testimony, documentation, or contact with family members to support their case at the exact moment the state generating their persecution has also eliminated the communication infrastructure that would allow that evidence to be gathered.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: Internet shutdowns are executed through a small number of technically accessible chokepoints. In most countries a handful of internet service providers operate under government license and are legally compelled to comply with shutdown orders issued by telecommunications regulators, which are themselves executive branch instruments. The shutdown order requires no judicial authorization in Iran, Ethiopia, Myanmar, or Sudan. It is an administrative act. The technical execution takes between minutes and hours. VPNs, which diaspora members frequently send instructions for to family inside, are themselves blocked through deep packet inspection technology that identifies and throttles encrypted traffic patterns. The technology enabling these shutdowns is frequently sold by Western companies, meaning the infrastructure of severance has a supply chain that runs through democratic countries whose own citizens are unaware of its export destination. On the diaspora side the mechanisms are different but equally immobilizing. Asylum proceedings in the US, UK, Canada, and EU countries require corroborating evidence of conditions in the home country, but immigration courts do not grant continuances simply because a blackout has made evidence gathering impossible. Deadlines proceed. Hearings proceed. The absence of communication from inside the country is noted but not accommodated. Western Union and similar remittance services, which are frequently the only financial lifeline diaspora members have to family inside, suspend operations during blackouts or periods of sanctions activation, meaning the severance is simultaneously communicative and economic.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A person in the diaspora whose country has gone dark is experiencing a specific kind of emergency that has no name in the institutional frameworks designed to help them. They do not know if the silence means their family has no internet or their family is dead. These are not equivalent possibilities and there is no way to distinguish between them. They call the same number continuously for days. They post in community Facebook groups asking if anyone has heard anything from their city or their neighborhood, assembling a crowd-sourced map of silence. They contact journalists who are also outside and also cannot get through. They wire money and do not know if it arrived. They file asylum evidence requests and cannot reach the witnesses who could provide them. The uncertainty is not a temporary discomfort. In places like Ethiopia during the Tigray conflict, blackouts lasted months. Families inside were experiencing active military violence during periods when diaspora members had no way to know if specific individuals were alive. People learned their parents had died weeks after the fact, from someone who had eventually crossed a border with a phone. The grief arrived delayed and without the context that would have allowed any preparation or response. The diaspora member sitting in London or Minneapolis or Toronto during this period is fully physically safe and completely unable to do anything, which is its own specific damage, and one that resettlement support systems, mental health services, and immigration courts are not structured to recognize or address.

—

It’s been 40 days since the blackout of internet. I haven’t heard from my parents. I don’t even know if they are okay or not. I’m loosing my mind. What should I do?

19. Bahai person in Iran who cannot access university education because of their faith, trying to plan their future.
Affected Groups: Bahai youth across Iran, estimated at between 300,000 and 350,000 community members nationally, concentrated in cities like Tehran, Shiraz, Isfahan, and Yazd where Bahai communities have historically been established for generations. Most acutely felt by teenagers and young adults in the years immediately following high school completion, where the university exclusion collides directly with the life stage at which educational trajectory determines everything that follows economically and socially. Particularly devastating for children of parents who were themselves excluded from university under the same policy across the preceding four decades, meaning entire family lines have now accumulated multigenerational educational deprivation inside a society that uses educational credential as the primary sorting mechanism for employment, social mobility, and professional legitimacy.
Legal & Bureaucratic Mechanisms: The exclusion is not written as an explicit anti-Bahai statute in a single document, which is part of what makes it so difficult to challenge. Bahai students are required to declare their religion on the national university entrance examination, the Konkur, which is administered by the Ministry of Science. The Konkur application requires applicants to identify as Muslim, Christian, Jewish, or Zoroastrian, the four constitutionally recognized religions. Bahai is not listed. A student who identifies as Bahai is either forced to lie about their faith, which violates a core Bahai religious principle around truthfulness and which can be used against them later if discovered, or to leave the field blank or mark other, which triggers automatic disqualification from the results processing system before their scores are ever evaluated. This means a Bahai student who achieves a perfect score on the Konkur is eliminated not by academic failure but by a data entry field. The mechanism is administrative rather than legislative, which allows the state to deny that a policy of exclusion exists while operationalizing one through form design. Bahai students who attempt to enroll through alternative pathways or who somehow gain initial admission have been expelled mid-degree upon their faith being identified, sometimes years into their studies, losing all accumulated credit with no refund or transcript that a subsequent institution will accept. The Institute for Higher Education, established by the Bahai community inside Iran as an underground alternative, has been raided repeatedly, its teachers arrested, and its students harassed, meaning even the self-generated workaround has been systematically dismantled by the state.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A Bahai teenager in Iran who has studied hard, who has performed well, who has done everything a meritocratic system asks of its participants, sits with their Konkur results and already knows the results do not matter. The form was the verdict. Around them their non-Bahai peers are selecting universities, choosing majors, building the credential architecture that will structure the next forty years of their working lives, and this teenager is planning something else entirely because planning around the university system is not an option available to them. The futures they can construct from inside Iran without a university degree are narrow and structurally subordinated, because Iranian professional licensing, civil service employment, and formal sector hiring are all credential-gated in ways that the university exclusion forecloses in cascade. Leaving Iran is the solution most Bahai families eventually arrive at, but leaving requires resources, requires a destination country willing to accept them, requires navigating an asylum system that may not immediately recognize religious persecution through administrative form design as the specific harm it is, and requires abandoning the community, the family network, the language, and the physical place that is also home. The ones who stay and build lives anyway do so in the informal economy, in underground educational networks, in community structures that the state periodically raids, always one investigation away from losing what they built. The exclusion does not announce itself as ethnic cleansing. It announces itself as a dropdown menu with four options, none of which include them.

—

I heard all of my friends has gotten into universities like Sharif and Tehran. I’ve always had better grades than them. I wish i could also go to university like a normal Iranian. I’m also praying to the same prophet than them. I don’t understand it. I really want to become someone. How can I get to university?

20. Woman in a country where abortion is banned who is pregnant and does not want to be.
Affected Groups: Women and girls of reproductive age across countries with full or near-full abortion bans including El Salvador, Nicaragua, Honduras, Malta, Poland post-2020 ruling, and across significant portions of the United States following the 2022 Dobbs decision, as well as women in countries where abortion is technically legal but functionally inaccessible due to provider refusal, geographic concentration of services, or cost barriers. Most acutely felt by women in poverty who cannot finance travel to a jurisdiction where abortion is legal, women in rural areas where geographic distance to any reproductive healthcare compounds every other barrier, undocumented women for whom crossing a border to access care carries immigration consequences, and girls who are pregnant as a result of rape or incest in countries where even these circumstances do not constitute legal exceptions. Particularly devastating for women carrying pregnancies with fatal fetal anomalies, where the ban forces continued gestation of a pregnancy with no viable outcome, and for women with conditions like lupus, pulmonary hypertension, or certain heart conditions where pregnancy carries a clinically documented risk of maternal death but where the legal threshold for a life-saving exception is written so narrowly that physicians cannot act until the woman is actively dying.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The mechanisms differ by jurisdiction but produce the same structural trap through different administrative architectures. In El Salvador the ban is total with no exceptions, enforced through a legal framework that has prosecuted women for obstetric emergencies including miscarriages that prosecutors argued were induced, meaning the law does not only prevent abortion it retrospectively criminalizes pregnancy loss in ways that require women to prove their miscarriage was not deliberate to avoid prison. In Poland the 2020 Constitutional Tribunal ruling eliminated the fetal anomaly exception that had accounted for the vast majority of legal abortions performed in the country, leaving a theoretical exception for rape and maternal life risk that physicians are functionally unable to use because the legal exposure for misreading the threshold falls entirely on the doctor, creating a professional incentive to wait until the clinical situation is unambiguous at the cost of the patient's deteriorating condition. In American states with trigger bans the medical exception language uses terms like substantial risk and serious health condition that are undefined in the statute, meaning hospital legal teams are making the operative interpretation rather than physicians, and those legal teams are calibrating their guidance to the institution's liability exposure rather than to the patient's medical need. Medication abortion, specifically mifepristone and misoprostol, is available through mail order services operating from states where abortion remains legal, but in ban states receiving or distributing these medications carries criminal exposure, and the postal interception of medication has been proposed and in some cases enacted as an enforcement mechanism. For women without the internet literacy, English proficiency, credit card access, or safe home address to receive discreet mail, this workaround does not exist in practice.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A woman who is pregnant and does not want to be, in a jurisdiction where abortion is banned, is living inside a clock that the law has decided she has no right to stop. The pregnancy is advancing every day that every option is unavailable or inaccessible. A woman in El Salvador who miscarries and arrives at a hospital bleeding is simultaneously a patient and a suspect, and the nurses and doctors around her are potential witnesses in a criminal case, which means the clinical relationship that should be the most protected and confidential of her life is structurally adversarial at the moment she is most physically vulnerable. A woman in Poland carrying a fetus with a condition incompatible with life outside the womb is required to continue that pregnancy to term and then deliver and lose a child, a grief she was not permitted to choose to spare herself. A woman in Texas who is septic from a pregnancy complication waits in a hospital where physicians have documented in sworn testimony that they watched her condition deteriorate while lawyers decided whether she met the exception threshold. A teenage girl pregnant from rape in Honduras carries a pregnancy the state has decided is more legally protected than she is. The specific cruelty embedded in total bans with narrow or nonexistent exceptions is that they are written as though the hardest cases are the least important ones, when in clinical and human reality they are the cases where the stakes of forcing continuation are highest and the argument for any humane exception is most obvious. The law does not see this because the law was not written to see it.

—

I was just curious and it was my first time. But now I’m pregnant. I’m in highschool. No doctor in Tehran is accepting to do my abortion if they find out they can arrest us both. I really can’t be a mom. How can I fix this?

21. Unmarried woman in a conservative Arab context who is pregnant and terrified.
Affected Groups: Unmarried women and girls across conservative Arab societies including Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Iraq, Jordan, Egypt, and the Gulf states, as well as within conservative Arab diaspora communities in Western countries where family honor structures operate independently of the surrounding legal environment. Most acutely felt by women with no financial independence, no passport control over their own documents, and no physically safe space outside the family home from which to make any decision. Particularly devastating for women who were raped, where the pregnancy is simultaneously evidence of the crime committed against them and the mechanism of their social destruction, and for domestic workers and migrant laborers in Gulf states whose visa status is tied to their employer, who is frequently also their primary threat, and who face deportation, imprisonment, or violence with no consular protection that functions in practice.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The legal and social mechanisms are so thoroughly fused in these contexts that separating them misrepresents how the trap actually works. In Saudi Arabia, Jordan, and Iraq, zina laws criminalize extramarital sex without distinguishing meaningfully between coerced and consensual acts in ways that protect the woman. A pregnancy is self-executing proof of the act because it is a physical fact that cannot be denied, while the circumstances producing it are subject to the same evidentiary standards that make rape nearly unprovable across these jurisdictions. In several Gulf states unmarried women who present at hospitals while pregnant have been reported to police by healthcare providers, meaning the clinical system designed to protect her health is also an enforcement arm of the law criminalizing her condition. Abortion access is legally foreclosed in almost every conservative Arab jurisdiction except in narrow maternal life circumstances, meaning she cannot resolve the pregnancy through legal medical means. Her passport and movement in many of these countries require male guardian permission under mahram frameworks, meaning she cannot travel to access care elsewhere without the permission of the family from whom she is concealing the pregnancy. In diaspora contexts the legal protections of the surrounding country technically exist but the family's ability to control her movement, her finances, her phone, and her social world means those protections require her to first physically escape an environment where she is being monitored, which requires resources and a safe destination she may not have.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A woman in this situation is managing several simultaneous emergencies that are each accelerating on their own timeline and that cannot all be resolved without the others becoming worse. The pregnancy is advancing. Her body will eventually make concealment impossible regardless of every other factor. The window in which any decision can be made is closing at a fixed biological rate that does not pause for the legal, social, and logistical barriers she is trying to navigate simultaneously while also maintaining the performance of normalcy that her survival inside the household requires. If her family discovers the pregnancy before she has any plan, the response can range from forced marriage to a man who may or may not be the father, to being sent to a country she may barely know, to honor violence, to being expelled from the household into a legal and social environment where an unmarried pregnant woman has no institutional category that generates protection. The healthcare system will report her. The legal system will criminalize her. The family system will adjudicate her according to honor logic that was never designed to produce outcomes oriented around her wellbeing. The one person whose physical survival and future is most immediately at stake is the one person who has the least access to any of the mechanisms that could affect the outcome. She is terrified not because she has misread her situation. She is terrified because she has read it exactly right.

—

I really liked him that’s why I slept with him. Now that he found out that I’m pregnant he broke up. If my baba finds out, I don’t know what will happen. How can I explain my pregnancy while I’m not married to baba?

22. Young Arab woman whose father has discovered she has a boyfriend.
Affected Groups: Young women and girls across Arab societies and within Arab diaspora communities globally, spanning every economic class and educational level because the honor framework that generates the threat operates independently of household income or parental education. Most acutely felt by women living inside the family home with no financial independence, no separate legal address, and no physical space that is not monitored or accessible to male family members. Particularly devastating for women in diaspora contexts in Western countries where the surrounding legal environment technically offers protection but where the family's control over her documentation, finances, phone, social network, and physical movement means the theoretical availability of outside help does not translate into practical accessibility, and for women whose boyfriend is from a different religion, ethnicity, or class background, where the discovery is processed not only as a morality violation but as a threat to family lineage and community standing that escalates the response considerably.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: In Arab majority countries the mechanisms of control are partly legal and partly administrative. Male guardianship frameworks in Saudi Arabia, though partially reformed, and their equivalents in Yemen, Iraq, and Jordan still govern a woman's ability to obtain a passport, travel, sign contracts, access certain medical procedures, and in some jurisdictions leave the family home without permission.
