36. First generation university student from a village who does not know how academia works and has no one to ask.
Affected Groups: First generation university students from rural and peri-urban communities across every income context, from villages in rural India, Nigeria, Indonesia, and Bolivia to working class and low income families in the United States, UK, and Western Europe where university attendance remains strongly correlated with parental educational background. Most acutely felt by students who arrive at institutions where the majority of their peers grew up in households where university attendance was assumed, where parents could decode administrative systems, where older siblings had already mapped the terrain, and where the informal knowledge required to navigate academic life was transmitted casually across dinner table conversations the first generation student never sat at. Particularly devastating for students at elite or research-intensive universities where the gap between the institutional culture they have entered and the one they came from is widest, where the unwritten rules governing everything from how to speak to a professor to what office hours are for to how to interpret the difference between a suggestion and a requirement are most densely layered and most consequentially misread, and for students who are simultaneously managing financial precarity, family obligation, and the psychological weight of being the person their entire community has invested hope in, where failure is not a personal setback but a communal one.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The mechanisms excluding this student are not policies of exclusion but architectures of assumption. University administrative systems are designed by and for people who already understand how universities work, meaning the information required to navigate them is either assumed to be known or buried in documents whose existence the student does not know to look for. Advising systems that could compensate for the absence of family knowledge are typically under-resourced, appointment-based, and require the student to know what questions to ask, which presupposes a map of the terrain they do not yet have. A student who does not know what an advisor does cannot make productive use of an advising appointment. A student who does not know that professors expect to be emailed, that office hours are not a summons but an invitation, that asking for an extension is a legitimate academic act rather than an admission of failure, that recommendation letters require months of relationship building rather than a last minute request, will systematically under-utilize every support resource the institution nominally provides. Financial aid systems in most countries are extraordinarily complex, requiring navigation of forms, deadlines, verification processes, and appeals mechanisms that middle class families manage with the help of high school college counselors and parental experience and that first generation students manage alone or not at all, meaning they leave money on the table not because it was unavailable but because the system for accessing it was opaque. Academic integrity policies, grading norms, citation conventions, and the distinction between legitimate collaboration and plagiarism are assumed knowledge that the institution rarely transmits explicitly, meaning first generation students are penalized for violations of rules they did not know existed in the form they were violated. Internship and career pipelines at elite institutions operate heavily through personal networks and informal signaling, through who attends which information session, who knows to apply to which program, who has a family friend to ask for an introduction, systems that are invisible to someone who has no existing node in the network.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A first generation student arriving at university is entering a world that was built by people like their classmates for people like their classmates, and where the knowledge required to survive and thrive in it is so thoroughly assumed that the institution has never had to make it explicit because everyone who designed the institution already had it. Their classmate from a professional family in the capital city knows that the grade on a paper is not the end of a conversation but the beginning of one, that visiting a professor to discuss feedback is expected and rewarded, that the professor's somewhat harsh written comments do not mean what they would mean if a boss wrote them on a work performance review, but rather are an invitation to a particular kind of intellectual engagement the student is supposed to understand and respond to. The first generation student reads the same comments and hears a verdict. They do not go back. They do not know that going back is a thing people do. By the end of first year the classmate has three professors who know their name and could write them a recommendation letter. The first generation student has attended every class, submitted every assignment, and is completely unknown to every member of faculty because they were waiting to be invited into relationships that were available the entire time but that no one told them required initiative to enter. The knowledge gap is not academic. Their intelligence brought them here and is sufficient for the work. The gap is cultural, a dense accumulated set of unwritten conventions about how this world operates that their classmates absorbed across eighteen years of proximity to it and that they are now expected to have without ever having been near it. The institution will not name this gap because naming it would require acknowledging that what it calls meritocracy is partly a test of whether you grew up knowing how the test works.

People are like each other here. Even I don't have a laptop. I miss the cattle and now I just should live in these long buildings and riding elevators. I don't know what an Integral is. Was it a mistake to come here?

37. Person in China who wants to search for information about Tiananmen and cannot.
Affected Groups: Chinese citizens across mainland China spanning every demographic, age group, and educational level, though most acutely felt by young adults born after 1989 for whom the information absence is total rather than partial, who have no personal memory of the event and no access to the historical record that would allow them to understand what they do not know they are missing. Particularly devastating for students and academics in history, political science, journalism, and related fields who are attempting to produce intellectually serious work inside a knowledge environment with a deliberately engineered hole in it, for family members of those killed or disappeared in June 1989 who cannot publicly name what happened to their relatives or find others who share their loss, and for individuals who have encountered fragmentary references to the event through leaked content, foreign travel, or contact with diaspora communities and who are now trying to fill in what they sensed was missing without tools the domestic information environment provides.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The censorship of Tiananmen Square is not a single policy but a layered and continuously maintained information architecture that operates across every medium simultaneously. The Great Firewall blocks access to foreign websites carrying historical documentation including Wikipedia, the New York Times, the BBC, Google, and academic databases, meaning the basic research tools available to every other university student on earth are inaccessible without a VPN, which is itself illegal for individuals to use without government authorization and which is subject to periodic crackdowns that make consistent access unreliable. Domestic search engines including Baidu return no meaningful results for searches related to the June Fourth Incident, a term that is itself filtered, along with numerical variants like 5.35 (representing the date in a format designed to evade filters), tank man, and hundreds of related search strings that the censorship apparatus updates continuously as users develop evasion vocabulary. Social media platforms operating in China including WeChat and Weibo deploy keyword filtering and image recognition technology that identifies and removes related content before it reaches other users, often without notifying the person who posted it that their content was removed. Academic publishing in China self-censors on this topic so thoroughly that the domestic scholarly literature contains essentially nothing, meaning a Chinese historian cannot build an academic career that engages seriously with this event without either leaving the country or abandoning the subject. Textbooks at every educational level omit the event entirely or reference it in language so elliptical as to convey nothing. Teachers who have raised it in classroom contexts have faced professional consequences sufficient to make the subject professionally dangerous for any educator with institutional exposure to protect.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A young person in China who types a search related to Tiananmen into a domestic search engine and receives either no results or propaganda-framed results is not experiencing a simple information gap. They are encountering the surface of an engineered absence that was constructed specifically so that they would not know it was there. The most complete censorship is not the kind that blocks access to known information but the kind that removes the knowledge that the information exists, and the Tiananmen censorship has been sufficiently total and sufficiently sustained across three and a half decades that the majority of young Chinese citizens do not know they are missing something rather than knowing they cannot access something they know exists. The person who senses the gap and goes looking for it encounters a system that was built in anticipation of exactly that curiosity, that returns nothing, that makes the search itself a potentially surveilled act on a platform that stores query histories, and that provides no indication of where the absence begins and ends because the shape of what was removed is itself concealed. If they find a VPN and reach the historical record, the experience is not simply informational. It is a confrontation with the fact that the society they were raised in, the educational institutions they trusted, the media environment they navigated daily, were all organized in active collaboration to ensure they would not know this. The information itself is devastating enough, the scale of the killing, the deliberateness of the suppression, the identities of those who ordered it and who continued to govern China for decades afterward. But the secondary realization, that the absence was manufactured, that it required continuous maintenance, that it implicated every institution they had been taught to trust, is a different kind of knowledge that does not resolve into any simple political position but that permanently changes the epistemic relationship between the person and every other thing those institutions have told them.

Today our teacher told us to write an essay on his majesty great mao our founding father, modern economics. I asked my father and he mentioned something a bout a square. How can I find my information about that?

38. Person in Iran trying to use a VPN that keeps getting blocked.
Affected Groups: The near-entirety of Iran's internet-using population, estimated at over 79 percent of the country, spanning every demographic, age, profession, and political orientation, because the filtering system that makes VPN use necessary affects not only political dissidents and activists but academics trying to access research databases, doctors consulting medical literature, engineers using professional tools, businesses conducting international commerce, artists accessing creative platforms, and ordinary people trying to use applications that hundreds of millions of people elsewhere in the world use without obstruction. Most acutely felt by professionals whose work requires consistent access to international platforms including researchers dependent on Google Scholar, academics submitting to international journals, software developers working with Github and Stack Overflow, and journalists attempting to communicate securely with sources or editors outside Iran. Particularly devastating for activists and protest organizers for whom VPN failure is not a productivity inconvenience but a safety emergency, where the moment of blocked access is frequently the moment of highest need, during a protest, during a crackdown, during an attempt to document state violence and transmit it outside the country before it can be confiscated or destroyed.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: Iran's filtering infrastructure, administered primarily through the Supreme Council of Cyberspace and implemented through a small number of state-controlled internet exchange points through which all Iranian internet traffic passes, uses deep packet inspection technology that identifies encrypted traffic patterns characteristic of VPN protocols and throttles or blocks them at the infrastructure level rather than at the application level. This is technically significant because it means the blocking is not based on identifying specific VPN services by name or IP address, though that also occurs, but on recognizing the shape of encrypted traffic itself, which means that as VPN providers develop new obfuscation techniques that disguise their traffic as ordinary HTTPS browsing, the filtering system is updated to recognize the new patterns, producing an continuous technical arms race in which the state has structural advantages including greater resources, full control over the network infrastructure, and the ability to simply slow all encrypted traffic to speeds that make VPN use functionally impossible without blocking it explicitly. The legal framework criminalizes unauthorized VPN use under cybercrime legislation that technically exposes users to prosecution, though enforcement has historically been selective and targeted at activists, journalists, and businesses rather than individual users, meaning the law functions more as a latent threat maintaining self-censorship than as a consistently enforced prohibition. State-approved VPNs are technically available for businesses through a licensing process that requires the user to agree to filtering of their VPN traffic, which defeats the purpose of a VPN for anyone using it to access filtered content. During periods of civil unrest, including the 2019 protests and the 2022 Mahsa Amini uprising, the filtering system was supplemented by bandwidth throttling severe enough to make video transmission functionally impossible, a technically deniable form of partial shutdown that disrupted documentation and coordination without generating the international attention a complete blackout would have produced.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A person in Iran trying to use a VPN that keeps getting blocked is caught inside a technical system designed to exhaust them into compliance through friction rather than through absolute prohibition. The blocking is rarely total and rarely consistent, which is deliberate. A VPN that works Monday and fails Tuesday, that functions on a phone but not a laptop, that connects in Tehran but not in Isfahan, that works at 2am but not at noon, produces a specific kind of learned helplessness that absolute blocking does not, because absolute blocking generates workarounds while intermittent blocking generates uncertainty about whether the problem is the VPN, the device, the network, or the user's own technical error. The person spends time they do not have troubleshooting a system that is not broken but is being deliberately degraded. They download a new VPN application. It works for three days and then stops. They find a protocol update. It works for a week. They join Telegram channels where people share working configurations in real time, a crowdsourced technical resistance that the filtering system monitors and incorporates into its next update. At the moment of greatest urgency, during a protest, during an attempt to reach a family member whose location is unknown, during an effort to send evidence of a human rights violation to a journalist outside the country, the VPN that worked this morning does not work now. The content they needed to transmit is on a device in a country whose government does not want it to leave. The window during which transmission was possible has closed. The filtering system did not need to be perfect. It only needed to be good enough to win the specific moment that mattered, and it was designed by people who understood exactly which moments those are.

Oh it just connected! How not to let it turn off? I don't have the budget to pay for those expensive configs.

39. Person whose government monitors all communications trying to speak honestly with anyone.
Affected Groups: Citizens across comprehensively surveilled states including China, North Korea, Iran, Russia, Belarus, Turkmenistan, Azerbaijan, and Ethiopia, as well as individuals in partially surveilled contexts including Egypt, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Turkey where monitoring is selective but sufficiently documented in the community's lived experience to produce behavioral modification across the broader population regardless of whether any specific individual is actively being watched. Most acutely felt by journalists, activists, lawyers, academics, and civil society workers whose professional function requires frank communication about politically sensitive subjects and who face the highest personal exposure if monitored communications are used against them, but also by ordinary citizens whose surveillance-induced self-censorship has no professional justification and is therefore pure loss, people who simply want to say what they think to someone they trust. Particularly devastating for individuals inside North Korea where the surveillance infrastructure is so total and the consequences of detected dissent so catastrophic that self-censorship has become so deeply internalized across generations that the external monitoring apparatus is increasingly supplemented by an internal one, where citizens have so thoroughly incorporated the surveillance logic into their own cognition that they self-censor thoughts before they become words, and for dissidents and activists in Russia and China who have watched colleagues and friends receive prison sentences based on private communications they believed were secure, producing a community-wide understanding that no channel is reliably safe.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The surveillance infrastructure across these states operates through several overlapping technical and legal layers that collectively eliminate the possibility of unmonitored communication through any standard channel. In China the Cybersecurity Law and National Intelligence Law legally compel domestic technology companies to provide security agencies with access to user data and encryption keys, meaning every Chinese platform, WeChat, Weibo, Baidu, Alibaba's communication tools, is a monitored channel by legal requirement rather than by voluntary cooperation. End-to-end encrypted foreign applications including Signal, WhatsApp, and Telegram are blocked through the Great Firewall, and VPN access required to reach them is itself monitored and periodically crackdowns render it unreliable. In Russia the SORM system requires all telecommunications operators to install FSB-accessible interception hardware directly on their networks as a condition of operating legally, meaning the surveillance infrastructure is physically embedded in the communication infrastructure rather than applied to it from outside. In Iran the National Information Network provides a domestic internet layer that operates independently of the global internet and that is fully accessible to intelligence agencies, while foreign encrypted communication tools are blocked with the same intermittent effectiveness described elsewhere. In all these contexts the legal frameworks compelling surveillance were passed as national security or counter-terrorism legislation, meaning they are framed as targeted measures against specific threats while their technical implementation enables mass collection that is indistinguishable in architecture from the targeted application. Metadata collection, who communicated with whom, when, for how long, and from which location, continues even where message content is encrypted, and metadata analysis at scale produces relationship maps and behavioral profiles that can identify dissent networks without ever decrypting a single message.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A person who knows their communications are monitored and who wants to speak honestly with another human being is facing a deprivation that has no clean name in political theory or psychology but that operates at one of the most fundamental levels of human need. Honest speech to a trusted other is not a luxury or a political right in the abstract. It is the mechanism through which human beings process experience, test understanding, maintain intimate relationships, resolve uncertainty, and sustain the sense that they are known by someone rather than merely performing a version of themselves for an audience that includes the state. A person who cannot speak honestly to anyone is not just politically constrained. They are cognitively and emotionally alone in a way that coexists with being constantly surrounded by people, because the people around them are also performing, also self-censoring, also present in the interaction while being absent from it in the way that matters. In China and Russia this produces documented phenomena that researchers have described as a pervasive social fog, where conversations between friends and family members systematically avoid entire categories of experience and opinion not through explicit agreement but through mutual understanding of what cannot be said, meaning intimate relationships are built on a foundation of shared omission that both parties maintain and neither names. The specific damage this does over years and decades is not primarily political. It is the slow erosion of the experience of being known. A person who has never been able to say what they actually think to another person, who has spent thirty years performing the acceptable version of themselves in every communicative context, who has internalized the surveillance logic so thoroughly that the unacceptable thoughts arrive already translated into safe language before they are spoken, has not just lost a political freedom. They have lost the experience of their own interior life as something that can be shared, which is one of the things that makes an interior life feel worth having.

Do they check our conversation too? I want to speak about somethings but I have nowhere to talk about them. I only trust quiet in-person conversations.

40. Elderly person who has been told to do everything online and does not know how and is too ashamed to ask their children again.
Affected Groups: Elderly individuals across both high and low income countries navigating the systematic digitization of services that were previously accessible through physical presence, paper forms, and human interaction, spanning pensioners in the UK managing Universal Credit and NHS appointments through mandatory online portals, elderly Americans navigating Medicare, Social Security, and banking through digital interfaces, elderly people across Scandinavia where digital government services have advanced furthest and paper alternatives have been most thoroughly eliminated, and elderly individuals in middle income countries like Brazil, Turkey, and South Africa where digital service delivery has been adopted at government level faster than digital literacy has penetrated older demographics. Most acutely felt by individuals in their late seventies and beyond who did not encounter computers during their working lives and for whom the interface logic of touchscreens, browsers, passwords, and dropdown menus is not intuitive but genuinely foreign, representing a cognitive model of interaction that was developed by and for people who grew up with it. Particularly devastating for elderly individuals living alone whose children are geographically distant or estranged, where the shame of repeated asking has already foreclosed that avenue, for those with early cognitive decline where the complexity of digital interfaces exceeds their current processing capacity without anyone having formally identified or accommodated that decline, and for elderly people in rural areas where the physical service alternatives that urban elderly can sometimes still access, a bank branch, a post office, a government service center, have been closed in cost-cutting processes that explicitly relied on digital alternatives as justification for the closure.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The mechanisms trapping this person are the aggregate consequence of a thousand individual digitization decisions made by institutions that modeled their users as people who use the internet comfortably, which describes the people making the decisions more accurately than it describes the full population being served. Government digital transformation programs across the UK, Australia, Estonia, and increasingly across the developing world have been driven by efficiency metrics that measure cost per transaction and processing speed, both of which favor digital delivery, while systematically failing to measure or account for the access costs borne by people who cannot use the digital channel without assistance. The legal frameworks governing service delivery in most jurisdictions do not specify a right to non-digital access in terms that are practically enforceable, meaning institutions can formally eliminate paper and in-person alternatives without triggering a rights violation even where the practical consequence is that a segment of the population loses functional access to services they are legally entitled to. Banking digitization has been particularly aggressive, with physical branch closures in the UK averaging over 50 per month in recent years, driven by the economic logic that maintaining physical infrastructure for a declining minority of in-person customers is not commercially justified, which is accurate from a narrow institutional perspective and catastrophic from the perspective of the elderly person for whom the branch was the only accessible interface. Password and security systems require users to maintain multiple complex credentials, receive verification codes on mobile devices, and navigate multi-factor authentication processes whose security logic is sound but whose usability assumptions exclude people who do not have consistent access to a smartphone, who cannot read small screen text without glasses they may not have with them, and who do not have the cognitive mapping of how these systems fit together that makes troubleshooting possible when something goes wrong.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: An elderly person who has been told to do everything online and cannot is sitting with a letter that requires a response through a portal they have tried to access three times and failed each time for a reason they cannot diagnose. The letter has a deadline. The portal has a login they cannot remember, a password reset process that sent a code to a phone number they may have changed, and a help function that directs them to an online chat assistant. They have asked their children how to do this before. They remember the particular quality of patience in the voice, the effortful gentleness that was not quite concealing the mild exasperation, the way the explanation went slightly too fast while feeling like it was going slowly, the sense that they were taking something from their child by needing this help that they could not give back. They have decided not to ask again. The deadline on the letter approaches. The benefit it concerns, a pension adjustment, a healthcare entitlement, a tax rebate, is not optional money. It is the money that covers a specific bill. Missing the deadline has consequences the letter describes in bureaucratic language that is itself difficult to parse. The institution that sent the letter designed the response process for a user who is not this person and did not consult this person or anyone like them when it made that design decision. The elderly person is not failing to use the system. The system was built without them in mind and then they were told it was for them, and the gap between those two things is where they are now sitting, alone with a letter and a deadline and a shame that has quietly foreclosed the human help that would have resolved it in ten minutes.

I don't want to ask my granddaughter again. I try my best but each time it fails, I don't know it's my card or me. How to just find the cloth in a real store?

41. Person whose son was killed by the state and has kept his son in their house to burry him in the morning as the government might keep the body as a hostage.
Affected Groups: Parents and families of individuals killed by state security forces across Iran, China, Egypt, Belarus, Venezuela, and other states where the practice of withholding or controlling the bodies of those killed during protests, in custody, or through extrajudicial execution has been documented as a systematic policy instrument rather than an administrative irregularity. Most acutely felt by families in Iran following the 2019 protests where Amnesty International documented cases of authorities demanding families sign documents attributing deaths to non-state causes before releasing bodies, and following the 2022 Mahsa Amini uprising where families of killed protesters reported being pressured to hold small private funerals, avoid public mourning, and refrain from speaking to media as conditions attached to body release. Particularly devastating for mothers who have become the primary public face of protest mourning across these contexts, whose grief is simultaneously the most politically potent and the most personally exposed position available, and for families in minority ethnic communities including Kurdish, Baluch, and Azerbaijani families in Iran where the killed individual was already politically marked before their death and where the family's vulnerability to retaliation for public mourning is highest.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The body becomes a state instrument through a cluster of legal and administrative mechanisms that are individually presentable as routine procedure while collectively functioning as a system of grief control. In Iran forensic examination requirements routed through state-controlled medical examiner offices create a legally mandated delay in body release that gives authorities time to assess the political exposure of the death and to prepare the conditions they will attach to release. Death certificates issued by these offices have in documented cases listed causes of death that contradict visible wound patterns, eyewitness accounts, and in some cases the family's direct observation of the body, meaning the official paper trail contradicts the physical evidence while being the only legally recognized record. Burial permits in Iran are issued by municipalities and can be conditioned on compliance with authority directives regarding funeral size, location, and timing without any of these conditions being formally written into the permit itself, meaning the coercion is administered orally and is therefore legally undocumented and practically unappealable. Security forces in documented cases have stationed themselves at gravesites before and during burials, photographed attendees, and in some cases interrupted funerals where attendance exceeded what authorities had informally authorized. The legal framework governing none of this is explicit. The coercion operates entirely through informal directives, implied threats, bureaucratic delay, and the family's accurate understanding of what happens to families who do not comply, derived from watching what happened to other families before them.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A parent who has kept their son's body in their home through the night is doing something that has no precedent in their understanding of how grief is supposed to work and that requires them to hold simultaneously the rawest possible human experience, the death of their child, and a level of strategic political calculation that the state has forced upon them at the moment they are least equipped to perform it. The house contains their dead son. It also contains a calculation about what the morning brings, who might come, whether the burial can happen before authorities are aware of it, whether the neighbors can be trusted, whether the people they most want present at the burial are the people whose presence most endangers it. The funeral that every cultural and religious framework they have ever known says should be a public gathering of grief, a communal acknowledgment that this person lived and mattered, must instead be a covert operation optimized for speed and minimal visibility. They cannot announce the death on social media without triggering surveillance. They cannot invite the extended family without increasing the gathering beyond what informal authority has permitted. They cannot bury their son in the family plot in the home village without the journey making the burial visible. The morning they are planning toward is not a burial in any of the senses the word has carried for them across their entire life. It is a disappearance they are performing for their son before the state can perform a different kind of disappearance for its own purposes. And when it is done, when the ground is closed, they will enter the next phase, in which they cannot speak publicly about how their son died, cannot organize with other families without risk, cannot access the justice system that in a functioning state would be the next thing a parent reaches for, and cannot grieve openly in a way that might convert their private loss into the public reckoning it deserves. The state killed their son. It is now also administering how that death is allowed to mean anything, and the answer it has arrived at is as little as possible, as quietly as possible, as finally as possible.

42. Person from a community that was massacred and who carries collective memory that the outside world has moved on from.
Affected Groups: Survivors and descendants of communities that experienced mass atrocities which have been insufficiently acknowledged, inadequately prosecuted, or actively suppressed from international memory, spanning Yazidi communities following the 2014 ISIS genocide in Sinjar, Armenian diaspora communities carrying the memory of the 1915 genocide across generations in a context where the perpetrating state continues to deny the historical record, Rohingya survivors displaced into Bangladesh camps following the 2017 military campaign in Myanmar, Guatemalan indigenous communities carrying the memory of massacres during the 1980s counterinsurgency that have never produced meaningful accountability, Congolese communities in the eastern DRC where successive waves of mass violence have occurred in conditions of such sustained international inattention that individual atrocities have no names in global memory, and Tigrayan communities following the 2020 to 2022 conflict in Ethiopia where mass killings occurred during a communications blackout that limited documentation at the time and reduced international engagement afterward. Most acutely felt by first generation survivors who carry embodied memory of specific events, specific names, specific faces, and who watch the world's attention move through their catastrophe on its way to the next one, and by second generation descendants who inherited the memory as the organizing fact of their family's emotional life without inheriting the world's sustained attention that would validate it as something that continues to matter. Particularly devastating for communities whose perpetrators remain in power, politically active, or unprosecuted, where the survivor must navigate a world in which the people responsible for what happened to their community face no consequence and in some cases hold positions of international legitimacy, and for communities whose massacre occurred within living memory but has already been reclassified by international institutions and media as historical rather than active, foreclosing the accountability mechanisms that only function while the event retains current status.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The mechanisms that abandon these communities operate through international legal and institutional frameworks whose architecture systematically privileges state sovereignty, geopolitical interest, and procedural completeness over survivor-centered accountability. The International Criminal Court's jurisdiction requires either state party membership or Security Council referral, meaning atrocities committed by or in states with powerful Security Council allies, Russia, China, the United States, and their client states, are structurally protected from ICC prosecution regardless of evidentiary sufficiency. The genocide determination process under international law requires a finding of specific intent to destroy a group in whole or in part, a legal threshold whose evidentiary demands are sufficiently high and whose political implications are sufficiently significant that states and international bodies systematically avoid the determination even where the factual record would support it, preferring language like ethnic cleansing, mass atrocities, or crimes against humanity that carry moral weight without triggering the legal obligations genocide determinations formally impose on signatories to the Genocide Convention. Truth and reconciliation processes, where they occur, are typically negotiated by political actors whose interest in the scope and depth of accountability is shaped by their proximity to the perpetrating structures, meaning the process that is supposed to give survivors official recognition of what happened to them is designed and administered by institutions that have structural incentives to limit that recognition. Statute of limitations frameworks in domestic legal systems across many perpetrating states have extinguished criminal liability for individual perpetrators who have lived long enough, meaning biological time is doing the work of impunity that political protection might otherwise have had to do more visibly. Reparations frameworks where they exist are typically grossly inadequate relative to the scale of harm and are conditional on survivors navigating bureaucratic verification processes that require documentation that was destroyed in the same violence that produced the claim.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A person who carries collective memory of a massacre that the outside world has moved on from is living inside a temporal experience that has no equivalent in the lives of people around them. For them the event is not over. It is not historical. It is the present tense of their family, their community, their identity, and their understanding of what the world is and what it will do to people like them when no one with power decides to intervene. The outside world's movement on from their catastrophe is not experienced as the natural passage of time but as a second abandonment that recapitulates the first one, the moment during the massacre itself when the international community was aware of what was happening and decided that other considerations outweighed stopping it. They are now watching the same calculation being made about the memory of what happened, that other considerations, news cycles, diplomatic relationships, compassion fatigue, the volume of competing catastrophes, outweigh sustained engagement with theirs. When they try to speak about it in contexts outside their community they encounter a specific social response that is not denial exactly but is a kind of polite completion, a nodding acknowledgment that registers what they have said as received and understood and that moves the conversation forward in a way that reveals the acknowledgment was not really engagement but a courtesy, the social equivalent of a door being gently closed. They learn to read the moment when a listener has given what they are willing to give and is waiting for the topic to change. They learn to manage how much of the memory they bring into a room based on how much the room can hold, which is almost always less than what they are carrying. Within their community the memory is a living thing with texture and detail and specific names and the faces of specific perpetrators and the specific geography of specific places where specific things happened to specific people who were known and loved. Outside their community it is a paragraph in a report that was read by people who then wrote other reports and moved to other assignments. The distance between those two versions of the same event is where this person lives, permanently, in a present that the world has reclassified as past without asking the people for whom it has not ended.

I go online and see people posting their daily life. Nobody even noticed that a few miles away, they have killed 40000+!! I feel like when 40000 people are already gone and the world goes by, my existence has absolutely no meaning. What should I do?

43. Indigenous woman in the Guatemalan highlands whose land has been taken by a mining company and who has no legal identity in the national system.
Affected Groups: Indigenous Maya women in the Guatemalan highlands, particularly from Q'eqchi', Mam, Kaqchikel, and Ixil communities, whose relationship to land is communal, ancestral, and governed by indigenous customary law that the Guatemalan national legal system does not recognize as equivalent to formal title. Also affects indigenous communities across the broader Latin American extractive frontier, including in Peru, Colombia, Bolivia, and southern Mexico, where the same structural pattern of legal invisibility enabling resource extraction repeats across different ethnic and geographic contexts. Particularly devastating for women within these communities, who face a compounded invisibility: they are often excluded from formal land governance even within indigenous customary systems, lack national identity documents at higher rates than indigenous men due to barriers at civil registry offices that assume Spanish literacy and urban accessibility, and carry the primary burden of subsistence agriculture on the communal land being extracted. Also acutely affects community members whose entire cosmological and cultural identity is inseparable from specific geographic territory, meaning dispossession is not only an economic injury but a destruction of the conditions under which their identity and community can exist at all.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The Guatemalan state grants mining concessions through the Ministry of Energy and Mines under a legal framework that treats subsoil resources as state property regardless of surface land tenure, meaning a community can have effective occupation of land across generations and a mining company can nonetheless receive a legal concession to extract beneath it without the community's consent being a formal legal requirement. The ILO Convention 169, which Guatemala has ratified, requires free, prior, and informed consultation with indigenous communities before extractive projects proceed, but the consultation mechanism as implemented by the Guatemalan state has been systematically documented by human rights organizations as procedurally deficient, conducted after decisions are made, in Spanish rather than indigenous languages, with community representatives selected by authorities rather than communities, and without binding effect even when communities formally reject the project. Land titling in indigenous highland communities is overwhelmingly informal, with communal tenure recognized within communities but unregistered in the national property registry, meaning that when a legal dispute arises the company arrives with a concession document and the community arrives with oral history. A woman within that community who lacks a cedula, Guatemala's national identity document, cannot be a party to legal proceedings, cannot register a complaint with the human rights ombudsman as a named individual, cannot access legal aid systems that require identity verification, and does not formally exist within the national legal architecture that is simultaneously destroying the conditions of her existence.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A woman whose family has farmed the same hillside for four generations watches excavation equipment arrive on land her community has never sold and never consented to surrender. She attempts to file a complaint with the municipal government. She does not have a cedula. She is told she cannot file. She travels to the departmental capital to obtain one. The civil registry requires a birth certificate. Her birth was registered by her community but not by the state. Obtaining a birth certificate requires witnesses who are themselves registered, fees she cannot produce, and navigation of a bureaucratic process conducted entirely in Spanish through systems she has no experience with. She returns without documents. The legal aid organization she reaches through a community network tells her the case is strong on paper under ILO 169 but that without community members who can be named parties in a legal filing the case cannot move forward. The community organizes a formal consultation rejection of the mining project. The company's lawyers argue the consultation was improperly conducted and the concession stands. The water source the community uses for drinking and irrigation runs orange within eight months of extraction beginning. She cannot sue. She cannot file. She cannot vote in the municipal election that will determine who oversees the company's environmental compliance because her identity does not exist in the system registering voters. The land was taken not through violence alone but through the prior construction of a legal architecture in which she was never included, which then used her exclusion as the instrument of her dispossession.

44. Colombian woman who was displaced by paramilitaries twenty years ago and is still living in a city she never chose.
Affected Groups: Colombia's internally displaced population, estimated at over eight million people and representing one of the largest internal displacement crises in the world, making Colombia second only to Syria in total displaced persons. Most acutely affects Afro-Colombian and indigenous communities from the Pacific coast, the Urab— region, the Magdalena Medio, and the Llanos Orientales, where paramilitary and guerrilla territorial control was most absolute and displacement most systematic. Particularly devastating for women who were displaced not only by generalized violence but by targeted sexual violence used as a weapon of territorial control, who arrived in cities as single heads of household with children, no urban work history, no social networks, and no documentation of the assets and land left behind. Also affects the now-adult children of the displaced generation, who grew up in urban peripheries in conditions of poverty their parents did not choose for them, who have no memory of the land their families lost, and who inherit the legal and economic consequences of displacement without inheriting any of the rural identity or community ties that gave their parents a coherent sense of what was taken. Twenty years of urban marginality has produced a second generation whose dispossession is invisible because it looks, from the outside, simply like urban poverty.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: Colombia's Victims and Land Restitution Law of 2011, Law 1448, created a formal framework for recognizing displacement victims, registering their claims, and theoretically restoring land. The Victims' Registry requires documented proof of displacement through a declaration process that must be initiated within a legally defined window, and for many displaced in the late 1990s and early 2000s the window has closed or the documentation required to substantiate claims was destroyed, never existed in formal terms, or was lost across two decades of urban survival. Land restitution requires that the original land parcel be identifiable, that no subsequent claimant has acquired competing title, and that the security situation in the territory of origin permits return, conditions that in many regions of Colombia are simultaneously and indefinitely unmet because the same armed actors or their successor groups still control the territories from which communities were expelled. The restitution judges created under Law 1448 face caseloads that structurally cannot be processed within any timeframe that corresponds to a human life. Displaced women who arrived in cities and entered the informal economy have no formal employment history, no pension contributions, no social security record, and no path to retirement that does not run through a formal labor market that never absorbed them. The urban land they occupy in peripheral neighborhoods is frequently informal, meaning the second displacement, through urban development or eviction, requires no legal proceeding against people who have no legal tenure to defend.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A woman who was twenty-three when paramilitaries burned her village in Urab— is now forty-three and has spent two decades in a peripheral neighborhood of Medell—n or Bogot— or Cali that she reached because someone on a bus told her there was space. She raised her children in a house she built incrementally on land she does not own, in a neighborhood the city does not fully recognize, working in domestic service or street vending or informal food preparation because those were the labor markets that required no documentation she did not have. She registered as a displaced person and received transitional assistance that covered months, not decades. She filed a land restitution claim and was told the parcel could not be identified with sufficient precision in the registry, or that a third party had acquired title in the intervening years, or that security conditions in her municipality of origin did not permit the process to advance. She is not legally a refugee because she never crossed a border. She is not legally homeless because she occupies a structure. She is not legally landless because her claim is pending. She exists in a set of administrative categories that describe her situation without providing any material remedy for it. Her children grew up watching her navigate a city that processed her as a problem to be managed rather than a person to be restored. The paramilitaries who displaced her were demobilized, some were prosecuted, some received reduced sentences, some are operating again under different names in the same territories. The land she left is still there. She is still here. Twenty years later the distance between those two facts has become the permanent architecture of her life.

I really miss my hometown and they didn’t let me see my hometown during these 20 years living in Bogotá. What should I do now?

45. Mexican person whose family member was disappeared and who knows that reporting to police is pointless or dangerous.
Affected Groups: Families of the disappeared in Mexico, numbering over 100,000 formally registered cases as of recent counts, with human rights organizations consistently estimating the true figure is substantially higher due to systemic underreporting. Most acutely affects communities in Tamaulipas, Veracruz, Guerrero, Jalisco, Sinaloa, and Guanajuato, where cartel territorial control and state institutional capture overlap most completely, but disappearances occur across all 32 states and at rates that have accelerated rather than declined through successive federal administrations. Particularly devastating for mothers, who in Mexico as elsewhere bear the primary weight of searching, and who have organized collectively into movements like the Madres Buscadoras precisely because the state has abdicated the function those movements are now performing with bare hands and rudimentary tools in fields and unmarked ground. Also acutely affects indigenous and Afro-Mexican communities where disappearances intersect with land and resource conflicts, communities in border regions where the disappeared were migrants whose families may be in another country entirely and who face the additional barrier of cross-border jurisdiction in seeking any accounting, and working-class urban families whose disappeared member was taken not in a context of organized crime membership but of proximity, of being in the wrong place, of owing money, of resisting extortion, of being young and male in a territory someone else decided to control.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: Mexico's General Law on Forced Disappearances, passed in 2017, created a formal architecture of response including the National Search Commission, state search commissions, and a national register of disappeared persons. The architecture exists on paper with considerable procedural sophistication and exists in practice as a system so under-resourced, so infiltrated by the same institutional actors implicated in disappearances, and so structurally dependent on family members doing investigative work the state will not do, that the law functions primarily as a legitimizing document rather than an operational remedy. Reporting a disappearance to municipal or state police in territories where those institutions have documented relationships with criminal organizations is not a neutral act. It is an act that in documented cases has resulted in the reporting family member being threatened, in information about the family's search being passed to the organization responsible for the disappearance, and in secondary disappearances of family members who reported. The Attorney General's office receives reports but the investigative follow-through rate is so low as to be functionally indistinguishable from non-investigation in the majority of cases. Forensic capacity is catastrophically insufficient relative to the scale of the crisis, with thousands of unidentified remains in state morgues that cannot be processed because the genetic databases, trained personnel, and funding required to match them to missing persons reports do not exist at necessary scale. Families who attempt to search independently, as the Madres Buscadoras do, operate without legal authority to excavate, without forensic support when they find remains, without protection when their searches bring them into proximity with the organizations that created the clandestine graves they are finding.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A woman's son did not come home on a Tuesday evening. She knows, from everything her community knows, that calling the municipal police is not reporting a crime but announcing to the people who may have taken him that his family is looking. She does not call. She begins asking quietly, carefully, in the ways that do not draw attention, because drawing attention in her municipality has consequences she has watched happen to others. She files a report eventually with the state search commission because someone tells her it is necessary to create a legal record. The commission acknowledges receipt. Nothing happens for six months. She joins a collective of mothers searching. They go on weekends with shovels and sticks to areas where community knowledge, the informal cartography of where bodies are put, suggests looking. They find remains. They do not know whose. They report the location to authorities. Forensic personnel arrive days later. The remains enter a system with a backlog measured in years. She does not know if her son is among them. She cannot know because the system that would tell her does not have the capacity to tell her within any timeframe that corresponds to how grief and uncertainty operate in a human body. She lives in a permanent present tense of not knowing, unable to mourn because mourning requires a fact she has not been given, unable to stop searching because stopping means accepting a silence the state has decided is sufficient. The disappearance took her son in one moment. The institutional failure disappears her every day afterward, incrementally, in the accumulation of unreturned calls and unprocessed evidence and forms acknowledged and never acted upon, until the search itself becomes the entirety of what remains of her life before.

—

My son did not come home ten days ago and his phone is off. I talked to my neighbors but they don’t help me at all. They just say not to ask around here in Veracruz. I don't know what to do.

46. Haitian person trying to navigate any official system after the state has functionally collapsed.
Affected Groups: The entire Haitian civilian population of approximately 11 million people, but most acutely those in Port-au-Prince and surrounding metropolitan areas where gang territorial control has rendered physical movement through the city a life-threatening calculation, and where the concentration of what remained of functional state infrastructure means its collapse is felt most totally. Particularly devastating for women and girls in gang-controlled territories where sexual violence is deployed as a systematic instrument of territorial governance rather than incidental to conflict, for the estimated 700,000 internally displaced persons living in camps and informal settlements without address, identity, or access to any administrative system, for families attempting to register births, deaths, or marriages that occurred during the period of collapse and for whom the absence of documentation will compound across every subsequent interaction with any system for the rest of their lives, for sick and injured people whose nearest hospital has been occupied, looted, or shuttered, and for the generation of children whose schooling has been interrupted not in months but in years, accumulating an educational deficit that no future stabilization will automatically repair. Also acutely affects Haitians in the diaspora attempting to send support, navigate dual legal obligations, or assist family members through systems that assume a functioning state exists on the receiving end.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The Haitian state's institutional collapse is not metaphorical but operational and physical. The civil registry offices where births, deaths, marriages, and identities are recorded have been burned, occupied, or abandoned in significant number across Port-au-Prince, meaning the documentary infrastructure that produces legal personhood is physically gone in ways that cannot be remedied by policy reform alone. The national identification system requires functioning offices to issue documents, functioning databases to verify them, and functioning infrastructure to connect them, none of which can be assumed. Courts have suspended operations across large parts of the country, meaning that legal disputes, property claims, inheritance proceedings, and criminal accountability have no functional venue. The national police force is numerically insufficient, outgunned, and in documented cases infiltrated by or complicit with the gang structures they are nominally opposing, meaning law enforcement as a neutral institutional function does not reliably exist. International aid systems that theoretically exist to fill state gaps require beneficiary registration, identity verification, and address confirmation that displaced populations without documents and without fixed addresses structurally cannot provide, creating the situation where the most devastated are least reachable by the systems designed to reach them. Remittance systems, one of Haiti's primary economic lifelines representing a larger share of GDP than almost any other nation, depend on physical money transfer locations that have been closed, looted, or made inaccessible by gang checkpoints that tax movement through territory they control.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A woman in Cit— Soleil needs to reach the hospital three kilometers away. Those three kilometers cross two gang territorial boundaries. The cost of passage, if passage is negotiable at all, is money she does not have or compliance she cannot survive. She does not go. A man whose wife died during the period of collapse needs to register her death to access their shared property and settle her affairs. The civil registry office in his arrondissement was burned. The nearest functioning office requires travel through territory he cannot safely cross. The death is unregistered. The property exists in a legal suspension that will outlast his own life if the system is not rebuilt. A family displaced from their neighborhood by gang expansion arrives at an aid registration point. They have no address because they have no home. They have no documents because their documents were left behind when they fled in the night. They are told registration requires identification. They do not receive assistance. A young man who witnessed a gang killing and knows the names of those responsible has no police station he can report to that will not expose him to the organization he is reporting. He carries the knowledge in silence because speaking it in any official direction is a death sentence and official directions have ceased to offer any protection that justifies the risk. The particular cruelty of state collapse as a lived condition is that every system a person might turn to in a crisis, the hospital, the police, the court, the registry, the aid organization, either does not function, cannot be safely reached, or requires as a condition of access the documentation that the collapse itself destroyed. The emergency has consumed the infrastructure of emergency response, leaving people to navigate the worst moments of their lives entirely alone, in a country that is simultaneously everywhere in international news and completely unreachable from inside it.

The other day I went to register my daughter for pre-school in Port-au-Prince but they said they cannot accept her without a birth certificate. What should I do?

47. Indonesian domestic worker in Hong Kong whose employer has taken her phone and she has one hour on Sunday to communicate with anyone.
Affected Groups: The approximately 400,000 Indonesian and Filipino foreign domestic workers in Hong Kong, representing one of the largest concentrations of live-in migrant domestic labor in Asia, and a workforce whose legal status is structurally engineered to maximize employer control and minimize worker autonomy. Most acutely affects Indonesian workers, who arrive through a recruitment agency system that charges fees equivalent to six months or more of salary, meaning workers begin employment already in debt to the system that placed them. Particularly devastating for workers from rural East Java, West Nusa Tenggara, and East Nusa Tenggara, where recruitment networks operate with minimal government oversight and where the social pressure of having accepted migration as a family economic strategy makes reporting abuse or abandoning a placement feel like a betrayal of everyone who invested in the departure. Also acutely affects workers whose employers have confiscated their passports, a practice that is illegal under Hong Kong law and routine in practice, workers who are deployed to households where they are shared between multiple family units in violation of their contracts, workers managing chronic illness or mental health deterioration in conditions of isolation and overwork with no access to healthcare they can reach without employer permission, and workers whose one Sunday off has been unilaterally cancelled by employers who face no meaningful enforcement consequence for doing so.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: Hong Kong's live-in requirement, embedded in the standard employment contract for foreign domestic workers, legally mandates that workers reside in their employer's home, structurally eliminating the physical separation between workplace and living space that labor protections in every other employment context assume as baseline. The two-week rule requires that workers whose employment is terminated, for any reason including employer abuse, leave Hong Kong or find new employment within two weeks, creating a legal mechanism that functions as a deportation threat whenever a worker considers reporting mistreatment or leaving a dangerous placement. The debt bondage produced by agency fee structures means that a worker who leaves a placement in the first months forfeits the salary that would have repaid the debt, returning home worse than when she left and owing money to networks with social reach into her home community. The confiscation of passports and phones, both illegal under Hong Kong law, is effectively unenforceable because enforcement requires the worker to report, reporting requires access to authorities, access to authorities requires physical movement the employer controls, and the legal consequences for employers found in violation are insufficiently punitive to deter the practice at scale. The Labour Tribunal and Immigration Department, the nominal venues for worker complaints, require in-person attendance during working hours that workers cannot attend without employer knowledge, and the process of filing, waiting, and adjudicating a claim extends across months during which the worker must maintain legal status through continued employment or face the two-week deportation clock. NGOs and legal aid organizations exist and do meaningful work, but reaching them requires the phone that has been taken and the time that has been reduced to one hour on Sunday in a city of seven million people.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A woman from East Java has not spoken to her children in three weeks because her employer took her phone on her first day and told her she could use it on Sundays. It is Sunday. She has one hour. She is in a park in Causeway Bay or Victoria Park or whatever open space is closest to the employer's apartment, surrounded by thousands of other domestic workers doing the same thing, trying to compress a week of isolation into sixty minutes of connection. She calls her children first. Then her mother. Then she has twenty minutes left and she needs to decide what to do with them. She has not been paid in six weeks. Her employer told her the salary is being held to cover household expenses she allegedly damaged. She does not know if this is legal. She does not know who to call. The NGO number she was given during her pre-departure orientation in Indonesia is on a piece of paper she kept in her phone case but her phone case is with her phone which is in the employer's bedroom. She tries to remember the number. She cannot. She uses ten minutes searching for it online on a borrowed phone. She finds a hotline. She calls. She is placed on hold. Her hour ends. She returns to the apartment. The following Sunday her employer tells her there are family activities and she is needed at home. She does not get her Sunday. The week after, her employer's mother visits from mainland China and she is told she will be shared between two households temporarily. This has been temporary for four months. She has not filed a complaint. Filing a complaint requires a process she cannot begin without the phone she does not have, during hours she cannot leave without permission she will not receive, through a system that will start a two-week clock the moment she tries to use it, in a city where the law that was supposed to protect her is written in a language she reads only partially and enforced at a threshold her employer has learned, precisely, never to cross.
