I injured my foot at work, but I don’t have legal status here. It’s getting worse and I can barely walk. Some people told me to go to the hospital anyway, others say it could cause problems for me later. I don’t know what the safer choice is. What should I do?

58. A student in a conservative family who got into a university in another city but has not told her parents yet.
Affected Groups: Young women in conservative families across Iran, Pakistan, Afghanistan, parts of the Arab world, Turkey, India, and within diaspora communities in Western countries where family authority over daughters' mobility and educational trajectories operates independently of the surrounding legal environment, as well as young women in conservative religious communities globally including certain evangelical Christian, ultra-Orthodox Jewish, and fundamentalist Mormon contexts where female higher education is viewed with suspicion or conditioned on proximity to family supervision. Most acutely felt by first generation university students whose families have no framework for understanding what university education means, what it requires, or what it produces in the person who undergoes it, and for whom the absence of a family map of this territory means the daughter is navigating not only the institutional challenge of gaining admission but the prior and more immediately dangerous challenge of gaining permission from people who have never been where she is trying to go and who therefore cannot evaluate whether it is safe or appropriate by any standard except the standards of immobility that their own lives were organized around. Particularly devastating for young women in households where the authority being negotiated is not only paternal but fraternal, where brothers who may be younger than her have been socialized into a guardianship role over her movements that the family structure enforces regardless of age, and for young women whose families have already identified a marriage prospect whose timeline would be disrupted by university attendance in another city, meaning the university admission is not only a negotiation about education but a collision with a parallel plan for her life that was made without her participation and that the family may consider more settled than she does.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The mechanisms operating against her are a dense layering of formal authority, informal control, and economic dependency that the university admission, however prestigious and however hard-won, does not by itself dissolve. In Iran a woman under twenty-six traveling to another city to study requires written permission from her father or husband to obtain dormitory housing through the university system, meaning the institutional pathway for acting on her admission runs directly through the family authority she has not yet confronted, and the university's own administrative structure enforces the family's veto before she reaches campus. In Pakistan and Afghanistan family permission is not formally embedded in university administrative systems in the same way but the practical barriers are equivalent, since housing in another city requires financial support the family controls, since traveling alone as a young woman without family sanction exposes her to social and physical risks the family's protection partially mitigates, and since proceeding without permission burns the family relationship that is also her safety net if everything else fails. In conservative diaspora contexts the legal environment of the surrounding country offers her formal protections, she is an adult, she has a legal right to attend university, no law prevents her from leaving, but the family's control over her finances, her documentation in some cases, her social network, and her psychological security means the legal freedom is not the same as practical freedom, and exercising it without family consent means accepting costs that the law does not protect her from, estrangement, social exposure within the community, the loss of the support structures that legal adulthood does not replace. The admission letter sitting in her possession or her email is legally sufficient to change her life. It is not socially or economically sufficient without the conversation she has not had.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A young woman who has gotten into a university in another city and has not told her parents yet is living in a specific kind of suspended time that has a physical texture, the weight of the knowledge sitting in her that no one else in her household shares, the way every dinner table conversation happens slightly around the thing that is not being said, the way she looks at her parents and performs normalcy while internally she is somewhere else entirely, already in the other city, already in the lecture hall, already the person the admission says she could become, and simultaneously still entirely in this house, this kitchen, this family, this set of expectations that have been organizing her life since before she was old enough to have opinions about them. The letter arrived and the world split into two versions and she is living in the gap between them waiting for the conversation that will collapse them into one. She does not know which one. The delay is not cowardice, though she will probably call it that in her own internal accounting. It is a rational response to genuine uncertainty about an outcome that will determine not just whether she goes to university but the entire subsequent shape of her relationship with the people she loves most and is most afraid of simultaneously. She is calculating. She is trying to find the right moment, the right framing, the right version of the conversation that produces the outcome she needs without destroying what she cannot afford to lose. She may be doing this calculation alone because there is no one in her immediate world she can think through it with, no one whose advice does not come attached to a stake in the outcome, no friend whose family is not connected to hers, no sibling who would not become an unwilling keeper of the secret or an inadvertent revealer of it. The admission has an acceptance deadline. The deadline is approaching at the same fixed rate as every other deadline regardless of whether she has found the right moment yet. The university does not know it is waiting for a conversation that may go very badly. It is simply waiting for her response. She is trying to make sure that when she gives it there is still a version of her life on the other side of it that is worth responding for.

—

I got into a university in another city, but no one at home knows yet. It’s sort of already assumed I’ll just stay here. They always bring up safety and what people will say. I keep thinking if I say it too soon, it’ll get shut down before it even becomes real. Is there a right time to tell them?

59. A migrant worker whose employer has withheld two months of wages and threatens to report him if he complains.
Affected Groups: Migrant workers across Gulf Cooperation Council states including Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain, and Oman under the kafala sponsorship system, as well as migrant workers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Jordan where similar employer-tied visa frameworks operate, spanning construction laborers from South Asia and Southeast Asia, domestic workers from the Philippines, Indonesia, Ethiopia, and Sri Lanka, and agricultural workers in Southern Europe and North America whose seasonal visa status creates equivalent dependency on employer goodwill regardless of the formal legal framework. Most acutely felt by workers whose visa status is explicitly tied to a single employer through sponsorship systems that make changing employers or leaving the job without permission a legal violation regardless of the employer's conduct, creating a structural situation in which the worker's legal presence in the country is contingent on the continued goodwill of the party who is harming them. Particularly devastating for domestic workers who live inside their employer's household and who therefore have no physical separation between their workplace and their living space, no colleagues who witness their treatment, no commute during which they exist in a public space where help could theoretically reach them, and no hours during which they are not under the direct supervision of the person withholding their wages, and for workers who borrowed significant sums from recruiters in their home countries to finance the migration, whose debt means that returning home without the wages owed to them does not restore their previous situation but delivers them into a debt crisis whose consequences for their family may be more severe than continued endurance of the wage theft.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The mechanisms trapping this worker were not assembled accidentally but are the structural outcome of labor frameworks designed to maximize employer control over migrant worker behavior by making legal status contingent on employer approval. The kafala system in its various Gulf implementations requires a migrant worker to obtain their sponsor's permission to change jobs, take another employment, or leave the country, meaning the employer holds three simultaneous vetoes over the worker's primary options for resolving a labor dispute, none of which can be exercised without employer cooperation. Wage theft in this context is not merely a labor violation but a power demonstration, the employer's withholding of wages communicates that the worker's recourse options are understood by the employer to be sufficiently limited that the violation can be sustained without consequence. The threat to report the worker to immigration authorities for complaints or for fabricated visa violations is not a bluff in most of these contexts. It is an accurately described power differential. Immigration enforcement in Gulf states, Malaysia, and Jordan processes complaints from employers about workers with a speed and institutional priority that complaints from workers about employers do not receive, meaning the same administrative system that is theoretically available to both parties in a labor dispute functions asymmetrically in practice, efficiently processing employer complaints and slowly or never processing worker complaints. Migrant worker access to labor courts and dispute resolution mechanisms in most of these contexts requires the worker to physically present themselves to an authority while their visa status is unresolved, which exposes them to detention pending resolution of status questions that the employer's threatened report may have already initiated. Legal aid organizations exist in some of these contexts but require the worker to have a phone, to know the organization exists, to be able to contact it without the employer monitoring the communication, and to be physically able to reach it, conditions that domestic workers living inside employer households and construction workers in labor camps with restricted movement frequently cannot meet simultaneously.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A migrant worker whose employer has withheld two months of wages and threatens to report him if he complains is inside a trap whose architecture he understood before he entered it, because workers from sending communities share information about conditions in destination countries through networks that predate any individual's migration, and the general contours of employer power over worker status are known. What he did not fully calculate, or calculated and accepted because the alternative was remaining in a situation with its own impossibilities, was what it would feel like to be inside it when it activated. Two months of wages is not an abstraction. It is the specific sum he calculated before departure would be sufficient to send home by a specific date for a specific purpose, a child's school fees, a parent's medical treatment, a debt installment whose non-payment has consequences for people who are not here and who do not know yet that the money is not coming. He is communicating home in a register that does not convey this because conveying it would produce worry that cannot help him from that distance and would confirm fears his family had about his departure that he reassured them were unfounded. He is performing stability for people who depend on him from thousands of kilometers away while being structurally unable to produce the stability the performance claims. The threat to report him is the employer's understanding that the worker's situation is more precarious than the employer's, that the worker has more to lose from a confrontation than the employer does, and that this asymmetry is sufficient to sustain the wage theft indefinitely. He is owed money for work he performed with his body over two months in conditions that were already difficult. The money is being withheld by someone who is legally empowered to also determine whether he is allowed to remain in the country, to change jobs, or to go home. The same hand that owes him wages holds the document that governs whether he exists legally in the place where the wages are owed. This is not a coincidence of his specific situation. It is the design.

—

My boss keeps saying he will pay me next week, but it has already been two months. Every time I ask again, he reminds me that I have no proper papers and says no one will believe me over him. I need the money to send home, but I am scared of making things worse. What should I do?

60. A woman in a small town who needs private medical advice but the only doctor knows her husband’s family.
Affected Groups: Women in small towns and rural communities globally where the density of social relationships between medical providers and patient communities eliminates the functional separation between clinical encounter and social network, spanning rural communities across the Middle East and South Asia where a single male physician serves an entire district and where his social integration into the community's prominent family networks is a precondition of his professional position, small towns across conservative parts of the United States, Eastern Europe, and Latin America where the local doctor has been embedded in the community for decades and where patient confidentiality is legally required but socially impossible to guarantee, and women in remote communities across sub-Saharan Africa where the community health worker is a neighbor, a church member, a market vendor, and a healthcare provider simultaneously with no institutional or physical separation between these roles. Most acutely felt by women seeking advice about reproductive health, sexual health, domestic violence, mental health, or any condition whose disclosure to their husband or his family would alter the power dynamics of their marriage or their standing in the community, and by women in communities where the physician is male and where consulting him about intimate health matters requires overcoming cultural prohibitions around discussing female bodies with men outside the family that the clinical framing of the encounter does not fully dissolve. Particularly devastating for women in communities where the local doctor is socially obligated to the husband's family through relationships of debt, loyalty, shared history, or reciprocal standing that create informal pressures on clinical confidentiality that no legal framework can reach, and for women whose medical need is urgent enough that delay carries clinical consequences but whose social situation makes the only available provider functionally inaccessible.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The mechanisms operating against this woman exist at the intersection of what the law requires and what social reality delivers. Medical confidentiality is legally mandated in virtually every jurisdiction through frameworks ranging from HIPAA in the United States to equivalent data protection legislation across Europe and the medical ethics codes of professional licensing bodies globally. These frameworks create legal obligations on providers but cannot reach the informal information flows that characterize small community social life, where what was learned in a clinical context migrates into social context not through deliberate disclosure but through the thousand small signals of changed behavior, altered social interaction, and community awareness that travel through tight social networks without anyone having explicitly said anything that could be identified as a breach. A physician who would never deliberately disclose a patient's information may mention to a mutual acquaintance that he has been busy, or may behave differently toward the husband at a subsequent social encounter, or may discuss a case in sufficiently anonymized terms with a colleague who is not anonymous to anyone in a community of four hundred people. The legal confidentiality obligation cannot regulate these transmissions because they are not legally identifiable as disclosures. In many low and middle income country contexts the legal framework exists but the enforcement mechanism, a medical licensing board capable of investigating and sanctioning a rural physician for confidentiality violations, is urban, under-resourced, and inaccessible to a rural woman who may not know it exists. Telemedicine platforms that might provide access to a geographically distant provider are available in some contexts but require internet connectivity, a private space in which to conduct a consultation, a device that is not shared with family members whose browsing history is visible, and a credit card or payment method that does not generate a household financial record requiring explanation.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A woman in a small town who needs private medical advice and knows that the only doctor knows her husband's family is performing a risk calculation at the exact moment she is least equipped to perform it, because the medical need that drives her to consider consulting him is by definition a moment of physical or psychological vulnerability, and the social calculation she must overlay on that vulnerability requires a clarity of judgment that vulnerability impairs. She is not being paranoid. Small town social networks transmit information with an efficiency and a completeness that urban dwellers systematically underestimate, and a woman who has lived her entire life in this community understands exactly how information moves through it because she has watched it move about other people across her entire life. She knows that what she tells this doctor in a room that is legally confidential will exist in a social environment that is not, and she knows this not as an abstract risk but as a lived and specific understanding of the relationships between the people involved. If her need is reproductive, a pregnancy she has not decided about, a contraceptive she wants without her husband's knowledge, a sexually transmitted infection whose presence would require an explanation she cannot give, the consequences of the information reaching her husband are not merely embarrassing but potentially dangerous in ways that the clinical encounter is not designed to assess or protect against. If her need is a symptom she has been dismissing that has now become urgent, the delay her social calculation produces has clinical consequences that accumulate silently while she weighs risks. She may drive to another town if she has access to a car and the freedom to use it without explanation. She may look for answers online in the privacy of a phone she keeps separately. She may ask a friend who asks a friend in a chain of informal consultation that degrades in accuracy with each transmission. She may wait. The waiting is the most common outcome and the most dangerous one, and it happens not because she does not understand the importance of seeking care but because she understands with perfect clarity the social cost of seeking it from the only person positioned to provide it, and has calculated that cost against the clinical risk and arrived at an answer that the medical system, which only sees the delayed presentation and not the calculation that produced it, will record as non-compliance.

—

There is something personal I need to ask a doctor about, but the only doctor in our town is a close friend of my husband’s family. Everyone here talks, and I do not trust that my visit would stay private. People keep saying I should just go, but I am scared. What should I do?

61. A woman in a village where her husband’s cousin is the police officer.
Affected Groups: Women in rural and peri-urban communities globally where law enforcement is embedded within the same kinship networks that govern family and community life, concentrated most densely in tribal and clan-organized societies across the Middle East, North Africa, South Asia, and sub-Saharan Africa where police recruitment patterns follow family and community lines, and in small rural communities across Eastern Europe, Latin America, and parts of Southeast Asia where a single officer or small detachment covers an entire district and where that officer's social integration into the community predates and supersedes their institutional role. Most acutely felt by women experiencing domestic violence, forced marriage, honor-based control, or financial abuse at the hands of a husband or his family, for whom the police officer who is supposed to represent the state's protective function is instead a member of the family structure generating the harm, and by women in communities where the officer's presence is not incidental to the family's power but constitutive of it, where the family's local dominance is partially built on the authority the officer's position provides and where challenging the husband means challenging a family that has a legal instrument. Particularly devastating for women in communities where the officer is not merely socially connected to the husband's family but actively participates in family councils and dispute resolution processes that determine how domestic matters are handled, meaning the line between law enforcement and family authority is not blurred but nonexistent, and for women who have already attempted to report and discovered that the report traveled back to their husband before any official response was generated, a common experience that forecloses future attempts not through explicit threat but through the demonstrated futility of the channel.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The mechanisms operating against this woman exist at the precise point where formal state authority and informal kinship authority share a body, a uniform, and a weapon. In most jurisdictions the legal framework nominally governing this situation includes domestic violence legislation, mandatory reporting requirements, and police conduct codes that prohibit officers from handling cases involving family members or close associates. These frameworks assume an institutional separation between law enforcement and community that does not exist in the contexts where this problem is most acute. Conflict of interest provisions in police conduct codes are designed for urban bureaucratic environments where the separation of officer from community is structural and where supervision is possible. In a rural district where a single officer covers several villages, where there is no supervising officer within practical reach, where complaints about officer conduct must be filed with a district headquarters that is geographically distant and administratively indifferent to rural domestic complaints, and where the officer has the discretion to determine which situations constitute reportable incidents and which constitute private family matters, the conflict of interest provision exists as text with no enforcement mechanism attached. Domestic violence reporting systems in many of these contexts route through the local officer as the first point of contact, meaning the architecture of the reporting system requires the woman to approach the person least likely to help her as the precondition for accessing any help at all. In customary law contexts across parts of Africa and South Asia, domestic disputes are formally or informally routed to community or family councils before or instead of state legal processes, and the officer's participation in these councils is expected and normalized, meaning his dual role as family member and law enforcement is not a corruption of the system but a feature of how the system was designed to operate in that community context. Women's shelters, legal aid organizations, and NGO support services that might provide an alternative pathway exist primarily in urban centers and require the woman to first leave the community, which requires resources, transport, and a destination she may not have.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A woman in a village where her husband's cousin is the police officer does not need to have been told explicitly that reporting is futile. She has watched enough to know. She has seen how disputes in this community are handled, who calls whom, whose version of events is recorded and whose is not, what happens to women who make formal complaints and how those women are subsequently positioned within the community narrative. She has absorbed this knowledge across years of living in a place where law enforcement and family authority share a face she recognizes at family gatherings, at the market, at the mosque or the church, a face that belongs simultaneously to the person who could help her and to the family that is harming her, and that resolves these dual memberships without apparent difficulty because in this community they were never understood as contradictory. If she calls the emergency number, if such a thing exists and functions in her area, the call may be routed to him or to someone who tells him. If she walks to the station, she is walking to a place where her presence will be known before she arrives and interpreted before she speaks. If she files a written complaint, the complaint will be handled by people who know him and who have calibrated their professional behavior around the social reality that he is part of. Her husband knows this. The husband's family knows this. The officer knows this. The architecture of her entrapment is held in place by everyone's accurate understanding of how power is distributed in this place, and her accurate understanding of the same distribution is what prevents her from approaching the one institution nominally designed to protect her. She is not without legal rights. She is in a place where legal rights require legal institutions to enforce them, and the nearest legal institution has his cousin's face.

—

My husband has been hurting me for years, and people keep saying if it gets worse I should go to the police. But the police officer for our area is his cousin, and they eat together every week. I do not know what “reporting” means when everyone belongs to the same family. What should I do?

62. An international resident living legally abroad is trying to access a service that requires identity verification, but their passport is from a sanctioned country not supported by the system. Customer support only loops them back into the same process. The core issue is structural exclusion.
Affected Groups: Legal residents and citizens of sanctioned or politically isolated states living abroad with valid residency status in host countries, most acutely affecting Iranians, Russians, Belarusians, Syrians, North Koreans, Cubans, Venezuelans, and Sudanese nationals who have legally relocated to Europe, North America, Latin America, or Southeast Asia through work visas, student visas, asylum status, or permanent residency. Particularly devastating for professionals in technology, finance, academia, and medicine whose work requires access to digital platforms, payment systems, and verification infrastructure that their passport of origin structurally excludes them from regardless of their legal standing in the country where they actually live and work. Also acutely affects stateless persons and those holding travel documents issued by states with limited international recognition, including Palestinian Authority travel documents, Kosovo passports in non-recognizing states, and Taiwanese passports in jurisdictions deferring to Beijing. Also affects people holding valid refugee travel documents issued under the 1951 Convention, which many identity verification systems do not recognize as equivalent to a national passport despite their legal status as internationally recognized travel documents. The population is not small, not marginal, and not composed of people attempting to circumvent systems. It is composed of people who are legally present, legally working, legally tax-paying, and structurally excluded by an identity verification layer that was designed without them.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: Digital identity verification systems used by banks, financial platforms, telecommunications providers, healthcare portals, government service interfaces, and employer onboarding systems are built on document recognition databases that reflect geopolitical rather than legal logic. A system that accepts passports from 180 countries but not Iran is not making a legal determination about the Iranian national standing in front of it. It is importing a sanctions framework designed for state-level financial flows and applying it as a binary individual exclusion at the identity layer, regardless of whether that individual is subject to any sanction, has any connection to sanctioned entities, or poses any compliance risk. OFAC and EU sanctions regulations contain general licenses and individual exemptions that technically permit service provision to individuals with no sanctioned activity, but compliance departments at financial institutions and technology companies have systematically overcomplied, applying blanket nationality exclusions because the cost of individual due diligence exceeds the revenue value of the customer and the reputational risk of a compliance error exceeds the reputational cost of excluding innocent people. Know Your Customer regulations require identity verification but do not specify that passport nationality must determine eligibility, yet vendor systems implementing KYC have operationalized it that way because national passport databases are the infrastructure they were built on. Customer support escalation paths at these institutions are staffed by agents with no authority to override system-level exclusions, trained on scripts that loop back to the same verification pathway, and operating without access to the compliance exceptions that theoretically exist. The result is a system where the exception that would resolve the individual's situation exists in policy and does not exist in practice because the practice was never built to implement the exception.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: An Iranian software engineer living legally in Germany on a work visa, paying German taxes, holding a German residence permit, attempts to open a business bank account to receive client payments. The bank's identity verification system does not accept Iranian passports. She submits her German residence permit. The system requires a passport as primary document. She calls customer support. She is told to submit her passport. She submits her Iranian passport. The system flags it and suspends the application. She calls again. She is told the matter has been escalated. Three weeks later she receives an email telling her the application cannot be processed and directing her to the same online portal that rejected her. She attempts a second bank. The same outcome in a different interface. She attempts a fintech platform. The platform's automated verification vendor does not include Iranian passports in its supported document list. The platform's customer support has no pathway for manual review. She attempts to use her German residence permit as a primary document on a third platform. The platform accepts it, begins verification, and then requires a second identity document from a supported country list that does not include Iran. She has no second document from a supported country because she is Iranian and has lived in Germany for three years and has not acquired German citizenship because the naturalization timeline is longer than her residence. She cannot receive payment from her clients. She cannot pay her suppliers. She cannot register the business that would make her self-employment legal under her visa terms. She is legally present, professionally credentialed, financially solvent, and institutionally invisible. The customer support agent she reaches on her seventh call is genuinely sorry and structurally unable to help and returns her to the portal. The loop is not a malfunction. It is the system operating as designed, which is to say as a compliance artifact that was never required to consider the human being standing inside it, legally, with nowhere left to escalate.

—

I’m living in another country now and I’m here legally, but I’m trying to sign up for something I need and the identity check keeps failing on my documents. My passport is from a country they don’t seem to accept, and support just keeps sending me back to the same verification page. It feels like the system has decided I’m the wrong kind of person before I even start. What am I supposed to do when it keeps acting like I don’t exist?

63. Person whose child died and whose culture requires specific mourning rituals they cannot perform in the country they now live in.
Affected Groups: Diaspora communities and migrants whose cultural and religious mourning practices fall outside the legal, logistical, or infrastructural frameworks of their host countries, most acutely affecting West African communities in Europe and North America whose mourning traditions require multi-day communal gatherings, specific food preparation at scale, and ritual practices that apartment living, noise ordinances, and workplace leave policies structurally prevent. Also affects South Asian Hindu and Sikh communities whose cremation traditions require specific ritual conditions including open-air or wood-fire cremation that is prohibited in most Western jurisdictions on environmental grounds, Muslim communities across Europe and North America whose requirement for burial within twenty-four hours of death collides with coroner hold periods, autopsy requirements, funeral home processing timelines, and cemetery availability that routinely extend that window to days or weeks. Particularly devastating for indigenous communities relocated far from ancestral land whose mourning practices are geographically specific, requiring return to particular places, rivers, burial grounds, or territorial spaces that are thousands of kilometers away and accessible only through international travel that immigration status, financial constraint, or document problems may make impossible. Also acutely affects communities whose mourning practices require the physical presence of religious specialists, elders, or community members who are themselves distributed across multiple countries by the same migration that displaced the grieving parent, meaning the ritual cannot be assembled even when its individual components theoretically exist somewhere in the diaspora.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The legal infrastructure governing death in most Western countries was built around Christian northern European mourning traditions and has been only partially and inconsistently adapted to accommodate religious and cultural diversity at scale. Coroner jurisdiction over unexpected or unattended deaths, which includes most deaths of children, imposes mandatory hold periods and autopsy requirements that are non-negotiable under law regardless of religious prohibition, meaning a Jewish or Muslim family whose faith requires burial within twenty-four hours has no legal mechanism to fulfill that requirement when the state has jurisdiction over the body. Cremation regulations in the United Kingdom, Germany, France, Australia, and most American states require enclosed cremation in licensed facilities at temperatures and conditions that preclude the ritual elements of open-air cremation central to Hindu and some indigenous traditions, and no exemption pathway exists in most jurisdictions because the regulations were written without those traditions as a consideration. Zoning laws governing noise, assembly size, food preparation, and the use of residential space prevent the communal mourning gatherings that many West African, South Asian, and Pacific Islander traditions require as the primary mechanism of grief processing, meaning the ritual is not merely inconvenient but legally impermissible in the spaces where the community actually lives. Workplace bereavement leave policies in most countries provide between three and five days for the death of a child, a duration calibrated to northern European mourning conventions and structurally insufficient for traditions requiring forty days of mourning observance, annual death anniversary rituals requiring community assembly, or the extended family presence that transforms grief from a private into a communal and therefore survivable experience. The body itself, in many traditions the site of the most critical ritual actions in the hours immediately following death, enters a legal and logistical system, the funeral home, the coroner, the crematorium, the cemetery, that treats it as a process to be managed efficiently rather than a sacred object requiring specific handling, and that system has no formal intake mechanism for ritual requirements that fall outside its operational assumptions.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A Ghanaian woman in London whose four year old dies unexpectedly is told by the coroner's office that the body will be held for up to three weeks pending autopsy and investigation. In her tradition the child must be buried within days, with the community present, with specific rituals performed by elders who know what to do with the grief of a parent who has lost a child. The elders are in Accra. The community is distributed across London, Birmingham, and Amsterdam. The body is in a refrigerated drawer in a facility she cannot enter freely or perform any ritual within. She calls her mother in Ghana who tells her what must be done. None of what must be done is possible. A Hindu father in New Jersey whose teenage son dies needs to perform the antyesti, the last rites, including ritual washing of the body by family members and cremation conditions that allow the spirit's release according to tradition. The funeral home tells him the body has been embalmed as standard procedure, a process that his tradition considers a violation of the body's integrity in death. The cremation will occur in an electric retort at a licensed facility. There is no option for the ritual fire his tradition requires. He performs what adaptations he can. He knows they are not enough. He knows this not as an opinion but as a theological fact within the framework that gives his son's death its only available meaning, and that framework is telling him that he has failed his child at the moment of his child's greatest need. A Lakota woman in Minneapolis whose infant dies needs to return to her nation's territory to perform burial rites connected to specific land. She is on a waiting list for housing assistance and cannot afford the journey. The infant is buried in a municipal cemetery in a city that was never home. The land that would have held her child correctly is a thousand miles away. The grief she carries is not only the grief of a mother who lost a child. It is the grief of a mother who lost a child and was then prevented, by poverty and distance and a legal system built around other people's traditions, from doing the one thing her culture told her she could still do for him.

My child left us today. My whole family came from pakistan for her burrial but, the there is no burial in Japan and they say that I have to burn my daughter’s body which is forbidden in Islam. I don’t have the money to take the body to Karachi either. I don’t know what to do.

64. Person who has survived something so extreme that no one around them can hold it with them.
Affected Groups: Survivors of atrocity-scale trauma whose experiences exceed the psychological and social capacity of their immediate community to witness, process, or remain present with, most acutely affecting survivors of genocide including Rwandan Tutsi survivors living among perpetrator communities or in diaspora, Yazidi women who survived ISIS captivity and sexual enslavement, survivors of the Cambodian Khmer Rouge whose entire social fabric including the people who would have been their witnesses was destroyed by the same event they survived, and Holocaust survivors who arrived in new countries to find that the scale of what they carried was incomprehensible to people whose war had been nothing like theirs. Also affects survivors of state torture in Chile, Argentina, Syria, and North Korea who return to societies where what was done to them in official facilities by official actors is politically contested or officially denied, meaning their testimony is not merely difficult to hear but actively threatening to social and political arrangements that require its suppression. Particularly devastating for child soldiers in Uganda, Sierra Leone, and the DRC who were both perpetrators and victims in ways that make their trauma narratively and morally illegible to communities structured around clean victim categories, survivors of sexual violence in conflict whose experience is unspeakable within cultural frameworks that locate the shame of the violation in the body of the person violated rather than the person who violated, and first responders, humanitarian workers, and forensic investigators whose professional exposure to mass atrocity is not recognized as trauma by institutions that required the exposure and now expect functional continuation as though the exposure did not occur.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The mechanisms here are not legislative but structural, built into the architecture of therapeutic, legal, and social systems that were designed to process trauma at an individual clinical scale and have no adequate framework for atrocity-scale experience. Refugee status determination systems require survivors to narrate their trauma coherently, chronologically, and credibly within interviews conducted by officials trained in legal assessment rather than trauma-informed reception, meaning the very neurological effects of extreme trauma, fragmented memory, non-linear recall, emotional dissociation, physical response during testimony, are interpreted as credibility problems rather than diagnostic evidence of what the person is describing. Asylum systems in the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia have formal credibility assessment criteria that systematically disadvantage survivors of the most extreme experiences because the most extreme experiences produce the most disrupted narration. Mental health systems in receiving countries offer therapeutic modalities developed for and validated on populations whose trauma occurred within functioning social contexts, whose support networks survived the event, and whose cultural frameworks for meaning-making are broadly compatible with Western clinical assumptions about selfhood, memory, and recovery. Survivors of collective atrocity whose identity, meaning, and psychological survival depend on communal rather than individual frameworks of sense-making are offered individual therapy. Survivors whose trauma is inseparable from political and historical context are offered clinical depoliticization. Legal systems that theoretically provide accountability for atrocity through international criminal tribunals require survivors to testify in processes that take decades, produce verdicts for a fraction of perpetrators, and offer no mechanism for the witness to be received as a full human being rather than an evidentiary instrument. Truth and reconciliation processes, where they exist, ask survivors to narrate publicly in formats designed for political rather than human purposes, and offer in return an official record that documents what happened without providing any structure for what to do with having survived it.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A Yazidi woman who was held by ISIS for two years, sold multiple times, and witnessed things that do not have civilian equivalents in the experience of anyone around her, is resettled in Germany or Canada or the United Kingdom. She is given an apartment, language classes, and a referral to a therapist who has a twelve week evidence-based trauma protocol and genuine care and no framework adequate to what this woman is carrying. The therapist has been trained on PTSD presentations from car accidents, childhood abuse, and combat exposure. What this woman experienced has no clinical category that captures it completely. The therapist does her best. The woman sits in the room and understands, with the clarity that extreme experience sometimes produces, that the person across from her cannot hold what she is about to say, not because the therapist is inadequate but because what she is about to say exceeds the holding capacity of any individual who was not there. She narrates a portion of it. She watches the therapist's face do the thing that faces do when they encounter the boundary of what they can receive. She stops. She has learned to stop at that boundary because continuing past it means being alone with the full weight of what she survived while also managing the person she was supposed to be helped by. She leaves the session having performed a edited version of her experience for an audience of one who could not hold the unedited version, and returns to an apartment in a city where no one on the street has any idea what she contains. A Rwandan survivor in Kigali lives among people who were perpetrators, neighbors of perpetrators, children of perpetrators, and people who have been through a national reconciliation process designed to make continued coexistence possible, which required the social suppression of the full weight of survivor testimony as a condition of political function. He cannot speak completely in the place where the thing happened because completeness is socially destabilizing. He cannot speak completely in diaspora because diaspora does not have the context to receive it. He cannot speak completely in therapy because therapy individualizes what was a collective annihilation. He exists in a permanent partial disclosure, releasing small amounts of the weight into conversations that can hold small amounts, carrying the remainder in a solitude that is not chosen but structural, produced by the gap between what he survived and what any available human context can witness. The research literature calls this secondary wounding, the additional injury produced not by the original event but by the failure of subsequent human contact to adequately receive it. The term is accurate and insufficient. It names the mechanism without conveying that for some survivors the secondary wounding is ongoing and total and constitutes the permanent condition of their life after survival, which is that they are alive and they are alone with it and the aloneness is not something that more therapy or more time or more well-meaning human contact will resolve because it is structural, produced by the absolute size of what they carry relative to the absolute limit of what any person who was not there can hold.

—

Nobody here understands me, my friends, my colleagues, not even my therapist. Nobody understand what I have gone through in Fur, it’s been 3 years nearly since I lost them, my own children who were fighting to breathe while they were hanged and I couldn’t help them just could watch and hear them calling me. What should I do?

65. Afghan Hazara person in Pakistan who faces ethnic persecution and cannot return to Afghanistan and has no legal status in Pakistan.
Affected Groups: Afghan Hazaras in Pakistan, concentrated most densely in Quetta in Balochistan and in Karachi, numbering in the hundreds of thousands and representing a population that is simultaneously persecuted in their country of origin by Taliban governance that has historically treated Hazaras as a target population for systematic elimination, and unprotected in their country of refuge by a Pakistani state that has never ratified the 1951 Refugee Convention and therefore operates no formal legal framework recognizing refugee status as a domestic legal category producing enforceable rights. Particularly devastating for Hazaras who fled Afghanistan after the Taliban's return to power in 2021 and who join a community that has been present in Quetta for decades and has experienced recurrent mass casualty attacks by Lashkar-e-Jhangvi and affiliated sectarian organizations targeting Hazara neighborhoods, markets, mosques, and snooker halls with a consistency and impunity that human rights organizations have documented as persecution meeting the legal threshold of crimes against humanity. Also acutely affects Hazara women whose educational and professional lives were already foreclosed by Taliban governance in Afghanistan and who arrive in Pakistan to find that their legal invisibility there forecloses the reconstruction of those lives in a different direction, Hazara men whose visible ethnic features, the particular physiognomy that makes Hazaras identifiable to persecutors in both countries, make moving through Pakistani cities a daily physical risk that documentation would not fully resolve but whose absence makes unresolvable, and the generation of Hazara children born in Pakistan who have no citizenship in any country, no passport from any state, and no legal existence in the national framework of the place where they have spent their entire lives.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: Pakistan's non-ratification of the 1951 Refugee Convention and its 1967 Protocol means that no domestic legal category of refugee exists that produces enforceable rights to residence, work, education, healthcare, or protection from refoulement. UNHCR operates in Pakistan under a memorandum of understanding with the government and issues Proof of Registration cards to registered Afghan refugees, but registration has been frozen, restricted, or administratively inaccessible at various points, meaning a significant portion of the Hazara population in Pakistan has neither Pakistani legal status nor UNHCR registration and exists in a complete legal vacuum where no institutional actor has a formal obligation toward them. Those who do hold UNHCR registration hold a document that the Pakistani state is not legally bound to honor and that does not prevent detention, deportation, or refoulement as a matter of enforceable right but only as a matter of administrative practice that varies by political context and has been suspended during periods of Pakistan-Afghanistan diplomatic tension or domestic political pressure around migration. The Pakistani government has conducted periodic mass deportation operations targeting unregistered Afghans, operations that do not distinguish between economic migrants and people fleeing targeted persecution, and that return Hazaras to a Taliban-governed Afghanistan where their ethnic and sectarian identity places them at documented risk of detention, forced disappearance, and execution. Employment without legal status exposes Hazaras to exploitation by employers who correctly calculate that a worker who cannot report to labor authorities has no floor on the conditions they can be made to accept. Children without documentation cannot enroll in Pakistani state schools in most provinces, and the community schools established within Hazara enclaves in Quetta operate without state recognition, meaning the education they provide produces no credential legible to any system the child might later try to enter. Movement outside Hazara neighborhoods in Quetta is a security calculation as well as a legal one, as Hazara men in particular have been targeted in targeted killings on roads leading out of their enclaves, producing a situation of de facto enclosure where the community is geographically confined by violence in a city where they have no legal right to be.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A Hazara man in Quetta has not left his neighborhood in four months. The road to the market where he used to work was the site of a targeted killing three months ago. The victim looked like him because the victim was Hazara and the targeting is ethnic and the faces are recognizable to the people doing the targeting. He has no Pakistani identity document. He has no Afghan document that would help him in Pakistan. He has a UNHCR card that he carries because it is the only piece of institutional recognition he possesses and because he has been told it offers some protection and because he does not entirely believe this but has nothing else to carry. His children have not been in school for two years. The community school in the enclave closed when the teacher left for Europe on a resettlement case that came through after seven years of waiting. His own resettlement application has been pending for four years. UNHCR's resettlement referral system operates on timelines that bear no relationship to the urgency of the situation on the ground, processing cases across years during which the situation generating the cases continues to produce casualties. He cannot return to Afghanistan because the Taliban's governance of Hazara regions has produced documented patterns of land seizure, arbitrary detention, and extrajudicial killing of Hazara men that make return not a risk calculation but a near certainty of harm. He cannot integrate in Pakistan because integration requires legal status he cannot obtain in a country that has not created a legal category for what he is. He cannot move forward on resettlement because resettlement moves on its own timeline in offices in Islamabad and Geneva that process his file as a case number while he lives his file as a life. He exists in a three-sided enclosure where every exit is sealed by a different combination of law, violence, and bureaucratic time, in a neighborhood in a city in a country that does not recognize him, waiting for a process he cannot accelerate, for a decision made by people who will never meet him, about whether he is sufficiently endangered to deserve the safety he is already not receiving.

66. Person from Tuvalu whose island is disappearing under rising sea levels and who is being told to migrate but has no country that will take them with full rights.
Affected Groups: The approximately 11,000 citizens of Tuvalu, a Pacific Island nation composed of nine low-lying atolls with a maximum elevation of approximately four meters above sea level, facing existential territorial dissolution within the lifetimes of people currently alive, and the broader category of climate-displaced persons from Kiribati, the Marshall Islands, and low-lying coastal and delta communities in Bangladesh, Vietnam, and the Maldives who face the same structural problem of displacement without a legal category adequate to their situation. Particularly devastating for elder Tuvaluans whose entire identity, cosmology, and sense of self is inseparable from specific land, ocean, and place in ways that relocation to a suburban neighborhood in Fiji or New Zealand does not preserve and cannot replicate, for communities whose collective land tenure systems, customary governance structures, and inter-generational relationships to territory have no equivalent in the individual property and citizenship frameworks of receiving countries, for those whose displacement is not yet complete meaning they exist in a permanent anticipatory grief for a loss that is ongoing and incremental rather than discrete and datable, and for the generation of children being raised knowing that the place their identity is rooted in will not exist in the form they know it for the duration of their lives. Also acutely affects the question of nationhood itself, as Tuvalu faces the historically unprecedented situation of a state potentially ceasing to exist as a physical territory while its people and government continue to exist, a situation for which international law has no precedent, no framework, and no agreed solution.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The 1951 Refugee Convention defines a refugee as a person fleeing persecution on the grounds of race, religion, nationality, political opinion, or membership of a particular social group, a definition that was written in the aftermath of World War Two to address state-sponsored persecution and that does not include climate displacement, environmental destruction, or the disappearance of a person's country beneath rising seas as a recognized ground for protection. No subsequent international legal instrument has created a binding legal category of climate refugee or environmental refugee that produces enforceable rights to admission, residence, or citizenship in another state. The Nansen Initiative and its successor the Platform on Disaster Displacement produced non-binding frameworks that acknowledge the protection gap without closing it. New Zealand's specific Pacific Access Category visa pathway offers a limited number of Tuvaluan nationals annual entry but caps the number at 75 households per year, requires applicants to have a job offer in New Zealand before applying, meet English language requirements, and meet health and character criteria, meaning the pathway is real and radically insufficient relative to the scale of the need and structured around individual economic contribution rather than collective existential displacement. The Falepili Union agreement signed between Tuvalu and Australia in 2023 creates a specific mobility pathway for Tuvaluans to live, study, and work in Australia, representing the most substantive bilateral response to climate displacement yet negotiated, but contains provisions giving Australia a say over Tuvalu's external agreements that critics have characterized as a sovereignty exchange, meaning the price of a partial solution to physical displacement is a partial surrender of the political independence that makes Tuvalu a state worth preserving. Citizenship law in virtually every potential receiving country is structured around individual naturalization pathways that dissolve collective identity into individual legal status, meaning a Tuvaluan who becomes a New Zealand or Australian citizen gains individual rights in a new country and simultaneously loses the legal expression of membership in a community whose collective existence has no equivalent legal vessel in the receiving country's framework.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A Tuvaluan family watches the king tide flood the cemetery where their grandparents are buried, the taro pits that their food sovereignty depended on, the land boundary markers that encoded four generations of family history in their physical placement. They are told by their government, by international organizations, by well-meaning foreign journalists, that they must plan to leave. They apply through the New Zealand Pacific Access Category. The father does not have a job offer in New Zealand because he has never been to New Zealand and knows no one there and the pathway requires the outcome of successful migration as a precondition of being permitted to migrate. The English language requirement scores them just below the threshold. They apply again the following year. The atoll's freshwater lens, the thin layer of fresh water that sits above seawater in the coral substrate and that the community drinks from, has been increasingly salinized by storm surges and tidal intrusion. The food they grow tastes of salt. The application is pending. A young Tuvaluan woman who relocated to Fiji under an earlier mobility arrangement lives in a suburb of Suva with no customary land rights in Fiji, no political rights as a non-citizen, and a relationship to place that Fiji's land tenure system, which reserves customary land for indigenous Fijians, structurally cannot accommodate. She is not a refugee because climate displacement is not a refugee ground. She is not an immigrant in the conventional sense because she did not choose to move for opportunity but because her country is becoming uninhabitable. She is not stateless because Tuvalu still legally exists and she still holds Tuvaluan citizenship in a state whose physical territory is disappearing beneath the ocean at a rate that international climate negotiations have failed to prevent and international law has failed to adequately address. She exists in a legal category that does not yet have a name, displaced by a process that has been documented for decades, by emissions produced overwhelmingly by countries whose per capita contribution to atmospheric carbon is hundreds of times greater than hers, without any binding legal mechanism that translates that disproportion into an obligation of those countries toward her. The sea is not a persecutor within the meaning of the 1951 Convention. It has no political opinion about Tuvaluans. It is simply rising, incrementally, on a timeline set by industrial decisions made in countries that will not be underwater, toward an outcome that was predictable and predicted and insufficiently prevented, and the people in its path have no legal instrument adequate to the size of what is happening to them.

67. Woman in Afghanistan under the Taliban who was a doctor and is now not allowed to leave her house without a male guardian.
Affected Groups: Afghan women and girls across all socioeconomic backgrounds under Taliban governance reinstated in August 2021, representing a population of approximately 14 million females whose legal personhood has been systematically dismantled through a sequence of edicts that have no parallel in the contemporary world in the speed and totality of their application. Most acutely affects professional women, including the estimated 3,000 female physicians who constituted a critical portion of Afghanistan's healthcare workforce, female judges, lawyers, teachers, engineers, and civil servants whose professional identities, institutional positions, and economic independence were annihilated by decree rather than eroded gradually, women in urban centers like Kabul, Herat, and Mazar-i-Sharif where relative liberalization over twenty years had produced a generation with professional formation, educational attainment, and social expectations that the Taliban's return extinguished in weeks, and girls currently between the ages of twelve and twenty-two who have been denied secondary and university education during the years their cognitive and professional formation would have occurred, producing a gap that no future policy reversal will restore because the years are not recoverable. Also particularly devastating for women from ethnic minority communities including Hazara, Tajik, and Uzbek women who face compounded persecution combining gender-based restriction with ethnic targeting, women who worked with international organizations or the former government and face security risk on top of movement restriction, and widows and women heading households without a male mahram whose ability to access food, healthcare, and economic survival is directly contingent on a male guardian they do not have.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The Taliban's governance framework operates through a series of edicts issued by the Supreme Leader and enforced through the Ministry for the Propagation of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice, reconstituted from its previous iteration and given expanded enforcement authority over public space, dress, movement, employment, and education. The mahram requirement, mandating that women be accompanied by a male blood relative for any movement outside the home, is not a social norm operating through informal pressure but an enforced legal requirement with documented consequences for violation including detention, beating, and the punishment of the male guardian held responsible for the woman's non-compliance. The cumulative architecture of Taliban edicts has banned women from secondary and university education, banned women from employment in Afghan and international NGOs, banned women from employment in the UN, banned women from parks, gyms, public baths, and open spaces, banned women from traveling more than 72 kilometers without a mahram, and most recently banned women from medical education, closing the pipeline that would have replaced the female physicians whose work the Taliban simultaneously requires because male physicians cannot treat female patients under their own gender segregation rules, producing a self-consuming policy contradiction whose resolution is the suffering of Afghan women who die of treatable conditions because no gender-compliant care pathway exists. International legal mechanisms including UN Security Council resolutions, ICC preliminary examinations into gender persecution as a crime against humanity, and diplomatic pressure from every major international actor have produced no material change in Taliban governance of women's lives, in part because the Taliban government is not internationally recognized and therefore not subject to treaty obligations, and in part because the leverage available to international actors has been applied at a threshold the Taliban has consistently demonstrated it will not respond to.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A woman who completed medical school under the previous government, who specialized in obstetrics because Afghan women were dying in childbirth at rates that a trained female physician could address, who built a practice, saved lives, trained younger doctors, and understood her work as both a profession and a form of service to women whose options were always constrained, woke up in August 2021 to a series of changes that arrived faster than her capacity to process them. She cannot go to her clinic without a mahram. Her brother accompanies her for the first weeks. Then the clinic is told female staff cannot work. Then the clinic closes. She is at home. She has been at home for three years. She has medical knowledge that is deteriorating from disuse, that women in her city are dying for lack of, that she spent a decade acquiring, and she cannot apply it because the distance between her house and the clinic where it is needed is a public street that she cannot walk without a male relative who is available and willing to accompany her every day at every hour her patients need her. A maternal patient who would have been her patient hemorrhages after delivery attended by an underqualified male practitioner who should not have been in the room under Taliban gender rules but was the only option because the female physician who should have been there is at home. A girl of fourteen who would have been her student sits at home where school used to be, in the years when her mind is most capable of formation, watching those years pass without the content that was supposed to fill them. The physician applies for resettlement through international humanitarian pathways. The pathways are oversubscribed by a factor that means years of waiting. She applies for a visa to a neighboring country to continue practicing. The visa requires documentation her bank can no longer easily provide because Afghanistan's banking system has partially collapsed under sanctions. She applies through a professional diaspora network that helps female Afghan physicians relocate. The process requires a job offer from a receiving institution. The receiving institutions have limited positions. She waits. She is forty-one years old and she is waiting in a house in a city where women are dying of conditions she knows how to treat, separated from those women by a door she cannot open without a permission structure that has decided her knowledge, her decade of training, her professional identity, and her physical autonomy all belong to a category of things women in Afghanistan are no longer permitted to have.

68. Sex worker in a country where it is criminalized trying to access insurance
Affected Groups: Sex workers across criminalized and partially criminalized jurisdictions globally, most acutely in the United States where federal and state law criminalizes most forms of sex work, in Southeast Asia including Thailand, the Philippines, and Indonesia where enforcement is inconsistent but criminalization is formal and stigma is absolute, in Latin America including Mexico, Brazil, and Colombia where legal frameworks vary by region but criminalization of clients, third parties, or the work itself creates structural exposure regardless of the worker's own legal status, and in countries operating under Nordic model legislation including Sweden, Norway, Iceland, Canada, and Ireland where the purchase but not sale of sex is criminalized, a legal distinction that does not protect workers from the displacement into more dangerous working conditions that criminalization of clients produces. Particularly devastating for transgender women who constitute a disproportionate share of street-based sex workers across multiple geographies and who face compounded discrimination at every institutional interface combining transphobia with sex work stigma, for undocumented migrant sex workers whose immigration status and work status simultaneously expose them to enforcement from multiple directions, for women of color in the United States for whom racialized policing intersects with sex work criminalization to produce arrest and incarceration rates far exceeding those of white workers doing equivalent work, for indoor workers whose access to digital platforms was curtailed by FOSTA-SESTA legislation pushing work onto streets where violence and health risk is demonstrably higher, and for workers managing chronic health conditions including HIV whose treatment access runs through healthcare systems that their work status makes dangerous to engage with honestly.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: Insurance systems in criminalized contexts present sex workers with a structural impossibility at the income verification stage. Health insurance through employer-based systems requires formal employment that sex work cannot produce in criminalized jurisdictions. Marketplace insurance under the Affordable Care Act in the United States requires income documentation for subsidy calculation, and income documentation requires either formal employment records or tax filings that accurately represent income source, both of which expose workers to legal risk because accurately documenting sex work income is a potential self-incrimination event depending on jurisdiction and because inaccurately documenting it as something else is tax fraud. Private health insurance applications ask occupational questions whose accurate answer flags the applicant in underwriting systems that use occupation as a risk and moral hazard variable, meaning honest disclosure produces denial or prohibitive premium loading while dishonest disclosure produces policy voidance at the claim stage when the truth is most consequential. Workers compensation does not exist for workers with no formal employment relationship. Disability insurance requires documented earned income from legitimate employment. Life insurance underwriting uses occupation as a mortality risk variable and sex work as a categorical exclusion in many underwriting guidelines, meaning a worker attempting to provide for dependents in the event of her death is structurally excluded from the primary instrument available for that purpose. FOSTA-SESTA, passed in the United States in 2018 with stated intent to combat sex trafficking, eliminated online platforms sex workers used to screen clients and communicate safety information, pushing workers toward street-based work and reducing their ability to negotiate conditions, with documented increases in violence following the legislation, while simultaneously making the digital financial infrastructure sex workers used to transact, PayPal, Venmo, Square, inaccessible through those platforms' terms of service updates following the legislation, meaning banking and financial service access contracted at the same moment physical safety conditions deteriorated.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A woman in Chicago or Houston or Atlanta who has been doing indoor sex work for six years, who screens clients carefully, who has built a regular clientele, who manages her work with the professionalism of someone who understands it as work, attempts to obtain health insurance. She cannot access employer-based insurance because she has no employer. She goes to the ACA marketplace. The subsidy calculation requires income documentation. She has cash income she has not reported because reporting it accurately would document a criminal act and reporting it inaccurately would be fraud. She estimates an income low enough to avoid documentation scrutiny and high enough to obtain subsidized coverage. The coverage she can afford has a deductible she cannot meet from documented funds without triggering questions about income source she cannot answer. She develops a health condition, the specific nature of which is less important than the fact that it is the kind of condition that people with insurance manage routinely and people without it manage until it becomes an emergency. She goes to a clinic that serves uninsured patients. The intake form asks her occupation. She writes self-employed. The clinician asks what kind. She says consulting. The clinician who she has been honest with before, in a moment of trust, receives the information and changes in the way that people who are not trained in non-judgmental care change, and the care she receives in the remainder of the appointment is different from the care she would have received had she said something else. She leaves with a prescription she can partially fill. She does not return. A transgender woman doing street-based work in New Orleans after FOSTA-SESTA removed the platforms she used to screen clients is injured by a client who correctly calculated that she has no recourse available to her that does not expose her to arrest. She goes to the emergency room. EMTALA covers her stabilization. The social worker who conducts the intake assessment files a report that triggers a process she did not consent to and cannot control. She is discharged without the follow-up care her injury requires and without the safety planning that her situation requires and back into the conditions that produced the injury because no institutional actor in the system she just passed through had both the mandate and the capacity to address those conditions in their totality. She did not seek insurance before the injury because seeking insurance required documentation she could not produce. She cannot seek it after because the injury has now produced a pre-existing condition that, in the private insurance market outside ACA protections, would have been a denial. She is uninsured and injured and she goes back to work because going back to work is the only financial option available to someone whose work cannot be documented, whose injury cannot be compensated, and whose insurance cannot be obtained through any pathway that does not require her to be something other than what she is.
