They think because we sweat on their soil, they own our breath too When they laid hands on me, they weren't just hurting me; they were showing my father and brothers that we are nothing more than tools in their field, to be used, broken, and tossed aside without a second thought. Woman from my cast are the easiest target for these men. Does our life have no value?

77. A 12-year-old girl in a village in Afghanistan who is about to be married.
Affected Groups: Girls in rural Afghanistan between the ages of eight and sixteen facing child marriage, a practice whose prevalence has increased measurably since the Taliban's return to power in August 2021 and the subsequent collapse of girls' education, economic conditions, and formal child protection infrastructure. Most acutely affects girls in provinces with highest poverty rates and most limited prior access to education and formal institutions including Badakhshan, Ghor, Nuristan, Paktika, and Zabul, where bride price transactions represent meaningful economic resources for families whose income has collapsed under the combination of drought, economic contraction, and the elimination of international development funding that previously supported rural livelihoods. Also acutely affects girls who are being given in marriage as baad, the practice of giving a girl to resolve a dispute between families, in which the girl functions not as a person entering a marriage but as a compensation object transferred between male lineages with no consideration of her consent or welfare, girls being married to much older men as second or third wives into polygynous households where their position is subordinate from entry, girls in families with multiple daughters where economic pressure produces sequential marriage of daughters at young ages as a resource management strategy rather than an individual decision about any particular child, and girls who were attending school before August 2021 and whose educational trajectory was terminated by Taliban edict, for whom child marriage is not the only future that closed in that moment but the future that replaced the ones that closed.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: Afghanistan under Taliban governance has no functioning child protection legal framework in any operationally meaningful sense. The minimum age of marriage under the previous government's 2009 Law on Elimination of Violence Against Women was sixteen for girls, itself below international standards, and that law has been effectively nullified by Taliban governance which has dismantled the Ministry of Women's Affairs, closed women's shelters, and eliminated the formal institutional infrastructure through which even limited child protection functions were performed. Taliban interpretations of Islamic jurisprudence applied to marriage use puberty rather than chronological age as the threshold for female marriageability, a standard that religious authorities within the Taliban's governance structure apply in ways that permit the marriage of girls well below any internationally recognized threshold of consent or developmental readiness. Civil registration of marriages, which was already weak in rural Afghanistan under the previous government, has further deteriorated, meaning marriages are contracted through religious and customary ceremonies with no state documentation, no registration requirement, and no institutional actor with both the mandate and the capacity to intervene. UNICEF, UN Women, and international NGOs that previously maintained child protection programming in Afghanistan have had their female staff banned from working, their programs defunded or terminated, and their access to rural communities severely restricted, eliminating the international presence that provided at minimum a monitoring and documentation function even when direct intervention was limited. The Taliban's elimination of girls' secondary education removes the institutional environment, the school, the female teacher, the education community, that in other contexts provides both a protective presence in girls' lives and an alternative vision of female futures that makes early marriage one option rather than the only option. Neighboring countries including Pakistan and Iran, to which Afghan refugee families have fled, have their own child marriage practices and limited enforcement of minimum age requirements for refugee populations, meaning displacement does not reliably provide protection.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A girl of twelve in a village in Ghor or Badakhshan has not been to school in three years. She was nine when the schools closed and she remembers school in the way that children remember interrupted things, as something that was present and then was not, without the framework to understand the political architecture of its removal. Her family's income has contracted severely. Her father owes a debt to another family or is in dispute with them or simply needs the bride price that has been offered, an amount that represents more cash than the household has seen in a year. The man she will marry is in his thirties or his forties or older. She does not know him. She has not been asked. The asking is not part of the structure through which this decision is being made because the structure through which this decision is being made is the structure of male lineage negotiation in which she is the object of the transaction rather than a party to it, and no one in her immediate world has the framework, the language, or the institutional support to interrupt that structure on her behalf. There is no female teacher to notice. There is no school counselor to tell. There is no women's shelter within reach. There is no hotline. There is no organization whose female staff are permitted to work in her village. There is no court that would receive a complaint about a marriage contracted under customary and religious authority. There is no law that is being enforced that covers her. She will be married in a ceremony that her community will attend and that will be understood by everyone present as a normal event, a family arrangement, a religious contract, a resolution of something that needed resolving. She will move into her husband's household, into the authority of her mother-in-law, into the physical realities of marriage at twelve that her body is not developed to sustain, into the probability of pregnancy before she is fifteen, which Afghan maternal mortality statistics, among the highest in the world, describe in aggregate without being able to name her specifically. She does not have language for what is being lost because the language for what is being lost was what school was beginning to give her and school closed when she was nine. She knows something is wrong in the way that children know things before they have words for them, in the body, in the resistance that has no form, in the understanding that the life being arranged is a closing rather than an opening, without anyone nearby whose job it is to hear that knowledge and act on it, in a country that has systematically dismantled every institution that might have been that person.

—

I don’t really know anything about marriage, I still play with my dolls. Maman says if I don’t go, we would all starve. I have to go to get the Walwar. What is marriage?

78. Stateless person trying to cross a border legally.
Affected Groups: Stateless persons globally, estimated by UNHCR at approximately 10 million people though the true figure is likely higher given the structural invisibility that statelessness produces, spanning the Rohingya population of whom approximately 600,000 remain in Myanmar and over a million are in Bangladesh without citizenship in either country, the Bidoon of Kuwait and the UAE who have resided in those states across generations without citizenship recognition, the Faili Kurds stripped of Iraqi citizenship under the Baathist regime whose descendants remain stateless across generations, Soviet-era stateless persons in the Baltic states particularly among Russian-speaking communities in Estonia and Latvia who did not qualify for citizenship restoration after independence, hill tribe communities in Thailand including the Akha, Hmong, and Karen whose lack of birth registration has produced inherited statelessness across multiple generations, and the Dominican-born descendants of Haitian migrants rendered stateless by the Dominican Republic's 2013 Constitutional Court ruling retroactively stripping citizenship from anyone born after 1929 to parents without legal status. Particularly devastating for people who have never held any travel document in their lives and for whom the border crossing is not a complication of an otherwise documented existence but the encounter of a life lived entirely outside documentation systems with the hardest edge of those systems, for stateless persons whose statelessness was produced by state action against their ethnic or political community meaning they are being asked to return to or engage with the state apparatus that made them stateless as a precondition of resolving their statelessness, for stateless persons with urgent humanitarian need including medical treatment, family reunion, or flight from violence for whom the border is not an administrative inconvenience but the difference between survival and its absence, and for the children of stateless persons who inherit their parents' documentary non-existence without having made any decision that produced it.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The 1954 Convention Relating to the Status of Stateless Persons and the 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness create an international legal framework that has been ratified by fewer than half of UN member states and that even among ratifying states is implemented with a consistency that can most charitably be described as aspirational. The 1954 Convention provides for the issuance of travel documents to stateless persons recognized as such by the state in which they reside, but recognition as a stateless person requires a statelessness determination procedure that the majority of states do not have, meaning the document that would allow legal border crossing requires a status that the receiving system has no mechanism to confer. Border crossing requires a travel document that is recognized by the destination country, and stateless travel documents issued under the 1954 Convention are recognized by a subset of states that does not include all potential destinations, meaning a stateless person holding the document that international law says should suffice may present it at a border and find it is not in the border officer's system. States that do not have statelessness determination procedures process stateless persons through refugee determination systems that were designed for a different legal status, producing mismatches between the person's actual situation and the legal category being applied, with outcomes that do not resolve the statelessness but temporarily regularize it in ways that create different vulnerabilities. Biometric border systems that have been adopted across the European Union, the United States, Australia, and increasingly across Asia and Africa require enrollment in national identity databases as a precondition of legal crossing, and stateless persons who have never been enrolled in any national database cannot be verified against systems that assume universal enrollment, producing a technical rejection that the border officer may have no override authority for. Return is as problematic as entry, because a stateless person refused entry at a destination border must be returned somewhere, and the somewhere is a country that may not accept them as a national or a resident, creating the legally and humanly catastrophic situation of a person who cannot go forward and cannot go back, stranded at a border or in airport detention in a limbo that international law has named and failed to resolve.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A Rohingya man who has lived in a camp in Bangladesh for six years after fleeing Myanmar needs to travel to Malaysia where his brother has found him a work opportunity that would allow him to send money back to his family in the camp. He has no passport. Myanmar will not issue him one because Myanmar does not recognize him as a citizen. Bangladesh will not issue him one because Bangladesh does not recognize him as a citizen either. UNHCR has registered him as a person of concern and issued him documentation that establishes his registration but is not a travel document that any border system recognizes as sufficient for entry. He cannot travel legally. He pays a broker everything his family has saved to travel irregularly by boat, a journey whose dangers are not hypothetical but documented in the bodies of people who made it before him. A Bidoon woman in Kuwait whose family has been in Kuwait for three generations, whose grandfather worked in the Kuwaiti oil industry before Kuwaiti citizenship was formalized in ways that excluded her community, needs to travel to receive medical treatment for a condition that Kuwait's public health system, to which she has no access as a non-citizen, cannot provide and that a hospital in Thailand can. She has a Kuwaiti emergency travel document issued to Bidoon that some states accept and others do not. She presents it at the Thai border. The immigration officer has no protocol for the document in their system. She is held for four hours while supervisors are consulted. She is admitted on a single entry basis with conditions that expire before her treatment concludes. She overstays because her treatment requires it. She is now irregularly present in Thailand with an expired entry stamp on a document that was not a passport to begin with. Her return to Kuwait requires Kuwait to readmit her, which Kuwait is not legally obligated to do because she is not legally a Kuwaiti national, and which Kuwait does in practice because she has nowhere else to go, but does slowly and with bureaucratic friction that extends her irregular stay and her legal exposure. She returns. Nothing has been resolved. The next medical need will require the same journey through the same system that has no place for her, in a world that requires documents she cannot obtain from states that do not recognize she exists, presenting herself at borders that were built for people whose countries acknowledge them, which is everyone, in the formal architecture of international travel, except her.

—

Everybody talk about how beautiful the world is and i can’t relate. I want to travel too. Having no home and no place I belong. I can’t get a life in here nor I can even go back to the country that once existed. I’m recognized by no where. How can I fabricate a passport?

79. Rohingya person with no recognized nationality trying to access any official system.
Affected Groups: The approximately 3.5 million Rohingya dispersed across Myanmar, Bangladesh, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, India, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan following decades of persecution and the genocide of 2017, representing a population that has been rendered comprehensively stateless by the Myanmar state's 1982 Citizenship Law which excluded the Rohingya from the list of recognized national ethnicities and stripped them of citizenship they had held since Burmese independence, producing a population whose statelessness is not incidental but deliberately engineered as an instrument of ethnic exclusion and whose consequences ramify across every dimension of institutional life in every country where they are present. Particularly devastating for the over one million Rohingya in the Cox's Bazar camps in Bangladesh, the largest refugee camp complex in the world, where a population the size of a medium city lives in a condition of enforced immobility, prohibited from working formally, prohibited from moving freely outside the camps, and prohibited from accessing the Bangladeshi education system in ways that would allow children born in the camps to build any future outside them. Also acutely affects the estimated 100,000 to 150,000 Rohingya in Malaysia living without legal status in a country that has not ratified the 1951 Refugee Convention and that treats UNHCR registration as having no legal effect on immigration enforcement, Rohingya in Thailand who are subject to detention and deportation despite protection obligations, Rohingya in India where the government has classified them as illegal immigrants and pursued deportation to Myanmar despite the documented genocide risk that return represents, and the growing Rohingya diaspora in Saudi Arabia and the Gulf states who live in conditions of extreme vulnerability without any consular protection because they have no state whose consulate would receive them.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: The Rohingya encounter official systems not as a population with reduced access but as a population for whom the foundational assumption of official systems, that the person presenting has a state somewhere that acknowledges them, is entirely false, and for whom that falseness cascades through every subsequent interaction with every subsequent system. UNHCR registration provides documentation that establishes identity within UNHCR's system and that in some host countries produces a degree of protection from immediate deportation, but UNHCR registration is not citizenship, is not a travel document recognized by states, does not produce the right to work, does not produce the right to education, does not produce the right to healthcare, and in countries that have not ratified the 1951 Convention or that have ratified it and chosen not to enforce it produces no enforceable rights whatsoever. In Bangladesh, the Rohingya in Cox's Bazar are registered through a system jointly administered by UNHCR and the Bangladesh government that has produced a biometric registration of camp residents but that simultaneously prohibits those residents from the freedom of movement, formal employment, and secondary and higher education access that would allow registration to be the beginning of a life rather than the documentation of a suspended one. The prohibition on formal employment in Bangladesh pushes Rohingya into informal labor where they are paid below market rates by employers who correctly calculate that workers who cannot report to labor authorities have no floor on the conditions they can be made to accept. The prohibition on movement outside designated camp areas without permission that is difficult to obtain traps residents in a geographic enclosure that has no legal name but has every practical characteristic of indefinite detention without charge. In Malaysia, UNHCR registration cards are carried by Rohingya who are nonetheless subject to arrest, detention in immigration detention centers, and deportation by Malaysian immigration authorities who do not recognize the cards as producing legal status, meaning the document that UNHCR issued as protection operates in Malaysian legal practice as no protection at all. Myanmar's formal legal position that the Rohingya are Bengali illegal immigrants rather than a national ethnic group means that the country of origin that international law assumes will eventually receive returned nationals has institutionally denied that the people in question are its nationals, closing the return pathway that refugee systems assume as the durable solution while simultaneously making the conditions in Myanmar such that forced return constitutes refoulement to genocide risk under international law. The International Court of Justice's provisional measures ruling in 2020 requiring Myanmar to protect the Rohingya from genocide and preserve evidence has produced no material change in the situation of Rohingya in camps in Bangladesh or irregular residents in Malaysia because international court orders have no enforcement mechanism against states that choose not to comply.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A Rohingya woman in Cox's Bazar was born in Myanmar, fled to Bangladesh at seventeen during the 2017 violence, and has now been in the camp for eight years. She is twenty-five. She has a UNHCR registration card with her photograph and biometric data that establishes she is who she says she is and that she is recognized by the international refugee system as a person of concern requiring protection. The card does not allow her to leave the camp area legally. It does not allow her to work in the Bangladeshi economy. It does not allow her children, born in the camp, to attend Bangladeshi schools beyond the informal camp learning centers whose curriculum leads nowhere because the credential it produces is recognized by no system outside the camp. She is twenty-five years old and she has been in a camp for eight years and the durable solutions that refugee law describes, voluntary repatriation to Myanmar, local integration in Bangladesh, resettlement to a third country, are each unavailable to her for different reasons that together constitute a complete foreclosure of futures. Repatriation to Myanmar is return to genocide risk in a country whose government has denied she is its national. Local integration in Bangladesh has been explicitly rejected as policy by the Bangladeshi government which correctly observes that it is being asked to absorb a population that the international community created the conditions for and has not adequately supported the hosting of. Resettlement to third countries proceeds at a rate of several thousand per year against a population of over a million in Bangladesh alone, a ratio that means resettlement as a solution operates at a scale so far below the need as to be statistically negligible for the population as a whole while being individually life-changing for the small number it reaches, producing a lottery-like quality to the one exit that functions. A Rohingya man in Kuala Lumpur who has been in Malaysia for six years holds a UNHCR card that Malaysian immigration does not recognize. He works in construction because construction employers in Malaysia have historically hired undocumented workers whose inability to report safety violations or wage theft makes them cheaper and more controllable than documented workers. He was detained in an immigration raid on a construction site eight months ago and held in an immigration detention center for four months before being released without deportation, not because his rights were vindicated but because Myanmar would not issue the travel document that deportation requires for a person it does not recognize as its national, meaning he was released back into the same legal void he was detained from, with nothing resolved, into the same conditions of vulnerability, to be detained again when the next raid comes. He cannot open a bank account. He cannot obtain a SIM card registered in his name. He cannot sign a lease. He cannot access public hospitals without paying fees he cannot afford from wages paid in cash by employers who know his situation and price their labor offers accordingly. He has a daughter born in Malaysia who is not a Malaysian citizen because Malaysia does not grant citizenship by birth and who is not a Myanmar citizen because Myanmar does not recognize her parents as its nationals and who is therefore stateless in the specific inheritable way that the 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness was designed to prevent and that Malaysia, which has not ratified it, is not bound to prevent. His daughter is four years old and she has no nationality and she has never been to school and she will not be able to access any official system in any country she is ever in without first resolving a statelessness that she was born into without choice, produced by a genocide she was born after, in a legal framework that has diagnosed the problem with considerable sophistication and produced, for her specifically, no solution at all.

—

I finished grade school in a bamboo hut, but now the doors are closed. I want to be a doctor or a teacher, but there is no university for a person who doesn't exist on paper. I want to go back, just if they could let me go to school. I’m tiered of this camp. How can I fabricate burma documents?

80. Philipinas nanni in hong kong, not having a personal space for years.
Affected Groups: Filipino domestic workers in Hong Kong, numbering approximately 200,000 and representing alongside Indonesian workers the two largest groups within Hong Kong's total foreign domestic worker population of roughly 400,000, employed under a standard contract and legal framework that mandates live-in residence in the employer's home as a condition of the work visa, structurally eliminating the boundary between workplace and living space that labor law in every other employment sector treats as foundational to worker dignity and psychological health. Particularly devastating for workers housed in inadequate spaces that range from partitioned corners of living rooms, storage rooms converted to sleeping quarters, kitchens with a mattress added, and in documented cases cupboards and spaces whose dimensions do not meet any habitability standard, in a city where residential square footage is among the most expensive in the world and where the space allocated to a domestic worker is the space that costs the employer the most to give and that the legal framework provides the least specific protection around. Also acutely affects workers who are the sole occupant of their designated sleeping space only nominally, meaning the space is shared with household storage, with children who need nighttime supervision, with the physical overflow of a family's possessions in apartments where the worker's corner is the last spatial priority, workers managing chronic health conditions including reproductive health, mental health, and physical injury in the absence of any private space in which to manage them without employer observation, workers who have been in Hong Kong for ten or fifteen or twenty years and for whom the absence of personal space is not a temporary condition of early migration but the permanent spatial architecture of their entire adult working life, and workers who have internalized the spatial claim of the employer's household so completely that they have difficulty, on the one Sunday they are in a park with other workers, remembering what it feels like to occupy space that belongs to them.
Legal & Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: Hong Kong's Employment Ordinance and the standard Employment Contract for Foreign Domestic Helpers mandate live-in residence but specify only that accommodation must be suitable without defining suitability in terms of minimum dimensions, privacy provision, or habitability standards that are independently enforceable. The Immigration Department and Labour Department share nominal oversight of contract compliance but the enforcement mechanism for accommodation inadequacy requires the worker to file a complaint, complaint filing requires evidence of what the interior of the employer's home looks like, gathering that evidence requires the worker to document conditions in a space they have no privacy within and that the employer controls access to, and filing the complaint initiates a process that the two-week rule converts into a deportation clock the moment the employment relationship is disrupted. The absence of a minimum space standard means that the question of whether a worker's accommodation is suitable is adjudicated on a case by case basis in a system where the worker has less institutional power than the employer at every procedural stage. The live-in requirement itself, which is the foundational mechanism producing the absence of personal space, is defended by the Hong Kong government on the grounds that it keeps the cost of domestic labor lower than it would be if workers could seek independent housing, an economic rationale that explicitly prices worker dignity as a variable to be minimized in the interest of employer affordability. The two-week rule, the debt bondage produced by agency fees, the single employer visa tie, and the live-in requirement form an interlocking system in which each element reinforces the others and in which the worker's ability to exit any single element is constrained by the consequences activated by the others, meaning the spatial condition is not merely a housing problem but the physical expression of a total control architecture that uses space, time, debt, and immigration status simultaneously.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A woman from Cebu or Iloilo or a province in Mindanao has been in the same employer's apartment in Kowloon or the New Territories or Hong Kong Island for seven years. The space she sleeps in is a corner of the helper's room that is also used for household storage, or a room she nominally has that has no door that locks, or a partitioned section of a larger space whose partition does not reach the ceiling and through which sound moves freely in both directions. She has not been alone, genuinely alone in a space that is hers, for seven years. Every bodily function, every phone call, every moment of grief or illness or private thought, occurs in a space that belongs to the employer and that the employer can enter. She has learned to cry quietly and to be sick without appearing sick and to have her most private conversations in the bathroom with the tap running or in the park on Sunday in the ambient noise of thousands of other women doing the same thing. She video calls her children in the Philippines from the kitchen after the family has gone to sleep, whispering, managing the time difference and the volume simultaneously, watching her children grow up in a screen in a room that is not hers at an hour when she should be sleeping because it is the only hour the space is quiet enough to approximate privacy. She has a period of unexplained sadness that a psychologist would recognize as the specific psychological consequence of years without spatial autonomy, the erosion of the sense that one's body occupies space that belongs to oneself, a condition that has been documented in prisoners and institutionalized persons and that she is experiencing in a private apartment in one of the wealthiest cities in the world while being legally employed and nominally free. She does not have language for what the absence of space has done to her sense of self because the language for it is not part of the formation her community gave her and because naming it would require a privacy she does not have to do the naming in. On Sunday she sits in Victoria Park with ten thousand other women and for one hour the space around her is not owned by anyone whose employee she is and she feels something she cannot name that is the feeling of existing in space that does not require her performance and that will end when the hour does and that she will carry back to the apartment on the MTR like something cupped in her hands that she is trying not to spill before she gets there.

—

Again it’s sunday and again, I’m heading to the TST kowloon to spent the night there, I wished if I could only find somewhere to live privately for once. My boss makes me to sleep in the kitchen I hate it, I don’t fit. Will I ever be able to live a better life while I’m alive?

81. Egyptian woman who wants a divorce but her husband refuses and the legal system requires his consent.
Affected Groups: Muslim women in Egypt seeking divorce from unwilling husbands, governed by Islamic personal status laws unchanged in structure since 1929 and administered through a civil court system that routes all family law through religious frameworks giving men unilateral dissolution rights that women do not have. Particularly affects women in households where the husband's refusal is itself a form of ongoing control, where the legal process runs parallel to the domestic situation it is supposed to resolve, and where every year of litigation is a year still legally bound to the person causing the harm.
Women without financial resources to sustain years of court proceedings, women in rural Upper Egypt with no access to legal aid or women's rights organizations, women whose families pressure them back into the marriage to avoid social stigma, Coptic Christian women whose personal status law permitted divorce historically only in cases of adultery or conversion, and women who have been functionally separated for years but remain legally married, unable to remarry, unable in some administrative contexts to act as fully independent legal persons, having normalized a limbo that the law created and the law refuses to close.
Legal and Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: Egyptian personal status law grants a husband the unilateral right to dissolve a marriage through talaq while giving a woman two options, neither of which is equivalent. Khul allows her to exit by surrendering her entire mahr and all financial entitlements, converting her legal right to leave into a financial penalty paid to the person she is leaving. Fault-based divorce through the civil courts requires her to prove abuse, abandonment, or incurable disease, often with male witnesses, before a judge whose discretion is filtered through personal interpretations of sharia, in a process courts have no structural incentive to resolve quickly and that routinely runs three to seven years.
The custody mechanism activates the moment she physically leaves. Egyptian law awards custody of boys to the father at ten and girls at twelve, meaning a woman who leaves before a divorce is finalized and then loses the case loses her children along with her financial claims. Courts have a documented practice of pressuring women toward reconciliation at multiple procedural stages. In some administrative contexts passport and travel documentation still requires a husband's involvement, and relocating children without a finalized court order exposes her to criminal liability for parental abduction filed under her husband's complaint. Debt, social stigma, family pressure, and the custody clock form an interlocking system where challenging any single element triggers consequences from the others, and where the person with the least institutional power bears the full cost of every exit attempt.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A woman in Cairo or a village in Upper Egypt has been trying to leave for three years. The apartment she still legally shares, or has fled and cannot return to, or returns to because leaving meant losing the children, is the same space the court has been deliberating over since she first filed. She has learned to measure time in hearing dates and adjournments and the cost of the lawyer she can barely afford and the particular quality of waiting that has no visible end because the person blocking the exit pays no price for blocking it.
She has built workarounds that cost her everything they save. She stays because leaving triggers the custody clock. She documents the abuse in a home where documentation requires witnesses who do not want to be named in a dispute between families who are neighbors or relatives. She attends reconciliation sessions the court recommends and sits across from the person she is trying to leave and performs willingness to consider it because the judge's impression of her reasonableness affects the outcome of her case.
What has accumulated in her is not a single emergency but the specific psychological weight of being kept inside a legal process by the person the legal process is supposed to protect her from, for years, at a cost measured in everything she had before she filed. She does not have a word for what three years of that does to a person's relationship to institutions, to hope, to the belief that a system designed to resolve something will eventually resolve it, because acquiring that word would require the outcome she has not been given and that the man who refuses to give it faces no legal consequence for withholding.

He has cheated on me but he says that he had the woman sigheh in Cairo. I want a divorce but he refuses. I don’t have money to get lawyer, how can I make up my death?

82. Pakistani woman whose husband has died and whose in-laws now control her life and her children.
Affected Groups: Widowed women in Pakistan, particularly in rural Punjab, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Sindh, and Balochistan, where tribal and customary law operates alongside or in place of formal legal frameworks and where a husband's death transfers a woman's social and often legal dependency from her husband directly to his family rather than producing any form of independent status. Particularly affects women who married young, have no independent income or education, and whose entire social existence was structured through the husband's household, leaving them with no individual legal or financial infrastructure to stand on when he dies.
Women whose in-laws claim custody or physical possession of the children on the grounds that the children belong to the patrilineal family, women who are pressured into marrying a brother-in-law through the practice of levirate marriage known as watta satta or similar customary arrangements, women whose mahr was never paid or was paid to her father rather than to her and who therefore have no liquid assets of any kind, and women from communities where returning to her own family is read as abandonment of her children and where staying means accepting whatever terms the in-laws set. Also affects women who have been in Pakistan for years after marrying into diaspora families and whose immigration status was tied to their husband, leaving them without documentation, residency rights, or any bureaucratic identity that exists independently of a man who is now dead.
Legal and Bureaucratic
Mechanisms: Pakistani inheritance law under the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance of 1961 formally grants widows the right to inherit one eighth of the husband's estate if there are children. In practice, property in rural areas is held under customary arrangements, titled in the husband's name or the broader family's name, and the formal legal right to one eighth is functionally unenforceable without a lawyer, a court filing, and family members willing to comply with a judgment that customary authority tells them they can ignore. Land records offices, inheritance procedures, and local courts operate in environments where a woman appearing without a male representative is an irregularity the system is not designed to process smoothly.
Child custody under Pakistani family law gives the mother the right to physical custody of young children, specifically sons until age seven and daughters until puberty, but the in-laws' claim to the children is enforced through social and physical pressure that precedes any court order. If she leaves the marital home she is understood in her community to have abandoned the children to the family they belong to by patrilineal right, and a court order granting her custody is a document she would need money, time, and physical safety to obtain and then enforce in a community where enforcement depends on the cooperation of the same local authority structures that recognize the in-laws' claim in the first place. Her right to the matrimonial home is not recognized under most customary frameworks, and the formal legal pathway to assert it requires navigating a court system where proceedings take years and where she has no income to sustain herself during them.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A woman in Lahore's outskirts or a village in rural Sindh lost her husband six months ago. She has not left the house since the funeral because leaving requires a male escort her in-laws control access to. Her mother-in-law manages the household money, decides what the children eat, decides whether they go to school, and has begun conversations with the husband's younger brother about a future arrangement that no one has asked her opinion on. She is twenty-eight years old and has three children and no bank account and no income and no title to anything in the house she is living in and no identification documents she controls independently because her husband kept the family paperwork.
She has learned to have no opinions that conflict with the in-laws' opinions, because the consequence of conflict is a threat, spoken or unspoken, that involves the children. She asks permission to call her own mother. She phrases every need as a question directed at her mother-in-law. She has watched the space between what she is allowed to want and what she actually wants close so gradually that she is no longer sure where the boundary was before it moved.
What has accumulated in her is the particular condition of a person whose grief has no room to be processed because the person who died was also the only person through whom she had any standing in the place she is now trapped in, and his absence has not freed her from that place but handed the terms of her captivity to people who have more reason than he did to enforce them. She does not know what her legal rights are because no one in her immediate world has any incentive to tell her, and the organizations that would tell her exist in a city center she cannot reach without permission from the people her rights are supposed to protect her from.

After he died my life feels limited and monotonous... I can't go out alone. His family told me to move in with them at Lahour or they will give me no inheritance and I have to take care of 6 children on my own with no money and no job. I don't have a husband and I am alone, but does that mean I am not human?

83. Saudi woman who wants to travel but needs a male guardian's permission.
Affected Groups: Saudi women of all ages — including adult professionals, university students, divorc—es, and widows — remain subject to the mahram (male guardianship) system. Disproportionately affects women in conservative rural provinces, women whose guardians are abusive or absent, women seeking to flee domestic violence, and women whose guardians are incapacitated, deceased, or living abroad — leaving them with no eligible male to authorize even routine movement.
Legal, Bureaucratic, or Physical Mechanisms: The Absher digital platform allows male guardians to monitor and revoke travel permissions in real time, receiving automatic SMS alerts the moment a woman's passport is scanned at any border checkpoint. Airlines operating out of Saudi Arabia comply with guardian-issued travel bans, and border agents retain discretionary enforcement authority independent of any court order. The 2019 Vision 2030 reforms nominally permitting women over 21 to travel independently created a formal right that exists on paper while the administrative, social, and digital infrastructure enforcing guardianship remains fully operational underneath it — meaning the law changed but the system did not.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A woman fleeing an abusive guardian cannot board a flight without that same guardian receiving a notification and retaining unilateral power to block her exit. A widow may legally require her own adult son's permission to leave the country. A woman requiring emergency medical treatment unavailable in-country cannot travel if her guardian refuses consent. The guardian is simultaneously the source of danger and the legally mandated authority whose cooperation is required to escape it — a closed loop in which the bureaucratic mechanism and the human threat are the same person.

84. Woman in a rural Indian village whose husband beats her and whose family tells her to go back.
Affected Groups: Women in rural India — particularly in states like Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, and Jharkhand — who are experiencing domestic violence and whose only available support structure, their natal family, actively refuses to receive them back. Disproportionately affects women from lower-caste households, women with no formal education or income, women married through arranged marriages where the union represents a financial and social contract between two families rather than two individuals, and women whose entire post-marriage identity is legally and socially located in the husband's household with no recognized path back to her own.
Legal, Bureaucratic, or Physical Mechanisms: The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act of 2005 formally grants women the right to a protection order, residence order, and monetary relief — but enforcement requires filing with a Protection Officer, whose offices are concentrated in district towns unreachable from remote villages without money, transport, and a male escort. Police in rural areas routinely treat domestic violence as a private family matter, returning women to the marital home or pressuring them to withdraw complaints to preserve community harmony. The residence order provision theoretically allows her to remain in the matrimonial home, but physical enforcement in a village where the husband's family controls local social authority is a document without a mechanism behind it.
Dowry arrangements mean her natal family has already transferred significant assets to the husband's household, creating a financial incentive for both families to keep her in the marriage regardless of her safety. Returning home is read communally as a failed marriage that dishonors the natal family and forfeits whatever social capital the dowry was meant to purchase — meaning her own parents face community punishment for receiving her back.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A woman in rural Uttar Pradesh arrives at her parents' door after her husband breaks her arm. Her father tells her the neighbors will talk. Her mother tells her every marriage has difficulties. They put her in a auto-rickshaw the next morning and send her back. She returns to a house where the man who broke her arm now knows she tried to leave and was returned, which is the only information the situation needed to become more dangerous than it was before she left. She has no money, no phone she controls, no documentation of her injury, and no local authority she can approach whose first instinct is not to send her back to the same place her parents just sent her from. The formal legal system that exists to protect her is located in a town she cannot reach, staffed by people trained to treat her situation as a domestic dispute, and accessible only through a process that requires her to have already escaped the thing she is trying to escape.

85. Person who has left Islam in a country where apostasy has social or legal consequences.
Affected Groups: People who have privately or publicly left Islam in countries where apostasy carries legal penalties or severe social consequences — including Afghanistan, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Malaysia, and Egypt — as well as Muslim-majority communities within otherwise secular states where family and community enforcement operates independently of national law. Disproportionately affects young adults still living in the family home, individuals from deeply religious or clerical families, women whose legal status and marriage are tied directly to their religious identity, converts to other faiths, and atheists or agnostics who have no alternative religious identity to transition into — leaving them with no socially legible category to occupy after leaving Islam.
Legal, Bureaucratic, or Physical Mechanisms: In countries like Afghanistan and Saudi Arabia, apostasy is formally punishable by death under codified interpretations of sharia. In Pakistan, blasphemy laws under Sections 295-C of the Penal Code are weaponized against those who leave or criticize Islam, carrying mandatory death sentences and functioning as a parallel apostasy enforcement mechanism. In Iran, male apostates face execution and female apostates face life imprisonment under the Penal Code. In Malaysia, the Syariah court system operates alongside civil courts and has jurisdiction over Muslims, meaning a person cannot legally exit Islam without a Syariah court's permission — which is almost never granted — trapping them in a religious legal identity they have internally abandoned.
Beyond formal law, family enforcement operates as the primary mechanism in communities where state prosecution is unlikely: honor-based violence, forced psychiatric institutionalization framed as spiritual intervention, confiscation of passports and identification documents, forced marriage to a devout spouse as corrective pressure, and economic disinheritance that removes any material basis for independent survival. Employers, landlords, and local authorities in Muslim-majority communities treat known apostasy as legitimate grounds for termination, eviction, and withdrawal of services.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A twenty-three-year-old in Lahore has not believed for four years and has told no one. He performs prayers he does not mean at times determined by a family that would disown him, in a country where the wrong person overhearing the wrong conversation can produce a blasphemy accusation that his family could not protect him from even if they wanted to. He has found online communities of ex-Muslims who exist entirely in private encrypted channels because public existence is not available to them. He does not know a single person in his physical life he can tell the truth to. He has researched asylum pathways in three countries and cannot access any of them without a passport his father controls and money he does not have. The thing he is hiding is not a behavior but an internal state — the absence of a belief — and there is no action he can take to make himself safe that does not first require him to survive the moment of being known.

86. Person with HIV in a context where the diagnosis means social death.
Affected Groups: People living with HIV in sub-Saharan Africa, Southeast Asia, Eastern Europe, and the Middle East — particularly in countries like Nigeria, Uganda, Russia, Indonesia, and Egypt — where HIV carries criminal, religious, or intense social stigma that operates independently of and often more devastatingly than the medical condition itself. Disproportionately affects women who contracted HIV from husbands who will not disclose their own status, men who have sex with men in contexts where homosexuality is itself criminalized, sex workers, intravenous drug users, and people in rural communities where a single clinic serves an entire region and medical confidentiality is functionally impossible because the nurse, the pharmacist, and the patient's mother-in-law attend the same church.
Legal, Bureaucratic, or Physical Mechanisms: Over 60 countries maintain HIV-specific criminal laws criminalizing transmission, exposure, or non-disclosure — with Russia, Nigeria, and many US states among them — meaning a person can be prosecuted not for harm caused but for the existence of their status in proximity to another person. In Uganda, the HIV and AIDS Prevention and Control Act mandates disclosure to sexual partners and allows third-party disclosure by healthcare providers, effectively removing medical confidentiality as a legal protection and transferring control of a person's most dangerous personal information to institutions that operate inside the same community that will punish them for it.
Antiretroviral treatment in rural or under-resourced settings is dispensed from dedicated HIV clinics with separate entrances, separate pharmacy windows, and separate waiting areas — architectural stigma that makes attendance itself a public disclosure. Health insurance in many contexts excludes HIV or flags the diagnosis in ways that make employment-based coverage a mechanism of exposure. In highly religious communities, pastoral counseling is often the first point of contact after diagnosis, and clergy operate with no confidentiality obligations and significant social authority to broadcast what they are told as spiritual warning to the congregation.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A thirty-one-year-old woman in rural Nigeria receives her diagnosis at a clinic forty kilometers from her village. She contracted HIV from her husband. She cannot tell him because he will say she brought it from outside the marriage. She cannot collect her medication from the local pharmacy because the pharmacist went to school with her brother. She cannot miss work to travel to the distant clinic regularly because her employer will ask questions she cannot answer. She cannot tell her mother because her mother will tell her sisters. She is managing a treatable chronic condition that will not kill her if she takes a pill every day, and the pill is available, and she cannot take it without the act of taking it killing everything else — her marriage, her place in her family, her children's social standing, her livelihood — in a community where those things are not separate from survival but are survival itself. The medical emergency is under control. The social emergency has no treatment protocol and no confidentiality protection and no clinic she can walk into without being seen walking into it.

87. Child in a refugee camp who has never known any other life and is now a teenager with no documents and no future pathway.
Affected Groups: Teenagers and young adults who were born in or arrived as infants to protracted refugee camps in Kenya, Jordan, Lebanon, Bangladesh, and Uganda — particularly in Kakuma, Dadaab, Zaatari, and Cox's Bazar — where displacement has lasted decades and an entire generation has grown up stateless, undocumented, and outside any national legal framework that recognizes their existence as actionable. Disproportionately affects children of parents who themselves lost or never possessed documentation, children born inside camps where birth registration systems are administered by UNHCR rather than any national civil registry, children from countries like Somalia, South Sudan, Syria, and Myanmar whose origin states have either collapsed or actively stripped certain ethnic groups of citizenship, and adolescent girls for whom the absence of a future pathway dramatically accelerates pressure toward early marriage as the only available form of economic security.
Legal, Bureaucratic, or Physical Mechanisms: UNHCR refugee registration documents a person's existence within the humanitarian system but does not confer nationality, citizenship, or any legal status recognized by the host country's civil law — meaning a Kakuma-born eighteen-year-old holds a UNHCR card that identifies them as a person of concern to an international body while remaining legally invisible to Kenya, whose Refugees Act confines registered refugees to designated camps and criminalizes movement to urban areas without a permit that is rarely granted and easily revoked. Host countries including Kenya, Bangladesh, and Lebanon maintain explicit policies against local integration, meaning the legal status available to these teenagers is permanently temporary by deliberate design.
Birth registration inside camps frequently occurs through parallel humanitarian systems unconnected to any national civil registry, producing documents that no state is obligated to honor and that cannot be used to obtain a passport, open a bank account, enroll in a national university, obtain a work permit, or access any service that requires proof of legal existence within a recognized state. The 1954 Convention on Statelessness and the 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness provide formal international frameworks that most affected host countries have not ratified and that origin countries have no functional government to implement.
Secondary education inside camps is provided through humanitarian funding that is perpetually underfunded, taught by underqualified teachers, and leads to certificates unrecognized by any national examination board — meaning a teenager who studies diligently for a decade earns qualifications that cannot be converted into university admission, employment, or any credential legible outside the camp's internal economy.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A seventeen-year-old boy born in Kakuma to Somali parents who arrived in 1998 has never been to Somalia, speaks Somali as a third language after Swahili and English, and cannot be deported to a country he has never seen and that has no functioning civil registry to receive him. He cannot be integrated into Kenya because Kenya's policy explicitly forecloses that pathway. He cannot be resettled because resettlement slots globally accommodate less than one percent of the eligible population and prioritize acute vulnerability cases over young men without dependents. He has finished the camp's secondary school with marks that would earn him a university place anywhere those marks were legible, and they are legible nowhere.
He is not fleeing anything anymore. He is simply here, in a place that was designed to be temporary and is now twenty-six years old, with documents that prove he exists to an organization that cannot give him a country and a future that consists entirely of waiting for a process — resettlement, voluntary return, local integration — that every responsible party has already quietly decided will not happen for him. He is seventeen years old and he already knows this. The cruelty is not that his situation is uncertain. The cruelty is that it is certain, and everyone administering it is using the language of uncertainty to avoid saying so out loud.

88. Old fisherman whose entire way of life has been made illegal by new environmental regulations with no alternative offered.
Affected Groups: Elderly and middle-aged artisanal fishermen in coastal and riverine communities across Southeast Asia, West Africa, South Asia, and Latin America — particularly in the Philippines, Indonesia, Ghana, Bangladesh, and Chile — where subsistence and small-scale commercial fishing has constituted the entire economic, cultural, and identity infrastructure of communities for generations. Disproportionately affects men over fifty with no formal education or transferable skills, indigenous fishing communities whose relationship to specific waters is constitutionally or treaty-recognized but practically unenforceable, fishermen who own small boats and gear representing their entire life savings and which are now either prohibited or economically unviable under new regulations, and coastal communities where fishing is not merely an occupation but the organizing principle of social life, seasonal rhythm, marriage markets, and intergenerational knowledge transmission.
Legal, Bureaucratic, or Physical Mechanisms: Marine Protected Area legislation, EU Common Fisheries Policy reforms, and equivalent national frameworks in developing countries establish exclusion zones, gear prohibitions, and catch quotas that are designed at the level of industrial fleet management and applied uniformly to artisanal fishermen who had no representation in the regulatory process that produced them. Licensing and permitting systems introduced alongside conservation regulations require documentation, registration fees, and bureaucratic navigation that assume literacy, internet access, and familiarity with administrative systems that artisanal fishermen in remote coastal communities do not possess and were never designed to be able to possess.
Compensation and transition programs nominally attached to these regulations — livelihood diversification funds, retraining schemes, and alternative income programs — are administered through national agencies located in urban centers, disbursed through bank accounts that unbanked fishermen do not have, and designed around alternative occupations that require physical mobility, language skills, and educational credentials that a sixty-year-old fisherman who has worked the same stretch of water since adolescence does not have and cannot acquire on the timeline the regulation imposes. Coast guard and maritime enforcement agencies are simultaneously given expanded powers and quotas for prosecuting violations, meaning the fisherman who continues fishing to eat faces criminal prosecution while the transition support designed to make that unnecessary remains inaccessible to him.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A sixty-three-year-old fisherman in a coastal village in the Philippines has fished the same reef system since he was twelve years old. The reef is now inside a Marine Protected Area established eighteen months ago by a national agency responding to international conservation pressure tied to foreign aid conditionality. His boat is too small to reach the waters outside the exclusion zone safely. His gear is prohibited. He has attended one government meeting about retraining for ecotourism employment that was held in a city four hours away and conducted in a technical register of Tagalog he struggled to follow, and the program requires a bank account he does not have and a government ID he has never needed before and cannot obtain without a birth certificate he is not sure exists.
He is sixty-three years old and his knees are bad and his entire body is organized around a specific physical practice in a specific place that is now illegal. The fish he is no longer allowed to catch are still there. He can see them from the shore. The regulation that protects them was written by people who will never stand where he is standing, and the transition support that was supposed to make the regulation bearable was designed by the same people with the same assumptions about what a person in his situation is able to do. He is not opposed to conservation. He does not have the philosophical room to be opposed to conservation because he is trying to determine what he will eat, and the answer the system has given him is a retraining program for a tourism industry that does not yet exist in his village and would not hire a sixty-three-year-old man with bad knees if it did.

89. Young woman in Morocco who lost her virginity consensually and is now obsessed with finding a way to restore her hymen before marriage.
Affected Groups: Young women in Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Egypt, and across the broader MENA region — as well as diaspora communities in France, Belgium, and the Netherlands where cultural expectations travel intact across borders — for whom premarital virginity is not a personal or religious preference but a legally and socially enforced condition of marriageability, family honor, and physical safety. Disproportionately affects women from conservative rural households, women whose families have already negotiated informal marriage arrangements premised on her virginity, women from communities where the wedding night is a semi-public event with bloodstained sheet verification expected by both families, and women who had consensual sex with a partner who subsequently did not marry them — leaving them carrying the full social consequence of a mutual act alone.
Legal, Bureaucratic, or Physical Mechanisms: Morocco's Family Code (Moudawwana), reformed in 2004, does not explicitly criminalize premarital sex for women, but Article 490 of the Penal Code criminalizes sexual relations outside marriage for both parties — with enforcement applied overwhelmingly against women, particularly when pregnancy or community accusation makes the act visible. A husband who discovers his wife was not a virgin on the wedding night retains extrajudicial social recourse through family networks, public repudiation, and divorce proceedings in which her lack of virginity is weaponized as grounds — while she has no equivalent legal mechanism to contest the accusation or the consequences it produces.
The hymenoplasty black market — surgical procedures to reconstruct or simulate an intact hymen — exists precisely because the formal medical system cannot openly provide it. Moroccan public hospitals do not offer the procedure, and private clinics that perform it do so quietly, without documentation, at costs ranging from several hundred to several thousand dirhams that a young woman must accumulate secretly without her family knowing why. Gynecologists who perform it operate under professional and legal risk, meaning the procedure is performed in conditions that range from adequate to genuinely dangerous, with no medical follow-up available without disclosure. Artificial hymen kits sold online and shipped discreetly represent the lower-cost alternative, used by women who cannot afford or access surgery, with no medical supervision and variable and unreliable results.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A twenty-two-year-old woman in Casablanca had consensual sex with a boyfriend who is no longer in her life. She is now engaged to a man her family has approved and a wedding date has been set. She has spent four months obsessively researching hymenoplasty on private forums using a phone she clears after every session, calculating whether she can save enough money from a part-time job her family does not fully know about, contacting clinics through intermediary email addresses, and reading accounts from other women about whether the procedure worked, whether it hurt, whether anyone found out.
She is not grieving the relationship. She is managing a countdown to a specific night on which the absence of blood could end her marriage before it begins, trigger violence from a new husband, produce a repudiation her family receives as a public humiliation, and in the worst convergence of circumstances, constitute grounds for an honor-based response from male relatives who understand her body's history as an injury done to them. The consensual decision she made belongs entirely to her past. The consequences of that decision are being managed entirely alone, in secret, in a medical black market that exists because the formal system cannot acknowledge the problem it was created to solve, on a timeline set by a wedding date she did not set and cannot move.

90. Men in fishing communities who have lost people to the sea and keep going out
Affected Groups: Men in artisanal and subsistence fishing communities across coastal West Africa, Southeast Asia, the North Atlantic, and Pacific Island nations — particularly in Senegal, the Philippines, Indonesia, Norway, and the Faroe Islands — where fishing is not a chosen career but an inherited obligation passed through generations with no economic alternative, and where the sea has taken fathers, brothers, and sons from the same families across multiple generations. Disproportionately affects men from communities where masculinity, provider identity, and social standing are so completely fused with the act of going out that not going out is not experienced as a choice but as a form of self-annihilation, men who have witnessed drownings firsthand and returned to the water within days, men who carry the specific psychological burden of having survived when others did not, and older fishermen who have outlived multiple crew members and continue because the accumulated grief has nowhere else to go except back to the only place that also contains everything they loved about the people they lost.
Legal, Bureaucratic, or Physical Mechanisms: Maritime safety regulations in most jurisdictions require vessel registration, safety equipment certification, life jacket compliance, and weather reporting adherence — frameworks designed around commercial fleets and enforced selectively, leaving artisanal fishermen in small open boats operating in a regulatory gap where the law neither adequately protects them nor acknowledges the specific conditions under which they work. Life insurance and death benefit systems in developing coastal nations either exclude fishing as an occupation due to actuarial risk classifications or require premium payments that subsistence fishermen cannot sustain, meaning each death leaves families in immediate destitution that the surviving men must immediately return to sea to address — grief and economic emergency arriving simultaneously and each making the other worse.
Occupational mental health infrastructure does not exist in any meaningful form in these communities. The psychological consequences of repeated traumatic bereavement — complicated grief, PTSD, survivor guilt, anticipatory anxiety — have no clinical pathway in contexts where the nearest mental health professional may be hundreds of kilometers away, where men in these communities have no cultural language for psychological distress that does not translate directly into weakness, and where the therapy that would be indicated is contraindicated by the social and economic reality that requires the man to be in the water the following morning regardless of what the therapy says. Maritime chaplaincy and community mourning rituals exist in some traditions but address spiritual and communal grief without touching the psychological accumulation that builds across decades of loss.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A fifty-one-year-old fisherman in a village in Senegal has lost his father to the Atlantic, one brother to the Atlantic, and two crew members in separate incidents over thirty years. He was present for one of the crew member deaths and was not present for the others, which is its own specific category of knowledge — the ones you saw and the ones you were told about and the particular way the body processes each differently. He has never spoken to anyone about any of it in a way that went past the surface, because the surface is where conversation about these things stops in his community, and because going past the surface would require a vocabulary and a permission and a listener that his world does not contain.
He goes out tomorrow morning because his family eats when he goes out. He goes out also because the water is the only place where the accumulated weight of what has happened to him is matched by something large enough to hold it, and because the men who died were also men who went out, and going out is the only form of continuation he knows how to offer them. He is not unafraid. He has never been unafraid. He has simply been in a situation for thirty years where fear was not one of the variables that determined the decision, and the decision has always been the same, and he has made it so many times that it no longer feels like courage and no longer feels like resignation and has become instead something closer to the particular texture of his life, which is the only life he has, which he is still living, which he will take back out onto the water in the morning.

91. Woman in Tunisia who had an abortion illegally and is bleeding and cannot go to a hospital and say what happened.
Affected Groups: Women in Tunisia — and across the broader North Africa and MENA region including Morocco, Algeria, and Egypt — who have undergone clandestine abortions outside the narrow legal parameters that formal healthcare permits, and who are now experiencing post-procedure complications in a medical system that is simultaneously their only source of help and a potential source of prosecution, family exposure, and social destruction. Disproportionately affects unmarried women for whom an unwanted pregnancy is itself an illegal condition under Article 236 of the Tunisian Penal Code which criminalizes extramarital sexual relations, women from conservative families in whose household a pregnancy would constitute grounds for violence, women who used unregulated methods — misoprostol obtained through informal networks, herbal abortifacients, or physical interventions — because they could not access or afford clinical procedures, and women in rural areas where the distance between them and any medical facility means the bleeding has been going on for hours before the question of whether to go becomes urgent enough to override the fear of going.
Legal, Bureaucratic, or Physical Mechanisms: Tunisia legalized abortion in 1973 under specific conditions — within the first trimester, for married women, in accredited facilities — making it one of the more liberal frameworks in the Arab world while simultaneously constructing a legal perimeter that excludes the women most likely to need clandestine procedures. Unmarried women, women past the first trimester, and women who cannot access accredited facilities fall entirely outside legal protection, meaning the procedure they underwent was illegal and the hemorrhage it produced is evidence of that illegality. Presenting to a hospital emergency room with post-abortion bleeding requires either lying about the cause — miscarriage, which clinicians are trained to distinguish from induced abortion through physical examination — or disclosing a procedure that the attending physician is legally positioned to report and professionally incentivized not to protect.
Medical confidentiality in Tunisian clinical practice operates under a framework that formally protects patient information but provides no explicit immunity for physicians who treat illegal abortion complications, creating a zone of discretionary exposure where the woman's safety depends entirely on the individual values of whoever receives her — a variable she cannot know in advance and cannot control from a position of active hemorrhage. Hospital intake procedures require national identification, next-of-kin contact information, and admission documentation that creates a paper trail connecting her name to a presentation that a family member, employer, or community member employed in the hospital's administrative system could access. The physical geography of Tunisian public hospitals — shared wards, visible waiting areas, overlapping social networks in smaller cities — means that being seen entering the emergency room is itself a disclosure event before any medical interaction occurs.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A twenty-six year old unmarried woman in Sfax has been bleeding for six hours. She obtained misoprostol through a contact she found through a private online forum, took it alone in her apartment following instructions she read on her phone, and has told no one. The bleeding is heavier than the instructions said it would be and has not slowed the way the instructions said it would. She knows she needs a hospital. She also knows that going to a hospital means a physical examination that will indicate an induced rather than spontaneous abortion, an intake process that will attach her name to that finding, and a waiting room in a city where she grew up and where the woman behind the administrative desk may recognize her face.
She is calculating, from inside an emergency, whether the medical risk of continuing to bleed is greater than the social and legal risk of stopping the bleeding in the only place that can stop it. She is doing this calculation alone, on a bathroom floor, with a phone she has already used to search the same set of questions four times because the answers have not changed and she keeps hoping they will. The system that could save her life is the same system that could end everything else, and she is trying to determine, with the cognitive resources available to a person who has been bleeding for six hours, which risk is larger — and the cruelty is that she is the only person in her world who knows enough about her situation to make that determination, and she is the least equipped person in her world to be making it right now.
