92. Woman in Bangladesh whose husband rapes her regularly and who has been told by everyone including her mother that this is normal and is her duty.
Affected Groups: Married women across Bangladesh — particularly in rural divisions including Rajshahi, Rangpur, Mymensingh, and Sylhet — for whom marital rape is not recognized as a legal category and therefore does not exist as a harm the state is equipped to acknowledge, investigate, or prosecute. Disproportionately affects women married young, often below the legal minimum age through the persistent operation of child marriage despite formal prohibition, women with no independent income or education who have no material basis for survival outside the marriage, women from deeply conservative communities where religious authority figures, family elders, and female community members collectively reinforce the understanding that a wife's body is a marital entitlement rather than a site of personal sovereignty, and women whose own mothers and grandmothers experienced the same thing and transmitted it forward not as trauma but as the basic terms of wifely existence — meaning the harm has no generational witness who can name it as harm because every available witness lived inside it too.
Legal, Bureaucratic, or Physical Mechanisms: Section 375 of the Bangladesh Penal Code explicitly exempts marital rape from the legal definition of rape through a spousal exception clause inherited directly from British colonial law and never removed, meaning the act is not merely unprosecuted but legally classified as something other than the crime it would be if committed by any other person. A woman cannot file a police report for an act the law does not recognize as a crime. She cannot access a legal aid lawyer for a harm that has no legal existence. She cannot approach a court for a protection order against conduct that the same legal system has pre-emptively defined as her husband's right.
Shalish — the informal village arbitration system administered by male community elders — is the first and often only dispute resolution mechanism available in rural areas, and it operates from a framework that treats marital sexuality as a matter of family privacy, regularly instructs women to be more accommodating, and has no conceptual category for the complaint she is bringing because the complaint requires a premise — that she has sexual autonomy within marriage — that the system does not recognize as a valid premise. Religious authority structures including local imams reinforce the same framework through Quranic interpretations that emphasize wifely obedience and frame sexual availability as a religious obligation, giving the harm a sacred justification that operates above both law and community arbitration.
National and international NGOs operating domestic violence helplines and shelter networks in Bangladesh address physical violence and can sometimes intervene in cases of severe battery, but marital rape as a standalone harm falls outside their operational frameworks because it falls outside the legal framework their interventions are designed to work within — meaning even the organizations theoretically positioned to help her are institutionally unable to name what is happening to her as the specific thing it is.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A twenty-four year old woman in rural Mymensingh has been married for six years and has three children and has never once in those six years understood what is happening to her at night as something with a name that belongs to the category of wrong. She was told before the marriage by her mother that this is what marriage is. She was told after the marriage by her mother-in-law that a good wife does not refuse. She was told by the imam at a community gathering that a wife's refusal is a sin. She has never encountered a single voice in her physical world that has offered her a different frame, and the absence of that frame is not experienced as oppression but as the basic texture of reality, because a harm that has never been named in any language available to you is not experienced as harm but as weather — as the neutral condition of the life you are living.
What has accumulated in her is not rage, because rage requires a target and a target requires a wrong and a wrong requires a framework for wrongness that she has not been given. What has accumulated is a formless and unaddressed exhaustion and a specific bodily knowledge that something is being taken from her on a recurring basis that she does not know how to refuse and has never been told she is allowed to refuse and would not know where to go with the refusal if she had it. She is twenty-four years old and she does not know that what is happening to her has a name in other languages. She does not know that in other places it is called a crime. She has never been given the single most basic instrument of resistance, which is the knowledge that there is something to resist, and the system surrounding her — legal, religious, familial, communal — has withheld that instrument with a thoroughness so complete that it does not feel like withholding. It feels like the truth.

Affected Groups: Tibetan residents inside the Tibet Autonomous Region, Qinghai, Sichuan, Yunnan, and Gansu provinces — where Tibetan populations exist under a security infrastructure specifically calibrated to treat cultural and religious identity as an ongoing counterterrorism problem. Legal, Bureaucratic, or Physical Mechanisms: The Patriotic Education Campaign requires monks, nuns, and laypeople to formally denounce the Dalai Lama and sign loyalty pledges to the state-approved Panchen Lama — creating a bureaucratic apparatus in which religious devotion to the exiled spiritual leader is converted into a documentable act of political disloyalty. The photograph was evidence of the old architecture. The processing he is about to undergo is the renovation he did not request. The checkpoint was the door.

95. Person in a conservative Pakistani family who has been sexually abused by a relative and knows that telling anyone would destroy the family and result in them being blamed.
Affected Groups: Children and young adults — disproportionately girls and young women, though boys are significantly affected and almost entirely silenced — within conservative Pakistani households across urban and rural contexts where the family unit functions as the primary social, economic, and reputational structure, and where the perpetrator is structurally embedded in that unit as a trusted elder, patriarch, or economically dominant relative. Also affects victims in joint family living arrangements where physical privacy does not exist, where the abuser has continuous and socially sanctioned access, where leaving the household is not an available option for a child or economically dependent young woman, and where the architecture of daily life requires the victim to sit across from their abuser at every meal, share domestic space with them through every hour of every day, and perform normalcy so completely that the performance eventually becomes indistinguishable from the interior condition it was meant to conceal.
Legal, Bureaucratic, or Physical Mechanisms: Pakistan's Protection of Children Act 2016 and amendments to the Pakistan Penal Code Sections 375-376 formally criminalize child sexual abuse, but prosecution requires a First Information Report filed with police who are institutionally disposed to treat intrafamilial abuse as a domestic matter requiring mediation rather than criminal investigation. Medical evidence collection requires immediate post-assault examination at a facility equipped to perform forensic documentation — a requirement that presupposes a victim who has immediate access to transportation, a trusted adult to accompany them, and the knowledge that evidence collection is time-sensitive, none of which describe a child being abused by a household elder in a conservative family where the abuse is ongoing and cumulative rather than a single reportable incident.
The two-witness requirement inherited from Hudood Ordinance frameworks, while formally reformed, continues to shape police and prosecutorial culture in ways that make intrafamilial abuse cases functionally unprosecutable without corroborating witnesses — and the only witnesses are family members whose first institutional response is the protection of family reputation rather than the protection of the child. Panchayat and jirga systems in rural and tribal areas, and informal family elder arbitration in urban conservative households, represent the actual first-response mechanism for family disputes — and these systems treat intrafamilial sexual abuse as a matter of family honor whose optimal resolution is silence, internal management, and the victim's continued accommodation of the family structure that produced the abuse. Disclosure to a religious figure — imam, maulvi — routes through a framework that treats family integrity as a religious value superseding individual harm and that has no mandatory reporting obligation and no referral pathway to secular child protection services.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A fourteen year old girl in Lahore has been abused by her father's elder brother for two years. He lives in the same house. The abuser will remain at the dinner table. She will be the disruption.
What she is carrying is not only the abuse. She is fourteen years old and she has already conducted the cost-benefit analysis that the adults around her would need to conduct if she told them, and she has arrived at the same conclusion they would arrive at, and so she has decided what they would decide, and she is living with a decision that was never really hers to make because the system made it for her before she was old enough to understand what was being decided.

96. A family whose house was destroyed in a war and who are living in the ruins of it because there is nowhere else to go and no one is coming to rebuild it.
Affected Groups: Families across active and post-conflict zones in Gaza, Syria, Yemen, Ukraine, South Sudan, and Mali — particularly those in secondary and tertiary cities and rural areas that fall outside the geographic and media priorities of international humanitarian response, and where destruction has been so total and so uniform that the concept of temporary displacement loses meaning because there is no intact structure within reachable distance to be temporarily displaced into. Disproportionately affects families who owned rather than rented, whose entire generational wealth was stored in the physical structure of the house and the land beneath it, elderly members who cannot be moved and will not leave, families with disabled members for whom the logistics of displacement are insurmountable, families who left during active conflict and returned to find their ruins occupied or their land seized and who are now living in the ruins as an act of legal and physical assertion of ownership against secondary dispossession, and families in areas where the political complexity of the conflict means that no single humanitarian actor has a clear mandate to operate and where the reconstruction aid that exists is conditioned on political developments that have not occurred and may not occur within any timeline connected to human survival.
Legal, Bureaucratic, or Physical Mechanisms: International humanitarian law under the Geneva Conventions and their Additional Protocols formally prohibits the targeting of civilian infrastructure and obligates parties to armed conflict to allow humanitarian access — obligations that are violated as a matter of operational strategy in most contemporary conflicts and that carry no enforcement mechanism capable of operating on the timeline of a family sleeping under open sky in January. UN Security Council Resolution frameworks authorizing humanitarian corridors and reconstruction aid are subject to veto politics that have no relationship to the temperature inside a collapsed building in winter, and donor conference pledges for reconstruction — Syria 2017, Yemen 2022, Gaza 2024 — are disbursed through governmental and NGO channels that require stable administrative counterparts, banking infrastructure, and security conditions that do not exist in the places where the destroyed houses are.
Property documentation requirements for reconstruction assistance programs administered by national governments and international agencies require land titles, building permits, and ownership records that were stored in the houses that no longer exist, in municipal offices that were also destroyed, in administrative systems that have ceased to function — creating a bureaucratic impossibility in which proof of loss is required to access assistance for loss, and the loss itself destroyed the proof. In conflict contexts involving ethnic or sectarian targeting, demographic engineering through destruction means that returning to and rebuilding on ancestral land is actively obstructed by the party that destroyed it, using secondary legal mechanisms — eminent domain declarations, anti-terrorism property seizure laws, new zoning classifications applied to rubble — to convert the physical destruction into permanent legal dispossession while the family is still living in the wreckage.
Insurance frameworks do not cover war damage in any standard policy. War risk exclusion clauses are universal and absolute, meaning that whatever financial instruments middle-class families in these countries possessed are precisely calibrated to be useless in the circumstance that has now occurred. Microfinance and reconstruction loan programs require income verification, credit history, and collateral — requirements that presuppose economic infrastructure that the same war that destroyed the house also destroyed.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A family of six in a destroyed neighborhood in northern Gaza or Aleppo or Hodeidah is living in the section of their house where two walls and part of a ceiling remain intact. The father has arranged salvaged concrete blocks and plastic sheeting to close the gaps. The children sleep in the interior corner where the structural risk is lowest, a calculation he has made by looking at the damage and reasoning from what he can see, which is not engineering knowledge but is the closest thing to it available to him. There is no glass in any window opening. The cooking is done over wood burned in a cleared space because the gas line is severed and the electricity has not existed for a period of time that has become difficult to measure because measuring it with any precision stopped being useful some months ago.
He is not waiting for aid in the way that the word waiting implies passivity. He has filed paperwork with three organizations. He has registered on two government lists whose administering agencies have subsequently been defunded or restructured or relocated. He has been told by an NGO worker, who was genuinely sorry, that his neighborhood is not currently in the priority zone, and that the priority zone is determined by access routes that do not reach his street, and that when the access routes change his case will be reviewed. He understood what was being said and thanked the NGO worker because the NGO worker was the first person in some time who had spoken to him as though his situation was a problem someone was attempting to solve rather than a condition someone was attempting to document.
His wife has stopped talking about rebuilding. This happened gradually and he noticed when it was complete. She talks about the children and the food and the immediate logistical problems of the day. She has moved her cognitive horizon to the distance that is manageable, which is the distance of the next several hours, and she has done this as a survival adaptation that he recognizes and respects and finds devastating in a way he cannot discuss with her because discussing it would require her to move her horizon back out to the distance where the devastation lives and she needs it where it is to get through the day.
The house they are living in the ruins of took his father thirty years to build, room by room, as money became available. It was finished the year before the war started. The family has nowhere else to go not because they have not looked but because the concept of elsewhere has been uniformly destroyed across the radius of everywhere they could reach, and because this ruin is theirs, and leaving it means losing it, and losing it means the thirty years and the father and the finished year before the war and everything stored in the structure beyond its walls — the marriage, the births, the specific arrangement of a life — become not just destroyed but abandoned, which is a different and in some ways worse thing, and so they stay, and they arrange the concrete blocks, and they do not talk about rebuilding, and the children sleep in the corner where the walls are most likely to hold.

97. Families separated between North and South Korea who have not been able to contact each other for decades and who do not know if the other side is alive, and for whom the political situation means this is simply the permanent condition of their lives.
Affected Groups: Elderly Koreans on both sides of the 38th parallel who were separated during the 1945 partition and the 1950 to 1953 war, now predominantly in their 70s, 80s, and 90s, for whom the statistical reality is that most of their separated family members have already died without contact ever being reestablished. Disproportionately affects those in rural and provincial areas of South Korea who lack the political connections or financial means to access even the extremely limited informal channels that exist, North Korean defectors now living in South Korea or third countries who are legally and practically cut off from family still in the North and whose contact attempts put those family members at direct risk of state punishment, families in which one side was categorized as politically suspect by either government during the war or its aftermath and who were therefore excluded even from the limited reunion programs that existed, and the children and grandchildren of the original separated generation who have inherited an unresolvable absence they did not experience firsthand but which has structured their family's emotional and biographical reality for their entire lives.
Legal, Bureaucratic, or Physical Mechanisms: The Korean Demilitarized Zone is one of the most heavily fortified borders on earth, with no civilian crossing permitted in any direction under any circumstance including medical emergency, imminent death, or bereavement. South Korea's National Security Act criminalizes unauthorized contact with North Korean nationals, meaning that a South Korean citizen who attempts to reach a sibling living in Pyongyang through any unsanctioned channel is committing a prosecutable offense regardless of the personal circumstances motivating the attempt. On the North Korean side, any contact with the South is treated as a political crime under a system of collective punishment that extends liability to the individual's children and grandchildren, meaning that a North Korean family member who receives an unsanctioned communication from the South does not simply risk their own safety but the multigenerational security of everyone connected to them.
The only sanctioned reunion mechanism, the inter-Korean family reunion program, operated intermittently between 1985 and 2018, was controlled entirely by both governments as a diplomatic instrument, required applicants to register through South Korean state agencies, selected participants by lottery from a waiting list that at its peak exceeded 130,000 people, and allowed successful participants a single meeting of several hours with family members they had not seen in decades, in a supervised setting, with no private communication permitted before or after. The program has been suspended since 2018 with no resumption scheduled. The majority of the registered 130,000 have died waiting. There is no appeals process, no emergency exception, no humanitarian carve-out for terminal illness or imminent death on either side, and no international legal framework with any enforcement capacity that applies to this specific situation, because the situation exists entirely within the domestic jurisdiction of two states that do not recognize each other and whose relationship is technically still a state of armistice rather than peace.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A woman in her late 80s living outside Busan registered with the family reunion program in 1994. She was not selected in any of the subsequent lotteries. Her brother was last seen in what became North Korea in 1950, when she was in her early teens and he was a few years older. She does not know if he is alive. She has no way to find out. There is no database she can query, no consular service she can contact, no intermediary organization with the access and mandate to answer the question on her behalf. The question of whether her brother is alive is not pending resolution. It is permanently unanswerable within any realistic projection of her remaining life, and she is old enough to know this with the kind of clarity that comes from having waited long enough to understand what waiting in this context actually means.
She has a photograph from before the war. She has described her brother to her children and her grandchildren in enough detail that they can picture someone they have never met and will never meet. This transmission of a person across generations through description alone is the only form of contact the political structure of the peninsula has permitted. Her grandchildren know his approximate age, his face from a photograph taken when he was a teenager, and the fact that he liked to fish. They do not know if he had children. They do not know what he became. They do not know if there are cousins.
She has not stopped thinking he might be alive because the not-knowing makes the stopping impossible. This is not hope in any comforting sense. It is the cognitive consequence of an information vacuum that the state has maintained for seven decades with complete success. When she dies, the question dies with her, because she is the one for whom it was a question about a person rather than a question about an abstraction. Her children will grieve the uncle they never met. Her grandchildren will explain to their own children that there was a great-great-uncle once, somewhere, and that no one ever found out what happened to him, and that this was not an accident but a policy, and that the policy is still in place.

98. A person in Iran who went blind from drinking methanol-contaminated bootleg alcohol because alcohol is banned and the only available supply is unregulated and sometimes lethal.
Affected Groups: Iranian civilians, predominantly young men between 18 and 35, from working class and lower middle class urban and peri-urban backgrounds where the price point of regulated black market alcohol exceeds what is financially accessible, who consume methanol-contaminated bootleg spirits produced domestically under conditions of total regulatory absence. Disproportionately affects residents of poorer urban neighborhoods in cities like Tehran, Isfahan, Ahvaz, and Mashhad where enforcement of the alcohol ban is heaviest and the supply chain is therefore most compressed and least quality-controlled, religious minorities including Christians and Zoroastrians for whom alcohol consumption is not prohibited by their own religious law but who are subject to the same Islamic Republic prohibition regardless and who therefore access the same unregulated supply, university students who drink socially and have no mechanism to assess the safety of what they are consuming, people with existing alcohol dependency for whom abstinence is not a realistic behavioral option and who will consume whatever is available, and the families of those killed or permanently disabled who have no tort claim, no compensation mechanism, and no legal acknowledgment that the state's prohibition policy was a proximate cause of what happened.
Legal, Bureaucratic, or Physical Mechanisms: The Islamic Republic of Iran prohibits the production, sale, and consumption of alcohol under laws derived from Sharia and codified in the post-1979 legal framework, with penalties including flogging and imprisonment. This prohibition does not eliminate demand. It eliminates the regulatory infrastructure that would otherwise govern supply. The result is a black market production environment in which ethanol intended for industrial or cosmetic use, or produced through uncontrolled fermentation processes, is sold as drinkable spirits with no testing, no labeling, no producer accountability, and no supply chain that any authority has either the mandate or the incentive to inspect for consumer safety.
Methanol is a byproduct of poorly controlled fermentation and is also present in industrial ethanol that is denatured specifically to make it undrinkable. It is colorless, odorless, and indistinguishable from ethanol without chemical testing. A lethal or vision-destroying dose is small. The consumer has no way to know it is present. There is no regulatory agency with jurisdiction over bootleg alcohol safety because the product's existence is illegal, which means the state's relationship to it is enforcement rather than harm reduction. Hospitals treating methanol poisoning victims are required by law to report them to authorities, which means that seeking medical treatment for alcohol poisoning carries a direct risk of criminal prosecution, and that the decision to go to a hospital involves weighing permanent blindness or death against arrest and flogging, and that some people make the calculation too late or in the wrong direction. The antidote for methanol poisoning is ethanol, administered intravenously in a clinical setting within a narrow treatment window, a fact whose irony the legal framework does not accommodate.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A 24-year-old in Isfahan drinks at a small gathering with friends on a Thursday night. The bottle was purchased through the same informal network that has supplied every social occasion he has attended since he was 19. He has drunk from similar bottles many times. There is nothing about this bottle that is distinguishable from the ones that did not blind him.
He wakes in the night with a headache he attributes to the alcohol. By morning the headache is severe and his vision is blurring at the edges. He does not go to the hospital immediately because going to the hospital means explaining what he drank and explaining what he drank means a report filed with authorities and a report filed with authorities means his parents find out through a police visit rather than a phone call, and he is calculating whether the vision problem is serious enough to be worth that, and he is doing this calculation while the methanol is completing its work on his optic nerves, which do not pause during the calculation.
When he does go, the window for the antidote has partially closed. He loses the vision in one eye completely. The other retains some peripheral function. He is 24. He will navigate the Iranian state's near-total absence of infrastructure for blind citizens for the rest of his life, in a country where his disability was caused by a law, compounded by another law, and where neither law will be named as a contributing factor in any official account of what happened to him. His medical record will describe methanol poisoning. It will not describe prohibition. The state that blinded him will not be a party to that description.

99. A woman in Iran that needs a c section but her husband wouldn’t let her get that in the middle of the labour
Affected Groups: Women in Iran across all socioeconomic backgrounds but disproportionately affecting those in rural and peri-urban areas where access to independent legal counsel, women's advocacy infrastructure, and alternative medical facilities is functionally nonexistent, women in marriages where the husband is the sole financial administrator and whose access to any medical facility is contingent on his physical presence and consent, women with prior cesarean sections for whom a vaginal birth after cesarean carries documented clinical risk and whose obstetric history makes the denial of a repeat cesarean not a preference dispute but a life-threatening obstruction, young women in first marriages where the power differential between husband and wife is at its most extreme and where the woman has the least accumulated social capital to resist or circumvent a husband's decision, women whose husbands hold religiously or culturally grounded objections to cesarean delivery on grounds of interference with natural process or suspicion of unnecessary medicalization, and women in hospitals where the institutional culture defaults to male guardian authority in the absence of explicit legal challenge, which no woman in active labor is in a position to mount.
Legal, Bureaucratic, or Physical Mechanisms: Iranian civil law derived from the Islamic Republic's interpretation of Sharia designates the husband as the legal guardian of the marital household with broad authority over decisions affecting the family unit. While Iranian medical law does not formally and explicitly require spousal consent for emergency obstetric procedures, the practical and institutional reality in most Iranian hospitals is that spousal consent is sought as a matter of protocol for surgical interventions, and that in the absence of the husband's agreement, medical staff default to deferral rather than intervention because the legal ambiguity around overriding a husband's stated objection exposes the hospital and the treating physician to liability that the formal emergency exception provisions in Iranian law are too vaguely drafted to clearly neutralize.
A woman in active labor is not in a legal position to assert her own medical autonomy in real time. She cannot instruct a lawyer. She cannot file an emergency court application. She cannot contact a women's rights organization that has the standing and speed to intervene in the next forty minutes. The Iranian judiciary has no emergency mechanism calibrated to the timeline of obstetric emergency. The formal legal right to emergency medical treatment that exists on paper operates on a timeline measured in days and weeks, and fetal distress operates on a timeline measured in minutes. Physicians who perform a cesarean over a husband's explicit objection risk professional sanction, civil suit, and in some interpretive frameworks criminal liability under laws that treat unauthorized surgical intervention as bodily harm, meaning the incentive structure for the medical team in the room points away from intervention even when the clinical picture points toward it. The woman's ability to consent to her own surgery is not the operative legal question in the room. The husband's refusal is.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: She has been in labor for nineteen hours. The fetal heart monitor is showing decelerations that the obstetrician recognizes and that have a meaning she explains to the husband in terms she has calibrated to be clear without being so alarming that he feels pressured, because she has learned from experience that men who feel pressured in this room make worse decisions faster. He says no. He says his mother delivered six children without surgery and his wife is strong. He says he has heard that doctors recommend cesareans for financial reasons. He is not entirely wrong that this happens in some hospitals and this is part of what makes the conversation harder than it should be.
The obstetrician is not indifferent. She is operating inside a structure that has not given her the legal clarity to act unilaterally without consequence to her license and her livelihood, and she has her own children, and she is trying to find the language that moves this man in the next few minutes because the monitor is showing her something she does not have much more time to negotiate around.
The woman on the table can hear this conversation. She is the subject of it and she is not a participant in it in any way that the room's power structure recognizes as decisive. She is in pain that has reorganized her capacity for abstract thought and she is frightened in a way that has a physical texture and she knows something is wrong because she has been in this labor long enough to know what wrong feels like and she cannot make the decision that would address it. Her consent is not what is being sought. Her body is the site of a legal and cultural negotiation between her husband and her doctor and the outcome of that negotiation will happen to her.
What happens next depends on which version of this story it is. In some versions the doctor finds the language. In some versions the husband changes his mind when the fear becomes concrete enough. In some versions he does not change his mind in time. In those versions the baby dies, or she dies, or both, or the baby survives with a hypoxic injury that will define the entire arc of a life that has not yet properly started, and the husband stands in a corridor afterward in a grief that is real and that coexists without apparent contradiction with the decision he made, and no law names what he did, and no court will be convened, and the medical record will describe the obstetric outcome without describing the room.

100. Person in China who wants to search for information about Tiananmen and cannot.
Affected Groups: Chinese citizens on the mainland across all demographics but disproportionately affecting university students and young adults for whom the internet is the primary and in many cases sole research medium and who have grown up entirely within the information environment the firewall has constructed, academics and historians working in fields adjacent to contemporary Chinese political history who cannot access primary sources, journalism, or international scholarship without tools that are themselves legally precarious, the generation born after 1989 for whom the event is not a suppressed memory but a genuine absence with no personal or familial reference point to prompt curiosity in a directed way, family members of the dead and the disappeared from June 4th who cannot publicly discuss what happened to their relatives and whose attempts to memorialize or seek accountability have been met with sustained harassment and detention by state security, and citizens in Hong Kong where the annual June 4th vigil held continuously for three decades was banned in 2020 under the National Security Law and where the specific local memory of the event as a site of civic identity is now itself a prosecutable political position.
Legal, Bureaucratic, or Physical Mechanisms: The Great Firewall of China, operated by the Cyberspace Administration of China in coordination with the Ministry of Public Security, blocks all foreign platforms on which substantive Tiananmen content exists including Google, Wikipedia in all languages, YouTube, and the full archive of international news organizations. Domestic platforms including Weibo, WeChat, Baidu, and Douyin are legally required under a series of internet content regulations most recently consolidated in the 2022 Provisions on the Management of Internet Information Services to proactively remove content related to the June 4th crackdown and to prevent its appearance without waiting for government instruction, meaning the censorship is partially automated and partially performed by platform employees whose jobs depend on its thoroughness.
Search queries containing direct references to June 4th, 1989, Tiananmen, tank man, or associated terms return either no results, redirected results pointing to state-approved narratives, or in the case of particularly sensitive combinations, trigger account flags. The specific date written numerically as 5/35 or expressed through other substitution ciphers developed by users to evade keyword filters is itself now a recognized evasion pattern and is filtered accordingly, meaning the cat and mouse dynamic between censorship infrastructure and user circumvention has run long enough that the infrastructure has absorbed most of the circumvention vocabulary. VPNs capable of bypassing the firewall are legal only for corporations with government approval and for use cases the state sanctions, and their use by private individuals for accessing politically sensitive content is prosecutable under cybersecurity laws carrying sentences of up to three years, with penalties applied not just to users but to individuals who distribute or recommend VPN tools to others. The 2015 National Security Law and the 2017 Cybersecurity Law together create a framework in which the act of seeking the information is legally categorized in proximity to the act of threatening state security, which is not a metaphor but a structural feature of how the laws are written.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: A 20-year-old history student at a university in Chengdu is writing a paper on Chinese political development in the late twentieth century. She is not a dissident. She is not politically radicalized. She has been assigned a topic that in any other national academic context would require engagement with June 4th as a primary event and she approaches the gap in her available sources the way any conscientious student approaches a research problem, which is by looking harder.
Baidu returns nothing usable. The Chinese language Wikipedia article is a stub that describes the event in terms so compressed and so drained of specificity that it communicates the fact of official discomfort more than it communicates any history. She tries search variations and gets variations of nothing. She finds a forum post that refers obliquely to something having happened in Beijing in 1989 without naming it and the post is four years old and the account that posted it no longer exists.
She knows something happened. She knows it the way you know the shape of a hole without being able to see what filled it, because the hole has a shape, because the absence has edges, because the consistency and thoroughness of the nothing she is finding is itself a kind of information. She knows that whatever it was was large enough to require this much erasure and she finds this more unsettling than specific knowledge would be because specific knowledge has boundaries and this does not.
She does not try a VPN because a classmate told her last year about a student at another university who was questioned by campus security after his internet activity flagged a pattern consistent with firewall circumvention, and the questioning itself, regardless of outcome, was enough to jeopardize his scholarship review. The risk is not theoretical. It is a social fact she has absorbed through proximity to people who have absorbed it through proximity to people who learned it directly.
She writes the paper without the section it should have. Her supervisor reads it and does not mention the gap because her supervisor is also a person living inside the same structure and has long since integrated its boundaries into her own professional judgment without experiencing this integration as censorship, which is the most complete form censorship takes. The paper is graded. The event remains the shape of a hole. She is twenty years old and she will carry the outline of that hole through the rest of her education without ever being formally told what its dimensions are or why she is not allowed to measure it.

101. Person in Iran trying to use a VPN that keeps getting blocked.
Affected Groups: Iranian civilians across all demographics but disproportionately affecting journalists, activists, and civil society workers for whom VPN access is not a convenience but the operational baseline for doing work that the state has categorized as threatening, university students and researchers whose academic access to international scholarship, datasets, and publishing platforms is entirely contingent on circumvention tools functioning on any given day, members of religious and ethnic minorities including Kurds, Baluchis, and Bahais who use international platforms to maintain community, document persecution, and communicate with diaspora networks, women and young people who use Instagram, Twitter, and Telegram not just for social connection but as the primary infrastructure of organizing that emerged visibly during the Mahsa Amini protests in 2022 and whose suppression was a stated goal of the internet shutdown that accompanied the crackdown, freelancers and remote workers whose income is denominated in foreign currency and processed through platforms that are sanctions-blocked or firewall-blocked or both simultaneously, creating a layered impossibility in which the economic lifeline and the political lifeline are severed by the same infrastructure, and Iranians attempting to communicate with family members abroad for whom the blocking of WhatsApp and Instagram during periods of civil unrest means that the people inside the country and the people outside it lose contact precisely when the outside world most needs to know what is happening inside.
Legal, Bureaucratic, or Physical Mechanisms: Iran's filtering infrastructure, administered by the Committee Tasked with Determining Offensive Content and implemented through the Telecommunications Infrastructure Company which is state-owned and operates as the mandatory gateway through which all Iranian internet traffic passes, maintains a blocklist covering tens of thousands of domains and employs deep packet inspection technology that identifies and disrupts VPN protocols at the traffic level rather than simply blocking known VPN server addresses. This distinction matters because it means that acquiring a new VPN server address, which is the standard circumvention response to IP-level blocking, does not reliably restore access when the protocol signature itself is being detected and throttled.
The 2021 User Protection Bill, passed by the Iranian parliament and implemented in stages, formalized the legal framework for what had previously been administratively managed filtering, mandating that all internet service providers route traffic through state inspection infrastructure, requiring domestic platforms to store user data on servers within Iranian jurisdiction and accessible to security services, and creating licensing requirements for any content service operating in Iran that effectively prohibit foreign platforms from operating legally while simultaneously prohibiting citizens from accessing them through circumvention. The penalty for VPN provision is prosecution under cybercrime laws. The penalty for VPN use is formally present in the legal framework but applied selectively and unpredictably, which is a more effective deterrent than consistent enforcement because inconsistent enforcement means no one can accurately calculate their actual risk level and the safest behavioral response to incalculable risk is avoidance.
During periods of civil unrest the Telecommunications Infrastructure Company has demonstrated the capability and the willingness to throttle total international bandwidth to speeds that render VPN protocols nonfunctional regardless of their technical sophistication, and to shut down mobile internet entirely across geographic regions, meaning that the circumvention arms race between Iranian users and Iranian filtering infrastructure is asymmetric in a fundamental way because the state controls the physical pipe and can simply reduce what flows through it to nothing, at which point the sophistication of the tool sitting on top of the pipe becomes irrelevant.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: It is a Tuesday in Tehran and she needs to submit a piece to the outlet she freelances for by end of day. The piece requires accessing sources hosted on platforms that are blocked. She opens the VPN she has used for eight months. It connects and drops. She tries again. It connects, holds for forty seconds, drops. This is new behavior from this particular VPN and she recognizes it as the signature of a protocol block rather than a server problem, which means switching servers will not fix it, which means this VPN has been caught up in whatever update the filtering infrastructure pushed in the last day or two.
She has three other VPNs installed. She works through them in order. Two fail to connect at all. The third connects and holds and she works quickly because she has learned that holding does not mean stable and she wants to get as much done as possible before it drops, which it does, eleven minutes later.
She is not panicking because she has been doing this long enough that the emotional register for this situation has flattened from crisis into grinding tedious problem. She posts in a Telegram group she is part of where people share working configurations. Someone has posted a new server address twenty minutes ago. She tries it. It works. She finishes the piece with twenty minutes to spare.
What she does not post in the group, because the group itself is on a platform that is blocked and accessed through a VPN and is therefore a nested circumvention whose security she does not entirely trust, is that she spent forty-five minutes of a deadline day doing systems administration for her own internet connection, that this is the third time this week this has happened, that the cognitive overhead of maintaining circumvention infrastructure on top of doing actual work is not something she can expense or explain to an editor or factor into a deadline negotiation, and that last September during the protests the entire system collapsed for nine days and she could not reach her sister who was in the street and did not know for three of those days whether her sister was in a cell or a hospital or fine, and that the VPN problem and the nine days are the same problem, and that the same office in the same building runs both, and that she is going to close her laptop now and make tea and then come back and do it again tomorrow.

Oh it just connected! How not to let it turn off? I don't have the budget to pay for those expensive configs.

102. Person whose government monitors all communications trying to speak honestly with anyone.
Affected Groups: Citizens living under comprehensive surveillance states including North Korea, China, Iran, Belarus, Russia, Eritrea, and Turkmenistan, but extending to anyone in a country where the legal framework permits bulk communications interception without individualized judicial oversight, which as of current international practice includes more countries than it excludes. Disproportionately affecting political activists, journalists, lawyers representing dissidents, trade union organizers, and members of religious minorities whose communications are of active interest to security services rather than swept up passively in bulk collection, but also and in some ways more insidiously affecting ordinary people who have no political engagement and no reason to believe they are individually monitored but who have absorbed enough ambient knowledge of surveillance capability to have modified their behavior preemptively without any direct state intervention being necessary, which is the condition the architecture is most efficiently designed to produce. Also disproportionately affecting people in close relationships with someone the state is actively watching, who become surveilled by proximity and who must decide whether to modify their own speech to protect themselves or maintain honesty and accept the transferred risk, therapists and medical professionals in countries where patient confidentiality has no legal protection against state access and where a patient's honest disclosure of political views or stigmatized behavior during a clinical encounter can be extracted and used, clergy in countries where confessional or pastoral communications are subject to intelligence collection, and the children of surveilled parents who grow up learning to partition their speech before they have the conceptual vocabulary to understand why they are doing it.
Legal, Bureaucratic, or Physical Mechanisms: The technical infrastructure of comprehensive communications surveillance operates at the level of the telecommunications backbone through systems like SORM in Russia, which legally mandates that all internet service providers and telecoms install Federal Security Service monitoring equipment directly on their networks and provide encryption keys on demand, and through China's Golden Shield which combines deep packet inspection, keyword filtering, and AI-assisted behavioral pattern recognition across all domestic platforms simultaneously. These are not wiretapping regimes in the traditional sense of targeted interception requiring individualized suspicion. They are architectures of total collection in which the question is not whether a communication is captured but which captured communications are surfaced for human review, a distinction that matters because it means the chilling effect operates independently of whether any specific person is ever actually read.
Legal frameworks in these countries impose on platform operators, telecommunications companies, and internet service providers affirmative obligations to store communications data for defined retention periods, to provide real-time access to security services on request, and in some jurisdictions to decrypt end-to-end encrypted communications or face the platform being blocked entirely, which is not a technical requirement to break encryption but a commercial pressure applied to companies who must choose between modifying their security architecture and losing an entire national market. Messaging applications that offer genuine end-to-end encryption and refuse to provide backdoor access are blocked at the infrastructure level, and their use through circumvention tools carries legal risk that the ordinary person without technical sophistication and high risk tolerance cannot practically navigate. The legal concept of incitement, extremism, discrediting state institutions, or spreading false information about state activities is defined broadly enough in Russian, Chinese, and Iranian law that the category of honest political speech that falls outside criminal exposure is narrow and its boundaries are deliberately unclear, because unclear boundaries produce more conservative self-censorship than precise ones do.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: He has a best friend he has known since they were seven. They are in their late thirties now and the friendship has the depth and texture that comes from three decades of shared experience and the friendship has also, in the last several years, developed a quality that neither of them has named directly, which is that there are things they do not say to each other on the phone or in messages and things they say differently in person than they would in writing and things they only say in person in certain places and not others.
This is not a conversation they have had. It is a behavioral adaptation that emerged between them organically through a process of each of them noticing what the other was doing and adjusting accordingly, the way people who care about each other absorb each other's caution. They have never sat down and said we need to be careful what we say and how we say it. They have simply become careful, and the carefulness has become part of the texture of the friendship, and neither of them thinks about it consciously most of the time, which is how he knows it has gone deep.
What he is aware of, when he lets himself be aware of it, is that there is a version of himself that exists only in his own head. This version has opinions about what is happening in the country that are fully formed and specific and connected to evidence and that he has never transmitted to another person through any medium he does not trust with his physical presence. He does not know with certainty that saying these things through other mediums would result in consequences. He knows that it might, and that the might is sufficient, and that the architecture was designed so that the might would be sufficient, so that the certainty would not need to be established because the possibility would do the same work at lower cost to the state.
What this produces, at the level of a life rather than a policy analysis, is a specific kind of loneliness that has no clean name because it is not the loneliness of having no one around you. He has his friend. He has his family. He has colleagues he likes. The loneliness is the loneliness of moving through all of these relationships with a part of yourself held in a room that you cannot let anyone else into through any channel you cannot physically control, and of not knowing, after enough years of this, how much of what you present to the people who know you best is you and how much is the version of you that has learned to be safe, and of suspecting that the line between those two things has been moving for long enough that you are no longer certain where it started.

Do they check our conversation too? I want to speak about somethings but I have nowhere to talk about them. I only trust quiet in-person conversations.

103. Elderly person who has been told to do everything online and does not know how and is too ashamed to ask their children again.
Affected Groups: Adults over 70 across all income levels but disproportionately affecting those in rural and small town areas where in-person government services, bank branches, and post offices have been closed on the explicit assumption that digital alternatives are adequate substitutes, those with low digital literacy whose relationship to computing technology began late or not at all and for whom the interface conventions that younger users navigate intuitively represent a genuinely foreign symbolic language rather than a minor inconvenience, elderly people living alone following bereavement whose spouse managed household administrative tasks including any digital components and who are now encountering systems they have never operated without a partner present, people with age-related vision deterioration, tremor, or early cognitive decline for whom the physical and cognitive demands of navigating digital interfaces create compounding failure points that the systems were not designed to accommodate, elderly immigrants for whom the language barrier compounds the interface barrier in ways that multiply rather than add, people whose fixed incomes place smartphones and reliable broadband outside reliable financial reach and who are therefore attempting to access digitized services through outdated hardware on unstable connections that the services themselves are not optimized for, and the specific and underacknowledged population of elderly people who have adult children who helped them initially and who have now asked enough times to have developed a precise and detailed internal map of the point at which their child's patience, however genuine and however well concealed, shifts register, and who have decided that the administrative problem they are facing is more bearable than returning to that moment again.
Legal, Bureaucratic, or Physical Mechanisms: The digitization of public services in the United States, United Kingdom, Australia, and across the European Union has proceeded through a policy framework that treats online access as a reasonable universal assumption and in-person or telephone alternatives as costly exceptions to be progressively defunded rather than maintained as genuine parallel infrastructure. The result is a service landscape in which the nominal alternative to the digital channel exists but is designed and resourced at a level that communicates its intended obsolescence. Government helplines operate on hold times calibrated to the staffing levels of a service the administering agency is not trying to scale. In-person service centers have been consolidated to a geographic distribution that requires rural elderly people without driving ability to arrange transport for what was previously a local errand. The Americans with Disabilities Act and equivalent frameworks in other jurisdictions create accessibility obligations for digital services that are inconsistently enforced and that address specific disability categories without addressing the broader and more diffuse condition of age-related digital alienation which does not map cleanly onto any protected characteristic.
Banking digitization has proceeded under regulatory frameworks that permit branch closure without affirmative obligation to maintain accessible in-person alternatives within any defined geographic or demographic radius, meaning that elderly people in areas of branch consolidation face account management requirements, fraud dispute processes, and benefits access systems that have been moved online by institutions that are not legally required to ensure the people affected can actually use them. The NHS in the United Kingdom, Medicare in the United States, and equivalent national health systems elsewhere have moved appointment booking, prescription management, repeat prescription requests, and correspondence with specialists substantially or entirely online, with telephone alternatives that require navigating automated menu systems whose design conventions are themselves a form of digital literacy test. Universal Credit in the United Kingdom is administered through an online journal system with no paper alternative as a matter of explicit policy, meaning that elderly people who qualify for means-tested benefits must maintain and operate an online account to receive them, and that failure to operate it correctly results in payment suspension without any mechanism for the person to know why the suspension has occurred or how to address it through a channel they can actually use.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: She is 78 and she has received a letter from the pension service telling her that she needs to verify her identity online to continue receiving her payments without interruption and that she has three weeks to do this and that if she needs help she can visit the website listed at the bottom of the letter. The website is where the help is. She reads this twice.
Her tablet is the one her son set up for her two years ago. She uses it to video call her grandchildren and to look at photographs and these are the operations she knows how to perform from the specific sequence of taps her son showed her and wrote down on a piece of paper she keeps next to the tablet. The piece of paper does not cover what the letter is asking her to do.
She tries. She types the web address from the letter into the place she thinks web addresses go and gets a search results page instead and clicks on what looks like the right thing and arrives at a page with many options none of which say what she needs them to say in language that connects to the language in the letter. There is a button that might be relevant. She presses it and is asked to log in and she does not have a login for this and the process for creating one requires her to enter her email address and she has an email address her son set up but she does not know what it is because she has never needed to type it, her son's phone just knows it, and she cannot call her son and ask him for her own email address, she cannot do it again, last time she called him about the tablet she heard in the background his wife say something she was not meant to hear and she has thought about it since, not because her daughter-in-law is unkind, she is not unkind, but because she heard it and it was said and now she knows the shape of how much space she takes up in that house when she calls with these questions.
She puts the tablet down and makes tea and sits with the letter. The three weeks becomes two weeks and then ten days. She is not ignoring it. She thinks about it with a frequency and an anxiety that would surprise her son if he knew, which he does not because she has not told him. She is trying to work out if there is a way to solve it that does not require her to ask. She looks for a phone number on the letter and finds one and calls it and is told by an automated voice that the average wait time is forty-five minutes and that she can also access this service online at the address she has already failed to navigate and she stays on hold for twenty minutes and then her hand gets tired holding the phone and she puts it down.
What she is experiencing is not technophobia, which is the word that would be used to describe her situation in a policy document if her situation were described at all. It is the specific experience of being a competent adult who managed a household and a family and a working life for fifty years, encountering a set of systems that have been designed by people who cannot imagine her, for users who are not her, with failure modes that land entirely on her, inside a social situation with her son that makes the most obvious solution feel like a cost she has already paid too many times. The payment deadline for the administrative problem is in ten days. The other problem has no deadline and no resolution and will still be there after the payment problem is somehow solved, which it will be, probably, because eventually the anxiety will outweigh the shame, or the deadline will force it, but she will go to her son already knowing the shape of what it costs, and she will try to need less next time, which is not something she will be able to control, which she already knows, and which is its own particular kind of quiet grief.

I don't want to ask my granddaughter again. I try my best but each time it fails, I don't know it's my card or me. How to just find the cloth in a real store?

104. Person whose son was killed by the state and has kept his son in their house to burry him in the morning as the government might keep the body as a hostage.
Affected Groups: Families of individuals killed by state security forces, extrajudicial execution squads, or during detention in countries including Iran, China, Egypt, Syria, Saudi Arabia, and Belarus, where the state's relationship to the body of someone it has killed extends beyond the death itself into a post-mortem exercise of control that serves explicit political functions. Disproportionately affecting families of political prisoners, protest participants, and dissidents whose deaths carry evidentiary weight the state wishes to manage, families in ethnic and religious minority communities whose dead are killed in contexts the state wishes to categorize differently than the family would categorize them, mothers and fathers of young men killed during protest crackdowns whose bodies if released uncontrolled would become the center of public mourning that the state correctly identifies as politically dangerous, families without financial resources or political connections who cannot access the informal channels through which wealthier or better-connected families sometimes negotiate the return of a body, families in which the killed person's political associations mean that the act of claiming the body is itself surveilled and potentially incriminating, and families who have already lost one member to the state and who understand with the specific clarity that comes from direct experience that the institution they are now negotiating with over the body is the same institution that produced the body and has both the motive and the demonstrated capacity to harm them further.
Legal, Bureaucratic, or Physical Mechanisms: In Iran the legal framework governing the return of bodies to families of those killed by state forces operates through the coroner's office, the judiciary, and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps or the security branch responsible for the death, none of which are independent of each other and all of which have institutional interests in controlling the circumstances of burial. Families are in many documented cases required to sign documents prior to receiving the body, documents that variously describe the cause of death in terms the state has determined, commit the family to burying the deceased in a specific location away from the family plot, prohibit public mourning gatherings, and in some cases include commitments not to speak to media or human rights organizations about the circumstances of the death. The signature is the price of the body. Families who refuse to sign do not receive the body. Families who sign and subsequently violate the commitments have described further harassment, arrest, and in some cases the subsequent disturbance of the grave.
The specific use of burial location as a control mechanism is documented extensively in the cases of executed political prisoners in Iran whose families have been directed to bury them in Khavaran, a mass grave site outside Tehran used for political prisoners since the 1980s, or in municipal cemetery sections geographically and symbolically separated from the family's community, preventing the grave from becoming a site of gathering. In China families of Uyghurs who have died in detention have in documented cases been unable to receive bodies at all, with deaths confirmed through official notification but bodies disposed of by the state without family involvement. In Egypt families of those killed during the Rabaa massacre in 2013 described negotiating with morgues controlled by security services for the release of bodies under conditions of surveillance and implicit pressure. The common mechanism across jurisdictions is the conversion of the body from the family's dead into state-controlled evidence and political instrument, with release contingent on the family's agreement to bury the political meaning of the death along with the physical remains.
Devastating Real-World Consequence: He brought his son home at two in the morning. He and his brother-in-law went together because he did not trust himself to drive and because moving a body requires two people and because he did not want to do it alone, not that part. His son is in the front room. He has washed him. He has done this with his own hands because it was the last thing he could do and he did it correctly, the way it is supposed to be done, because his son deserved that regardless of what the night was or what the morning will be.
He has not slept. He is sitting in the room with his son because he does not want to leave him alone and because he is thinking about the morning with the part of his mind that is still capable of practical thought, which is not all of it but is enough. He knows what the morning carries. He has spoken to other families. He knows that men will come and that they will want to take his son to a place that is not the family plot where his own father is buried and where his son should be buried and that they will have a document they want him to sign and that the document will say his son's death was something other than what it was.
He is not going to sign it. He has decided this. He made the decision sometime in the last two hours sitting in this room and it is not a decision he is uncertain about but it is a decision whose consequences he is tracing forward with the part of his mind that is doing the practical thinking, and the consequences extend beyond him to his wife who is in the next room and has not stopped crying since he brought their son home, and to his daughter who is seventeen and who he can hear is also awake, and to his brother-in-law who drove with him tonight and who has his own family and who will also be present in the morning and who did not sign up for what the morning might mean.
He has a phone. There are people he could call, organizations, journalists outside the country who would want to know. He has not called them yet because calling them changes what tomorrow is in ways he has not fully mapped, and because calling them from this phone may already be known, and because he is sitting with his son and the calls can wait until his son has had this last quiet hour. He will make them before dawn. He has decided this also.
What he cannot decide, what sits outside the reach of the practical thinking, is how to hold in the same mind the fact that his son is here in this room, washed and at rest, and the fact that his son was alive four days ago and had opinions about football and ate too quickly and called him twice a week without being asked to, and the fact that the men who will come in the morning represent the same authority that decided his son's life was worth less than the political problem his son represented, and the fact that he is going to have to speak to those men in the morning in a way that is strategic rather than honest because being honest with them will not get his son buried next to his grandfather and will not protect his daughter and will not achieve anything that his son, who had opinions about football and called twice a week, would have wanted achieved at the cost of his family's safety.
He sits with his son. Outside it is still dark. He has a few more hours before he has to be the person who can do what the morning requires, and he is using them to be, for a little longer, just the father, in the room, with his boy.
